docs.title: Auto-Completion (IntelliSense)
docs.text: The XML Editor includes smart auto-completion that helps you write XML faster and with fewer errors.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The XML Editor with a schema-backed document - typing < shows context-valid element suggestions

When you type < in the XML Editor, a popup appears showing only the elements that are valid at your current position. This is based on your XSD schema.

Inside a start tag, typing a space (or pressing Ctrl+Space) suggests the attributes of that element - from your XSD schema, or, in XSLT stylesheets, from a built-in XSLT 3.0 catalog that needs no schema at all.

docs.title: 1. Smart Element Suggestions
docs.text:
• Context-Aware: Shows only valid child elements for your current location
  • Position-Aware: Inside an xs:sequence only the elements that may follow the siblings already present are offered - an element that has reached its maxOccurs (or an xs:choice whose alternative is already there) disappears from the list. Elements that already exist after the cursor are respected too, so you cannot insert a child in the wrong order. Completion is strict about position: only what the schema allows at exactly that spot is listed.
  • Repeatable elements: When the element you are inside may itself repeat (for example a FundsXML <Fund> with maxOccurs="unbounded"), only its remaining children are offered - the list does not start over with the first child just because the element can occur again. Only a repeatable group (xs:sequence / xs:choice with maxOccurs above 1) starts over once all of its members are present.
  • Namespace-Aware: Suggestions are inserted with the prefix your document declares for the element's namespace. A child of a type imported from another namespace (e.g. c:street when the document declares xmlns:c="…") is inserted as <c:street></c:street>; elements in the default namespace stay unprefixed. Typing the local name (<st) still matches c:street.
  • Based on Schema: Suggestions come from your loaded XSD schema
  • Reduces Errors: You can't accidentally add invalid elements

docs.title: 2. Path-Specific Values
docs.text:
Elements with the same name at different locations show their correct values:

Location Suggested Values /Document/ControlData/Version 4.0.0, 4.0.1, 4.1.0 /Document/Report/Version V3, V3S1, V3S2

docs.title: 3. Automatic Tag Closing
docs.text: When you type an opening tag like <element>, the editor automatically adds the closing tag </element>.

docs.title: 4. Attribute Suggestions (Schema-Bound XML)
docs.text:
New in 2.6.0

When your document is bound to an XSD schema, the editor also helps with attributes:

  • Where: Place the cursor inside a start tag (for example after <Fund) and type a space, or press Ctrl+Space
  • What: All attributes the schema declares for that element, including those from attribute groups
  • Order: Required attributes come first, followed by the optional ones
  • Details: The tooltip shows each attribute's type and its documentation from the schema
  • No duplicates: Attributes that are already in the tag are not suggested again
  • Insertion: Accepting a suggestion inserts name="" and places the cursor between the quotes, ready for the value
  • Values: If the attribute's type is an enumeration or xs:boolean, its values (true / false) open right after the attribute is inserted; Ctrl+Space inside the quotes shows them again

docs.title: 5. XSLT Stylesheets (Works Without a Schema)
docs.text:
New in 2.6.0

XSLT stylesheets get auto-completion even when no schema is bound. The editor knows every XSLT 3.0 instruction and declaration (including newer ones such as xsl:iterate, xsl:mode, xsl:accumulator, xsl:merge and xsl:evaluate).

Element suggestions follow the context you are in:

Cursor position Suggested elements Directly inside xsl:stylesheet Declarations (xsl:template, xsl:variable, xsl:output, …) Inside xsl:choose xsl:when, xsl:otherwise Inside a template or other instruction Instructions (xsl:value-of, xsl:if, xsl:for-each, …)

Attribute suggestions appear when you type a space inside an XSLT start tag such as <xsl:variable, <xsl:template or <xsl:param (or press Ctrl+Space there):

  1. Required attributes first - for example name for xsl:variable
  2. Then the element's own optional attributes - for example select or as
  3. Then the standard attributes every XSLT element accepts - use-when, expand-text, xpath-default-namespace, exclude-result-prefixes, version, and others

Attributes already present in the tag are left out, and accepting one inserts name="" with the cursor between the quotes.

Attribute value suggestions: when you insert an attribute that only allows a fixed set of values, the values open automatically (press Ctrl+Space inside the quotes to show them again), for example:

Attribute Suggested values method on xsl:output xml, html, xhtml, text, json, adaptive indent and other yes/no attributes yes, no order / data-type / case-order on xsl:sort ascending, descending / text, number / upper-first, lower-first validation strict, lax, preserve, strip on-no-match on xsl:mode text-only-copy, shallow-copy, deep-copy, shallow-skip, deep-skip, fail visibility public, private, final, abstract (depending on the element) version 3.0, 2.0, 1.0

Good to know:

  • Any prefix bound to the XSLT namespace works - not only xsl:
  • Literal result elements (for example <html> or <div> inside a template) get no XSLT attribute suggestions
  • Start tags that span several lines are supported: press Ctrl+Space after a line break inside the tag

docs.title: Step 1: Load an XSD Schema
docs.text:
If your XML already references its schema (via xsi:schemaLocation), it is picked up automatically - and if you add or change that reference while editing, the new schema is picked up on the next validation run and IntelliSense follows automatically. Otherwise, bind one yourself:

  1. Open your XML file in the editor
  2. Click the "No XSD" indicator in the status bar (or the toolbar's Schema button - Set XSD Schema…)
  3. Select your XSD file

The indicator changes to "XSD: name", and the binding drives both auto-completion and schema validation.

docs.title: Step 2: Use Auto-Completion
docs.text:
1. Position your cursor where you want to add an element
  2. Type <
  3. A popup shows valid elements for this location
  4. Use ↑/↓ arrow keys to navigate
  5. Press Enter to insert the selected element
  6. Press Escape to close without selecting

docs.title: Step 3: Add Attributes
docs.text:
1. Place the cursor inside a start tag, after the element name (e.g. <xsl:variable|)
  2. Type a space, or press Ctrl+Space
  3. Pick an attribute - the editor inserts name="" with the cursor between the quotes
  4. If the attribute has a fixed set of values, they appear right away - pick one with Enter (or press Escape and type your own value)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
1. Inside <document>, type <
   → Shows: header, body, footer

2. Inside <body>, type <
   → Shows: section, article, aside

3. Inside <section>, type <
   → Shows: title, paragraph, list

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Key Action < Open auto-completion Space (inside a start tag) Suggest attributes Ctrl+Space Open auto-completion on demand (elements, attributes or attribute values, depending on the cursor position) ↑ ↓ Navigate suggestions Enter Insert selected element or attribute Escape Close popup > Close the current tag

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text: Benefit Description Faster Writing No need to remember element names Fewer Errors Only valid elements are suggested Schema Compliance Your XML always matches the schema Easy Learning Discover available elements as you type

docs.title: No Suggestions Appearing?
docs.text:
• Make sure an XSD schema is loaded
  • Check that your cursor is inside an element
  • Verify the schema file is valid

docs.title: Wrong Suggestions?
docs.text:
• Check that the correct schema is loaded
  • Verify the XML structure is valid up to your cursor position

docs.title: Nothing Offered Although the Element Is Empty?
docs.text: The list also honours the elements that already exist after the cursor. If you type < directly in front of the first existing child of a sequence, nothing may legally go there - move the cursor after the last child that belongs before your new element.

docs.title: The First Child Is Offered Again Inside a Repeatable Element?
docs.text: It no longer is. Earlier versions treated a repeatable element like a repeatable group and restarted its content model. If you want to add another occurrence of the element itself, close the current one and type < after it.

docs.title: No Attribute Suggestions?
docs.text:
• Make sure the cursor is inside the start tag, after the element name and before >
  • For ordinary XML files, an XSD schema must be bound - attributes come from the schema
  • In XSLT, only XSLT elements get attribute suggestions; literal result elements such as <div> do not
  • Attributes that are already in the tag are intentionally not offered again
  • In a start tag that spans several lines, press Ctrl+Space to open the list

docs.title: Prefix Missing or Unexpected?
docs.text: Prefixes are taken from the xmlns declarations of your document. If the namespace of the suggested element is not declared at all, the prefix used inside the schema is inserted - add the matching xmlns: declaration to the root element.

docs.title: Contributing to FreeXmlToolkit
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in FreeXmlToolkit! Contributions of every kind are welcome: bug reports, feature ideas, documentation fixes and code.

By participating you agree to follow our Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Ways to Help
docs.text:
• 🐞 Report bugs — see Reporting Bugs
  • 💡 Suggest features — open a feature request
  • 📖 Improve the documentation — the user guide lives in docs/
  • 🛠 Contribute code — see Development Setup and Pull Requests
  • ❤️ Sponsor the project on GitHub Sponsors

Questions are welcome on the Issues page too — but please check the user guide and the FAQ & Troubleshooting page first.

docs.title: Reporting Bugs
docs.text:
You can send a report straight from the application with Help → Report a Problem…, or open an issue on GitHub. Before opening an issue, search the existing issues to see whether it has already been reported. A good bug report contains:

  • The version (Help → About FreeXmlToolkit) and how you installed it (installer, portable, Scoop, Homebrew, built from source)
  • Your operating system and version
  • Steps to reproduce, what you expected and what happened instead
  • A minimal sample file (XML, XSD, XSLT, …) that shows the problem — please remove confidential content first
  • The relevant part of the log file: Settings → Files & Cache → LOG FILES → Open log folder

docs.title: Security Vulnerabilities
docs.text: Please do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues. See the Security Policy for how to report them privately.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Java 25 with JavaFX 25 — we use the Liberica Full JDK, which bundles JavaFX. The build uses preview features (--enable-preview).
  • Git. Gradle is provided by the wrapper (./gradlew), no separate installation needed.

docs.title: Build and Run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/karlkauc/FreeXmlToolkit.git
cd FreeXmlToolkit
./gradlew run                                    # start the application
./gradlew test                                   # run all tests
./gradlew test --tests "ClassName.methodName"    # run a single test
./gradlew clean build                            # clean build

The UI tests use TestFX and need a display. On a headless Linux machine run them with xvfb-run ./gradlew test. The full suite takes a while — run the tests related to your change while you work, and the full suite before opening a pull request.

Every pull request runs the whole suite on GitHub Actions (workflow Tests): it is split into four parallel jobs and takes about half an hour. The job summary lists failed tests and the line coverage; the HTML test report of a failed job and the coverage report are attached to the run as artifacts. To run one of the four parts locally: ./gradlew test -PtestShards=4 -PtestShard=0 (0 to 3).

docs.title: Coding Guidelines
docs.text:
The project has detailed architecture notes in CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/ (architecture, domain model, quick reference). The most important rules:

  • English everywhere — comments, JavaDoc and the source texts of the interface.
  • Translations — the interface texts live in src/main/resources/i18n/messages.properties (English) and messages_de.properties (German). In FXML write the English text and run scripts/i18n-extract-fxml.py: it replaces it with a %Layout.key reference and adds it to the English bundle. In Java use I18n.t("key") / I18n.t("key", args…) (MessageFormat). Add the German text for every new key — I18nBundlesTest fails for missing keys or mismatched placeholders.
  • Tests — add unit tests for new features and bug fixes; make sure existing tests still pass.
  • UI styling — consult STYLE_GUIDE.jsonc before changing or creating UI. Use the existing -fxt-* design tokens and CSS classes instead of hard-coded colors.
  • Icons — use the IconifyIcon control with Bootstrap Icon names (bi-*, icons.getbootstrap.com). IconifyIconCoverageTest fails for unknown names. Menu items and context menus always have an icon and text.
  • Layout in FXML, behaviour in Java — panels, pages and dialogs load their layout from src/main/resources/pages/…/<ClassName>.fxml via FxmlViews.load(this, …). @FXML handlers must be public (required by the native packages). FxmlContractTest checks every FXML against its class.
  • Commands for model changes — XSD/XML/JSON model changes always go through a command and the CommandManager (undo/redo), never by modifying the model directly from UI code.
  • Never block the UI thread — load and compute in the background (ThreadPoolManager / FxtGui.executorService) and update the UI with Platform.runLater().
  • Network access only through ConnectionService, so proxy settings are respected (HttpCallsGuardTest enforces it).
  • Circular references — XSD types can reference themselves; always guard tree traversals.
  • Keep classes focused; split large classes and remove unused code.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The user guide is an MkDocs site in docs/, published at karlkauc.github.io/FreeXmlToolkit. When you change a feature, update the matching page. New pages need an entry in the nav section of mkdocs.yml. To preview locally:

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
1. For larger changes, open an issue first so we can agree on the approach before you invest time.
  2. Fork the repository and create a branch from main.
  3. Keep pull requests focused — one feature or fix per PR.
  4. Write commit messages in the Conventional Commits style used in this repository, e.g. feat(xsd): …, fix(grid): …, docs: ….
  5. Make sure the tests pass and add screenshots for UI changes.
  6. Fill in the pull request template and link the related issue (Closes #123).

docs.text: FreeXmlToolkit is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. By submitting a contribution you agree that it is licensed under the same terms.

docs.title: Debugger (XSLT, XQuery, Schematron)
docs.text: FreeXmlToolkit has an interactive debugger for XSLT stylesheets, XQuery files and Schematron schemas: breakpoints (conditional, hit counts, logpoints, template/function/input-node breakpoints), stepping, variables and watches, call stack, coverage and an output-to-source mapping.

docs.title: Starting a Debug Session
docs.text:
Debug (Transform panel, next to Run Transform), Tools → Debug with XSLT…, the Transform ▾ toolbar menu, Run ▾ → Debug Transform (active XSLT document) or Shift+F5 start a full interactive debugger that lets you pause a transformation, step through your stylesheet, and inspect state - similar to debugging in an IDE. It opens the stylesheet as a document (every saved stylesheet already shows its breakpoint gutter, see below) and the DEBUG dock below the editor, so the stylesheet stays visible while you step. The dock shares its space with the OUTPUT panel (OUTPUT | DEBUG strip).

The debugger runs what the editor shows: the stylesheet's text in the editor - unsaved changes included (Messages then notes Debugging the editor text of … (unsaved changes included)) - and, for included or imported modules that are open, their editor text too; modules that are not open are read from disk. The stylesheet needs a file once (a new one must be saved first), so relative xsl:include / xsl:import hrefs resolve and every module reports its own location. It uses a Saxon processor of its own, so a normal transformation started during a paused session is not affected. Started from the Transform panel, the input is the panel's INPUT (the file set there, otherwise the active document) - exactly as for Run Transform; started with Run ▾ → Debug Transform on an XSLT document, it is the toolbar's Input target.

docs.title: Debug Configuration
docs.text:
Tools → Debug Configuration… (on a saved stylesheet) sets how it is debugged, saved per stylesheet:

  • Input - the Run target (the XML document the Run button uses) or a file.
  • Parameters - one name=value per line, passed as stylesheet parameters.
  • Output - automatic (from xsl:output) or XML / HTML / XHTML / TEXT / JSON.
  • Pause on entry, even with breakpoints - stop at the first instruction although breakpoints are set (without breakpoints the run pauses on entry anyway).

Debug saves and starts the debugger, Save only saves. With a saved configuration, Debug with XSLT (Shift+F5) and Run ▾ → Debug Transform on that stylesheet use it. Tools → Re-run Last Debug (Ctrl+Shift+F5, ⌘⇧F5) repeats the last debug run with the same stylesheet, parameters and format, reading its input again (the file, or the open document it came from).

docs.title: Setting Breakpoints
docs.text:
• Every saved XSLT document has a breakpoint gutter in the editor's left margin, whether or not the debugger is running: click the slot next to a line to toggle a red breakpoint, or press F9 (Tools → Toggle Breakpoint) on the caret line. The click does not move the caret. Set your breakpoints first, then start the debugger - the run stops at the first one instead of pausing on entry. A stylesheet that was never saved has no gutter (save it once - its file location anchors the breakpoints).
  • Breakpoints match the file and line, so a line in lib/a.xsl never triggers a breakpoint set in another a.xsl.
  • An instruction whose start tag spans several lines can carry its breakpoint on any of those lines - e.g. on the <xsl:value-of line of a multi-line select. Saxon reports the instruction at the line where the start tag ends, so the run pauses (and the arrow shows) there; the breakpoint itself stays where you set it and counts the hits. Run to Cursor works the same way.
  • Breakpoints are persisted per file: they are back when you reopen or debug the same file, they survive Restart, and they stay in the gutter after the session ends.
  • Breakpoints in included modules count too: open lib/a.xsl, set a breakpoint, debug the main stylesheet - the run pauses there. The debugger scans the main stylesheet's xsl:include / xsl:import hrefs at start to pick them up; a module it could not find that way joins as soon as it is opened during the session (pause, jump, or opening it yourself).
  • The Breakpoints panel lists every breakpoint of the session grouped by file (a header with the file name and count, then line, condition, hit-count rule, log message and how often it was hit in this run); Remove, Edit…, Template…, Clear all and Break on ▾ sit in a small toolbar above the list, and the Delete key removes the selected entry. Double-click an entry to jump to that line.
  • Right-click an entry for Enable / Disable / Remove All in and for Export Breakpoints… / Import Breakpoints…: all line, template and function breakpoints with their settings go to a text file (absolute paths) and can be loaded into another session - an imported breakpoint replaces one on the same file and line.
  • Breakpoints follow your edits: inserting or deleting lines above a breakpoint moves it with its code (also during a debug session), and deleting a breakpoint's line removes it. Replacing the whole text - reloading the file after an outside change, reformatting the document - leaves the breakpoints on their line numbers. The debugger runs the editor's text, so breakpoints and the run agree also before you save.
  • Disable a breakpoint to keep it (with its condition and hit rule) without it stopping the run: untick its checkbox in the Breakpoints panel, or right-click its gutter slot → Disable Breakpoint / Enable Breakpoint. A disabled breakpoint shows a hollow marker in the gutter and a greyed row; it counts no hits. Clicking a hollow marker removes the breakpoint, as for any other.
  • Mute in the DEBUG header switches all breakpoints off at once for the session (they are drawn hollow); stepping and pausing still work. Muting is not saved - the breakpoints' enabled state is.
  • When a run completes, breakpoints it never reached are flagged: their gutter dot turns amber and the Breakpoints panel marks the row ⚠ … not reached in the last run. Usually the line has no instruction Saxon traces (a closing tag, a comment, an attribute on its own line) - move the breakpoint to the instruction's first line - or the code there did not run for this input. A stopped or failed run flags nothing; the next run clears the flags.
  • A breakpoint stops once per execution of its line: an instruction nested inside another one on the same line (e.g. <x><xsl:value-of select="@n"/></x>) does not stop the run a second time. Stepping (Step Into) still visits every instruction.

docs.title: Logpoints
docs.text:
A logpoint writes a message instead of (or before) pausing - printf debugging without editing the stylesheet. Right-click a gutter slot → Add Logpoint…, or set a Log message in Breakpoint Properties:

  • The message may contain {xpath} parts, evaluated at that moment like an attribute value template: item {@id}: {count(line)} lines, total {$total}. {{ and }} are literal braces; a failing part reads {ERROR: …} and the rest is still logged.
  • Each message appears in Messages as level LOG with the logpoint's file and line.
  • Pause when hit (off for a new logpoint) decides whether the run also stops there.
  • Condition and hit count apply: the message is written at the hits that pass both.
  • In the gutter a logpoint is a diamond - blue when it only logs, red when it also pauses.

docs.title: Template, Function and Mode Breakpoints
docs.text:
To stop whenever a component runs - wherever it is defined, also in included modules - use Template… in the Breakpoints panel. Choose what to break on and its name (the dialog suggests the names declared in the stylesheet and its modules):

Break on Pauses when Example Template rule (match) a template with that match pattern is entered item, order/line[@qty] Named template the named template is called footer Function the function is called f:total or just total (any prefix) Any template in mode a template runs in that mode summary

Patterns compare without spaces. These breakpoints are listed under Templates & functions below the line breakpoints (checkbox to disable, Delete to remove), are saved with the main stylesheet, pause even when the template has no line breakpoint, and are silenced by Mute. The status names what was entered (· template match="item").

docs.title: Break When an Input Node Is Processed
docs.text:
To stop when the stylesheet reaches a particular node of the input, open the input XML, put the caret on the element and right-click → Break When Processed (shown while a debug session runs). The run pauses whenever that element becomes the context node - a template rule matched it or a loop reached it - once per visit, not at every instruction that runs while it stays the context. The status reads · input node /order/item[2] (orders.xml:3).

The breakpoint is listed under Templates & functions in the Breakpoints panel (checkbox, Delete), saved with the main stylesheet and silenced by Mute; right-click the element again → Remove Break When Processed to drop it. The node is identified by its position in the file, so editing the input above it moves it out of reach.

docs.title: Break on Errors and Messages
docs.text:
The Breakpoints panel's Break on ▾ menu pauses the run independent of line breakpoints:

Option Pauses Default Dynamic errors when an instruction fails at run time (division by zero, a failed cast, error()) - at the failing instruction, with its context item and variables intact, so you can see why. The status reads error FOAR0001: … in red; Continue lets the error end the run as usual on Only error codes… limits Dynamic errors to the codes you list, comma-separated, e.g. FOAR0001, XTDE0640; XTDE* stands for every code starting with XTDE. Empty = every error. The menu shows the current list every error xsl:message terminate="yes" before a terminating message is emitted (also when terminate is computed, e.g. {if (…) then 'yes' else 'no'}) on Every xsl:message before every xsl:message off

The choices are saved. Mute silences these as well. Static errors (the stylesheet does not compile) are not run, so there is nothing to pause at - they appear in Messages.

docs.title: Conditional Breakpoints
docs.text:
A breakpoint can carry an XPath condition: the run pauses at that line only when the condition is true at that moment - for example @id = '4711' inside a template that runs for every item, $total > 1000, or position() = last().

  • Right-click the gutter slot of a line → Add Conditional Breakpoint… (a line without a breakpoint) or Breakpoint Properties… (a line with one), Remove Condition, Remove Hit Count Rule, Remove Breakpoint. In the Breakpoints panel select an entry and press Edit…. Both open the Breakpoint Properties dialog with the condition and the hit count.
  • An empty condition makes the breakpoint unconditional again.
  • A breakpoint with a condition or a hit-count rule shows a question-mark marker in the gutter; its tooltip names the rules and the hits of the current run.
  • The condition is evaluated like xsl:if test (effective boolean value): the context item and every variable in scope at that line are available, plus the stylesheet's namespace prefixes. A non-empty node sequence is true, an empty one false. position() and last() refer to the item being processed (the 2nd of 5), the same as in watches; inside a predicate (item[position() = 1]) or a path step they keep their usual meaning.
  • The dialog checks the condition and the log message while you type: a syntax error ($total >, an unclosed { in a log message) appears in red below the fields and OK stays closed until it is fixed. Variables, the stylesheet's namespace prefixes and its own functions are not checked there - they are only known at the line during the run.
  • When the run pauses because of a condition, the status says so (· condition: @id = '4711'). If the condition cannot be evaluated (a typo, an undeclared variable), the run pauses anyway and the status shows the error in red - a broken condition never silently skips the breakpoint.
  • The condition is checked every time the line runs, so a breakpoint inside a large loop costs time on each pass. Conditions are saved with the breakpoint (per file, like all breakpoints).
  • Cost. A pass that does not pause only collects what the condition can see (the context item, the focus and the variable values); the Variables table, the XSLT context and the call stack are built only when the run actually pauses. Logpoints work the same way. Measured over a loop of 10,000 items (median of 15 runs, DebuggerPerfBenchmark):
Scenario (10,000 passes) Before Now Condition that is never true 97 ms 66 ms Logpoint that never pauses 95 ms 64 ms Condition, 12-level call stack per item (1,000 items) 46 ms 28 ms

The remainder is the XPath evaluation itself, roughly 4 µs per pass - a condition in a loop of a million items adds about four seconds. A debug run without any breakpoint takes 29 ms for the same loop.

docs.title: Hit Counts
docs.text:
Every breakpoint counts its hits during a run - a hit is a pass of its line where its condition (if any) held. The count is shown in the Breakpoints panel (· 5 hits) and in the gutter tooltip, and starts over with every run and Restart.

In Breakpoint Properties → Pause on you can restrict pausing by the count:

Pause on Pauses at hit every hit 1, 2, 3, … (default) exactly the N-th hit N only - e.g. the 500th item of a loop the N-th hit and later N, N+1, … every N-th hit N, 2N, 3N, …

Condition and hit count combine: condition @type = 'B', exactly the 3rd hit pauses at the third item of type B. When a hit-count rule makes the run pause, the status says so (· hit 3 (hit = 3)). Hit-count rules are saved with the breakpoint, the counts are not.

docs.title: Starting and Stepping
docs.text:
Without breakpoints the run pauses at the first instruction (Pause on entry, a toggle in the header - switch it off to run straight to the first breakpoint). The header controls are icons - hover one for its name and key:

Control Key Description Continue F5 Resume until the next breakpoint Run to Cursor Ctrl+F10 (⌘F10) Run to the caret line of the stylesheet (Tools → Run to Cursor, or right-click a gutter slot → Run to Here). A one-shot stop: breakpoints on the way still pause and cancel it; it works while breakpoints are muted. Without a running session it starts the debugger (like Run ▾ → Debug Transform) and runs to that line instead of pausing on entry Pause F6 While the run is going: break in at the next instruction - e.g. to look into a long loop or an endless recursion without a breakpoint (the status reads paused by request) Step Into F7 Step into the current instruction - the next stop is the next line that runs (inside a called template or function too) Smart Step Into Shift+F7 When the paused line calls several things (f:a(1) + f:b(2), an xsl:call-template next to an xsl:apply-templates), a menu at Step Into lists them - pick the one to stop in. Also a right-click on Step Into. One call steps straight into it; none is a plain Step Into. The run stops when that function / template is entered, even while breakpoints are muted Step Over F8 Execute the current instruction without descending Step Out Shift+F8 Run until the current template/function returns Restart Run again from the start with the same breakpoints; the stylesheet is read again from the editor, so your edits (saved or not) are picked up Stop Abort the running transformation Mute Toggle: the run does not stop at any breakpoint (steps still pause) Coverage Toggle (remembered): from the next run on, record which lines run - see Coverage Show in editor Jump the editor to the currently paused line Show input Select the input document at the paused context node (see below) Evaluate Alt+F8 Open the value window on the selected frame's context item with the XPath field ready - evaluate any expression in that frame (its variables in scope); Up / Down in the field recall earlier expressions ✕ End the session and close the DEBUG dock (OUTPUT stays)

Steps move line by line: instructions nested on the paused line (a literal element with its xsl:value-of inside) do not stop again, and instructions without a source line are skipped. A line that runs again later (the next loop iteration, a recursive call) is a new stop.

The step keys only act while the debugger is paused and F6 only while it runs; otherwise F5 and F8 keep their usual meaning. A single long evaluation (one huge XPath expression) is not interrupted - Pause takes effect at the next instruction. The paused line is tinted in the editor and a green arrow marks it in the gutter; a hit breakpoint shows a yellow arrow over the red circle.

How much slower is a debug run? The debugger watches every instruction, so a debug run takes about 1.5 to 2 times as long as a normal transformation, with or without breakpoints. Saxon's own trace instrumentation is almost free; the time goes into following the call stack and recording which instruction wrote which output. Breakpoints on lines that never run cost nothing extra. Measured with DebuggerPerfBenchmark (median of 15 runs, stylesheet compiled in each run):

Workload Normal run Debug run Factor 10,000 items, one template 20 ms 29 ms 1.5 100,000 items, one template 153 ms 278 ms 1.8 1,000 items, 12-level recursion each 14 ms 23 ms 1.6

Variables, the call stack and the XSLT context are only collected when the run pauses, so stepping and hitting breakpoints do not slow the run between pauses.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text: With Coverage on in the DEBUG header, every run records which stylesheet lines ran. After the run, the breakpoint gutter shows a green bar next to each line that ran (the tooltip says how often) and a red bar on the lines of every template or function that never ran for this input - dead code, or a hint that the test input lacks a case. Messages lists those templates and functions (Never ran: template match="…"); double-click one to jump to it. The markers stay until the next run. Recording costs next to nothing (a 100,000-item run: 278 ms without, 282 ms with coverage).

docs.title: Inspecting State
docs.text:
The context node in the input. At every pause the line of the current context node (.) is tinted blue in the input XML document - the stylesheet's paused line stays yellow and in front. Show input in the header switches to the input document at that line. The input is the file the run read (Transform panel INPUT, FOP XML input, the Run target), or the open document whose text was transformed; a node from a document loaded with doc() / document() is shown in that file, which opens behind the stylesheet. Attributes and text nodes point at their element's line, the document node at the root element.

Below the header, the paused state is shown in two tab groups side by side: Variables | Watch on the left (the state at the pause point), Call Stack | Messages | Breakpoints | Output on the right (navigation, log and the output so far). Drag the divider between the groups to give one side more room - the position is remembered, and so is the tab you last chose in each group (a tab the debugger brings forward by itself, like Messages after a failed run, does not change that choice). Messages and Breakpoints show a count badge on their tab; Messages is highlighted when output arrives while another tab of its group is in front, and a failed run brings Messages to the front so the error is readable at once. In Watch and Breakpoints the Delete key removes the selected row.

docs.title: Why Did This Template Match?
docs.text:
Right-click a template rule in Call Stack → Explain Match… to see which rules of the frame's mode could process its context node. Every rule pattern is tested against the node and listed:

  • ✓ wins - the rule XSLT picks: highest import precedence, then highest priority, then the last one in the stylesheet;
  • matches, loses - with the reason (lower priority, lower import precedence, earlier in the stylesheet);
  • no match - the remaining rules of the mode.

Each line shows the pattern, its priority (default when computed from the pattern, e.g. item 0, * -0.5, item[@n] 0.5) and its module and line; double-click opens the rule. Imports and includes are followed; rules in other modes are left out. When no rule matches, the built-in rule applies.

docs.title: Changed Values
docs.text: Values that changed since the previous pause in the same template or function are shown in bold blue - in Variables (including variables that are new there) and in Watch. Pausing in the item template for the second item marks $label and position(), but not a global that stayed the same. The comparison is per frame: selecting an outer frame in Call Stack compares with that frame's previous pause. A new run starts without markers.

docs.title: Exploring Structured Values
docs.text: Variables is a tree: a node value unfolds into its attributes and child nodes (element → @id, <item>, text(), …; indentation whitespace is skipped), a sequence into its items [1], [2], …, a map into its entries and an array into its members - built as you expand them, at most 500 children per row. Every row knows the XPath that reaches it from its variable, e.g. $order/item[2]/@sku: Open Value… opens that node in the value window, Add to Watches adds the path as a watch, a click on its value opens it. Values are shown on one line; the tooltip and the value window show them in full.

docs.title: Values in the Code
docs.text:
While the run is paused, the stylesheet shows the current values next to the declarations: $fundName = DEMO FUND 01 appears in a yellow tag at the end of the xsl:variable / xsl:param line, as in the screenshot above.

  • Shown are the locals of the template or function the run is paused in, declared up to the paused line, and the global variables and parameters that have been evaluated so far (Saxon evaluates a global on first use).
  • A declaration over several lines shows its value on the line where the start tag ends.
  • Long values are cut at 80 characters - click the value in Variables to see it whole.
  • The values disappear when the run continues and as soon as you edit the stylesheet (they would no longer match their lines).

docs.title: Values Under the Mouse
docs.text: While the run is paused, rest the mouse on a variable reference ($total, $f:rate, also inside {$x} value templates) in the stylesheet: after half a second a small popup shows its value and type, evaluated in the selected call stack frame. Select an XPath expression (e.g. count($items) * 2) and rest the mouse inside the selection to evaluate the whole expression. Open in value viewer in the popup opens the full value. Errors (an undeclared variable, a typo) are shown in the popup; nothing happens while the run is not paused.

docs.title: Inspecting an Outer Frame
docs.text: At every pause the innermost frame is selected in Call Stack, and Variables shows the pause as described above. Select another frame to see the state of a calling template or function: Variables then lists that frame's context item (.), its own local variables and the globals, under a banner such as Frame 3 of 5: template match="/" · main.xsl:4, and the Watch expressions are re-evaluated in that frame (its context item and variables). Opening a value, Copy Value and the value window's XPath use the selected frame as well. Select the top frame to return to the pause. position() / last() are shown for the innermost frame only. The 32 innermost frames carry values; a deeper frame shows an empty table with a note.

docs.title: Viewing a Value in Full
docs.text:
The Value column of Variables and Watch shows only the start of a value (a node can be thousands of characters long). Click a value - or select the row and press Enter, or right-click → Open Value… - to open it in its own value window:

  • The complete value, pretty-printed (toggle Pretty print), with XML syntax highlighting and line numbers; Wrap wraps long lines, Copy copies the whole value. A sequence shows one item per line and its item count.
  • An XPath field below that runs against this value: a single node is the context item (item[1]/price, count(//item)), $value is the whole value ($value[2] for a sequence), and every variable of the pause stays in scope. Run (or Enter) shows the result with its item count and time; Copy result copies it.
  • Value windows are separate, resizable windows - keep several open next to the editor. They show the pause they were opened at (paused at file:line), stay open while you step, and close when the debug session ends. Clicking the same value of the same pause again brings its window to the front.
  • Right-click → Copy Value copies the full value without opening a window.
  • A Watch value is re-evaluated in full for the window (the table keeps a shortened version).
  • Call Stack frames open the same way (select a frame and press Enter, or right-click → Open Value…; double-click still jumps to the line): the window shows that frame's context item, and its XPath field sees that frame's own local variables plus the globals - so you can inspect the state of a calling template, not just the innermost one. The 32 innermost frames carry these values; deeper frames show only their name and location.
Panel Shows Variables The context item (.), position() / last(), the XSLT context (scope XSLT: the current mode when it is a named mode; inside xsl:for-each-group current-grouping-key() and current-group(); inside xsl:matching-substring regex-group(0…n); the tunnel parameters passed down, marked (tunnel); accumulator-before('…') of every accumulator that applies to the context node's document), every local variable in scope, and every global variable evaluated so far - with their real values and XDM types (globals not yet evaluated are not forced, that would change the evaluation order). Click a value to open it in full Watch Your XPath expressions, evaluated against the paused context item with all variables in scope: count(item), $total, string(@id), position(); the stylesheet's namespace prefixes are available. Type an expression into the field above the table and press Add, or right-click a variable → Add to Watches; Remove (or the Delete key) drops the selected one, a double-click or F2 edits an expression in place. Watches are saved per stylesheet and come back with its next debug session. Re-evaluated at every pause; errors are shown in the row. Click a value to open it in full Call Stack Template and function frames, innermost first (a template rule running in a named mode shows mode="…"; a loop - xsl:for-each, xsl:for-each-group, xsl:apply-templates - shows the item its body is working on, e.g. ForEach (3 of 222), and xsl:iterate its round, (iteration 4)), each with its module and line (the instructions nested inside them are dimmed); double-click a frame to jump to it - also into an included module. Selecting a frame switches Variables and Watch to that frame (see below). Enter or Open Value… opens the frame's context item and variables Messages xsl:message output and Saxon warnings live, as they happen, with their location; double-click jumps to the line. A failed run shows its error here too. The toolbar filters by level (Messages / Warnings / Errors - terminate="yes" counts as an error) and by text, Copy copies the selected messages (or all shown ones), Clear empties the list. The tab badge always counts all messages Breakpoints All breakpoints of the session with Remove / Clear all above the list, see above Output What the transformation has written so far, refreshed at every pause - see where in the result you are; when the run finishes, the complete results (the principal one also in OUTPUT). The serializer may hold back a just-opened start tag until it knows whether the element stays empty, so the text can lag by one tag. With xsl:result-document a selector switches between the principal and each secondary result (kept in memory - a debug run writes nothing to disk; xsl:result-document itself needs Settings → Schemas & Validation → PARSER → Allow XSLT extension functions, off by default). Documents (n) lists what the run loaded with doc(), document() or collection(); click a file to open it. Copy copies the shown text

docs.title: From the Output to the Stylesheet
docs.text: Double-click a line in the DEBUG dock's Output tab - while paused or after the run - to open the instruction that wrote it: the xsl:value-of, xsl:text, literal element or copy that produced that text. The jump uses the debugged run's own record of who wrote what, so it works for the principal output; secondary xsl:result-document outputs are not mapped. The serializer writes an element's start tag only together with the next thing it writes, so a click on a start tag can land on the first instruction inside that element.

docs.title: The Result
docs.text: When the run ends the status reads Finished · N ms · M chars → OUTPUT and the result is shown in the OUTPUT panel. DEBUG stays in front so Messages remain readable - the OUTPUT toggle lights up to show it has new content. A stopped run shows Stopped, a failed one Error: ….

docs.title: Debugging XSL-FO stylesheets
docs.text: The PDF / FOP panel's TOOLS → Debug stylesheet… runs an XSL-FO stylesheet in the same debugger (the page-size parameters are passed on). The FO it produces lands in OUTPUT and can be rendered with the panel's Render PDF from FO… - see PDF Generator.

docs.title: Debugging XQuery
docs.text:
The debugger runs XQuery too. Open a saved .xq / .xquery file and press Shift+F5 (or Run ▾ → Debug Query): the query runs against the same Input as Run Query (the most recently active XML document, or the one picked in the Input selector); a query without an input runs without a context item.

Everything above works the same way: breakpoints in the query's gutter (click, F9, conditions, hit counts, logpoints), stepping, Variables (the let and for variables of the FLWOR expression, function parameters), Watch, the Call Stack with function frames, Break on errors, Coverage and the Output tab. fn:trace() output appears in Messages (label: value). Smart Step Into offers the functions declared with declare function. What Saxon traces in a query is coarser than in a stylesheet: a stop is a let clause, a constructed element or attribute, or a function call - a for or where clause has no stop of its own. Explain Match is for template rules and does not apply.

docs.title: Debugging a Schematron
docs.text:
A Schematron can be debugged too. Open a saved .sch file and press Shift+F5 (or Run ▾ → Debug Schematron, or the Run button): the debugger checks the Input - the most recently active XML document, or the one picked in the Input selector shown for Schematron tabs. Behind the scenes SchXslt compiles the Schematron to XSLT (the same compiler validation uses) and the debugger runs that XSLT, but everything you see is the .sch:

  • Breakpoints go into the .sch gutter, including included files (sch:include). A breakpoint on an sch:assert or sch:report stops once for every node its rule fires on, before the test is evaluated - add a condition (for example $n gt 5) to stop only for some. A breakpoint on an sch:rule stops when the rule fires.
  • Stepping goes from rule to sch:let to assert to report; SchXslt's own driver code is skipped. Functions written in the Schematron (xsl:function) can be stepped into.
  • Variables show the sch:let values of the rule (and the global ones); Watch and hover evaluate XPath with the Schematron's sch:ns prefixes.
  • When the run ends, Messages lists every failed assert (warning) and successful report with its text and the location of the node; a double-click jumps to the .sch line. The Output tab shows the SVRL report.

The .sch file is compiled as saved - unsaved changes are not included (a note in Messages says so). The mapping follows the structure SchXslt produces (one template per rule, one test per assert and report, matched by their text). Rules of abstract patterns (is-a), whose context and tests are rewritten by the compiler, have no .sch lines to stop at; abstract rules used through sch:extends work, they stop at the abstract rule's asserts. Quick-fix code (SQF) is not part of the run.

docs.title: XML Digital Signatures
docs.text:
Note: Signing, signature validation (including detailed and PKIX trust/chain/revocation/timestamp validation) and self-signed certificate creation live on the Sign & Encrypt page of the Unified Shell. Click Sign & Encrypt in the activity bar to open it as a tab in the main editor area. The same page encrypts and decrypts XML - see XML Encryption. On the command line: fxt-cli sign and fxt-cli verify (Command Line).

This tool lets you digitally sign XML documents and verify signatures. A digital signature proves that a document is authentic and hasn't been changed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Signing, validation and certificate creation live on the Signature page (screenshot may show an older layout)

docs.title: What Can You Do?
docs.text:
In the Unified Shell, click Sign & Encrypt in the activity bar. The page opens as a tab in the main editor area, and the side panel on the left lists the actions in order of use (Encrypt, Decrypt and Inspect Encryption are described in XML Encryption). Click an action to show it on the page; the current action is highlighted, and the status message of the previously selected action is cleared:

Action Description Sign XML File Sign a document with your keystore (default) Validate Signature Check if the signed document is valid (plus a detailed report) Create Certificate Generate your own digital ID (keystore) Expert Mode PKIX trust validation against a trust store, with optional revocation check

docs.title: How the Page Is Organized
docs.text:
Every action uses the same layout, from top to bottom:

Part Shown for Description Header All actions The name of the selected action DOCUMENT Sign XML File, Validate Signature, Expert Mode The XML file to work on - the active document by default; Browse picks a different file KEYSTORE Sign XML File, Create Certificate The keystore file, alias and passwords (see below) - you enter them only once, both actions share them Action form All actions The options of the action and its primary button (e.g. Sign Document) Status line All actions The outcome of the last action

docs.title: The KEYSTORE Section
docs.text: Field Description Keystore row The selected keystore file, its name on its own line (full path as tooltip). Until you pick one it reads "No keystore — choose or drop a .jks / .p12", and clicking it works like Change. Click Change to browse, pick a favorite from the star menu, or drop a file from your file manager (.jks, .keystore, .p12, .pfx) Keystore alias Name of the key entry in the keystore Keystore password Password protecting the keystore file Alias password Password protecting the private key

docs.title: 1. Create a Certificate
docs.text:
Before signing documents, you need a digital certificate (like a digital ID card).

Certificate creation form with DN details

docs.title: Key Type
docs.text: RSA 2048 (default), RSA 3072, RSA 4096, or an elliptic curve key EC P-256, EC P-384, EC P-521. EC keys sign with ECDSA and receive encrypted documents with ECDH-ES (XML Encryption); RSA keys sign with RSA or RSA-PSS and receive with RSA-OAEP.

docs.title: Certificate Details (Distinguished Name)
docs.text:
All fields are optional - blank ones are simply omitted from the subject.

Field Description Example Common Name (CN) Your name or the certificate name John Smith Organization (O) Your company or organization Acme Corp Organizational Unit (OU) Your department IT Security Locality (L) Your city Vienna State (ST) Your state or province Vienna Country (C) Two-letter country code AT Email Contact e-mail address john@example.com

docs.title: Keystore Security
docs.text:
The alias and passwords come from the page's KEYSTORE section - all three are required:

Field Description Keystore alias Alias of the new key entry; also names the output folder and files Keystore password Password to protect the keystore file Alias password Password to protect the private key (can be same as keystore)

docs.title: What Gets Generated
docs.text:
The certificate parameters are fixed - there are no algorithm or validity options:

Property Value Key RSA, 2048 bits Signature algorithm SHA256withRSA Validity 1 year from creation Type Self-signed (issuer = subject)

The files are written to certs/<alias>/ in the application's working directory:

File Content <alias>_KeyStore.jks The Java keystore with the private key and certificate <alias>_publicKey.pem The certificate as PEM <alias>_privateKey.pem The encrypted private key as PEM (encrypted with the keystore password) summary.txt Alias, passwords and certificate details in plain text - keep it private

docs.title: How to Create a Certificate
docs.text:
1. On the Sign & Encrypt page, choose Create Certificate in the side panel
  2. Fill in the alias and both passwords in the KEYSTORE section
  3. Fill in the Distinguished Name fields
  4. Click "Create Certificate"
  5. The status line shows the path of the new keystore, which is selected automatically - you can sign with it right away
  6. Keep the keystore file and passwords safe!

Important: Remember your passwords! They cannot be recovered.

Tip: If you leave the alias or a password blank, the field is highlighted in red when you click Create Certificate. The highlight clears as soon as you start typing.

docs.title: 2. Sign an XML Document
docs.text:
Document signing interface

Sign XML File is the action the Signature page shows first. The DOCUMENT row is pre-filled with the active document.

docs.title: The Sign Form
docs.text: Section Description DOCUMENT The XML file to sign (the active document by default); Browse picks a different file KEYSTORE The keystore file, Keystore alias, Keystore password and Alias password SIGNATURE OPTIONS - Signature type Enveloped (default), Enveloping or Detached (see below). With Detached selected, a hint explains that a separate <name>.sig.xml is written - validate that file and keep both files in the same folder SIGNATURE OPTIONS - Signature method, Digest, Canonicalization Automatic picks RSA-SHA256 for RSA keys and ECDSA-SHA256 for EC keys; also RSA-SHA384/512, RSA-PSS (SHA-256/384/512) and ECDSA-SHA384/512. Digest SHA-256 (default), SHA-384 or SHA-512. Canonicalization exclusive (default), inclusive or C14N 1.1, each with or without comments. SHA-1 is not offered and is rejected on verification Sign Document Runs the signing; the outcome appears in the status line CERTIFICATE Show certificate details loads the certificate of the selected keystore/alias: subject, issued/expires, serial, signature algorithm, key usage and the SHA-256 fingerprint (with a copy button)

docs.title: Signature Types and Output Files
docs.text:
There is no output-file picker: the result is written next to the original, which is left untouched, and opened in the editor automatically.

Type Structure Output file Enveloped The ds:Signature element is inserted into the signed document <name>.signed.xml Enveloping The signed content is wrapped inside the signature document <name>.signed.xml Detached A standalone signature document referencing the original file by relative URI <name>.sig.xml

Detached signatures: keep the .sig.xml file together with the original document - the signature references the file by name and cannot be verified without it.

docs.title: How to Sign a Document
docs.text:
1. Open the Sign & Encrypt page and choose Sign XML File in the side panel
  2. Select your keystore in the KEYSTORE section - click Change, pick a favorited keystore from the star menu next to the keystore row (see Favorites Integration below), or drop a keystore file (.jks, .keystore, .p12, .pfx) from your file manager onto the KEYSTORE row (Expert Mode's trust store row accepts drops the same way)
  3. Enter the keystore alias, keystore password and alias password
  4. Check the DOCUMENT row - it shows the active document; click Browse to sign a different file
  5. Pick the signature type (Enveloped, Enveloping or Detached)
  6. Click "Sign Document"
  7. The signed file (<name>.signed.xml or <name>.sig.xml) opens in a new editor tab in the background; the Signature page stays in front and offers Validate this signature

Unsaved changes: signing reads the document from disk. If it has unsaved changes, you are asked "Save changes to first?" - Save and Continue signs your current text, Use Saved Version signs the file as last saved, Cancel stops.

Tip: Missing inputs are highlighted in red when you click Sign Document: signing without a keystore marks the keystore entry, and a blank alias or password marks that field. The highlight disappears as soon as you start typing.

docs.title: 3. Verify a Signature
docs.text: Verifying a signed document

docs.title: How to Verify a Signature
docs.text:
1. Right after signing, click Validate this signature below the status line - it switches to Validate Signature with the signed file and runs the check. Otherwise open the signed XML file in the editor (it becomes the active document)
  2. On the Sign & Encrypt page, choose Validate Signature in the side panel
  3. Check the DOCUMENT row - it shows the active document; click Browse to check a different file
  4. Click the Run Validation button
  5. See the result in the status line (failures additionally open an explanatory dialog)

For a detailed report (validity plus signing-certificate details), use the outlined Validate (Details) button instead - it also checks the document in the DOCUMENT row, and the report opens as Signature-Report.txt in a new tab.

docs.title: Validation Results
docs.text:
Each validation outcome explains in plain language what happened and what to do about it.

Result Meaning Valid (green status) The signature is authentic and the document is unchanged No signature found (red hint) The document doesn't contain a signature - sign it first Invalid signature (error dialog) The document was modified after signing. The dialog names what failed: the signature value itself or a specific reference Certificate cannot be used (dialog) The signature does not embed an X.509 certificate, only references it, or uses an unsupported algorithm. Ask the sender for a signature that embeds an RSA X.509 certificate, or use Validate (Details) Weak algorithm (rejected) The signature uses SHA-1, which is rejected for security reasons. Re-sign the document with SHA-256 or SHA-512 Error (dialog) Something else went wrong - the dialog includes collapsible technical details

docs.title: What the Verification Checks
docs.text: Check What It Means Authenticity The signature was created by the certificate holder Integrity The document hasn't been changed since signing Certificate The signing certificate is valid

docs.title: 4. Expert Mode - Trust Validation
docs.text:
In addition to checking that a signature is mathematically valid, you can check whether the signing certificate is actually trusted.

Expert Mode: trust store, revocation check and Validate (Trust)

Basic validation confirms that a signature is intact and matches its certificate. Trust validation goes further: it checks the signing certificate's chain against a trust store - a collection of certificate authorities you trust - to decide whether the certificate really comes from a trusted source (PKIX path validation).

Expert Mode shows the DOCUMENT row, the TRUST STORE section and one action:

Control Description DOCUMENT The signed XML file to check - the active document by default; Browse picks a different file Trust store row The trust store to validate against - default (cacerts) until you pick one. Change opens a file chooser (.jks, .p12, .pfx, .keystore); the star menu lists your keystore favorites; dropping a file onto the row works too Trust store password (optional) The password of the trust store, if it has one. This field is separate from the keystore password Check revocation (OCSP/CRL) Also verify that the certificate has not been revoked Validate (Trust) Runs the validation on the document in the DOCUMENT row and opens the report

docs.title: How to Run Trust Validation
docs.text:
1. Open the signed XML document, then choose Expert Mode on the Sign & Encrypt page (the DOCUMENT row shows the active document; Browse picks a different file).
  2. (Optional) Click Change in the trust store row to choose the trust store to validate against - or pick a favorited keystore from the star menu next to the trust store row. By default the application uses the JVM's built-in cacerts store, which contains well-known public certificate authorities.
  3. (Optional) If your trust store is password-protected, enter its password in the Trust store password field below the trust store row.
  4. (Optional) Tick Check revocation (OCSP/CRL) to also verify that the certificate has not been revoked.
  5. Click Validate (Trust).
  6. A trust report (Signature-Trust-Report.txt) opens in a new tab.

docs.title: What the Trust Report Tells You
docs.text:
Item What It Means Trusted Whether the signing certificate chains up to a certificate in the trust store Trust anchor The trusted certificate (certificate authority) at the top of the chain Revocation Whether the certificate has been revoked (only when revocation checking is on) Timestamp Timestamp information found with the signature, if any

Note: A signature can be mathematically valid but not trusted if its certificate is self-signed or issued by an authority that is not in your trust store. Trust validation is the step that tells the two situations apart. Certificates created with Create Certificate are self-signed, so they are only trusted if you add them to the trust store you validate against.

docs.title: Favorites Integration
docs.text:
Save frequently used files for quick access:

  • Add Favorite (Ctrl+D) - Add the active document to favorites
  • Favorites (Ctrl+Shift+D) - Show/hide the Favorites activity panel

The Favorites panel provides quick access to your saved keystores, XML files, and signed documents.

Keystore and trust store files (.jks, .p12, .pfx, .keystore) are their own Keystore favorite type with a lock icon. On the Signature page, the keystore row (KEYSTORE section) and the trust store row (Expert Mode) each carry a star menu listing your keystore favorites - pick one to select it without browsing the file system. See Favorites System for details.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
The Signature page has no shortcuts of its own; the shell-wide favorites shortcuts are the useful ones here:

Shortcut Action Ctrl+D Add the active document to favorites Ctrl+Shift+D Toggle the Favorites panel

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep your keystore safe - It's your digital identity
  • Remember your passwords - They cannot be recovered
  • Signed files are new files - The original is not modified
  • Delete or protect summary.txt - Certificate creation writes your passwords into it in plain text
  • Use strong passwords - At least 12 characters with mixed case, numbers, symbols
  • Backup your keystore - Store copies in secure locations
  • Check validity regularly - Certificates expire after the validity period (one year for certificates created here; Show certificate details in the Sign form shows the days remaining)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution Wrong password Double-check keystore and key passwords A field is highlighted in red The input is missing - select a keystore or fill in the alias/password; the highlight clears while you type Key not found Verify the key alias exists in the keystore Validation fails The error dialog names what changed - the document was modified after signing "Certificate cannot be used" The signature doesn't embed an RSA X.509 certificate - ask the sender to re-sign with the certificate embedded, or use Validate (Details) "Weak algorithm" (SHA-1) SHA-1 signatures are rejected for security - re-sign the document with SHA-256 or SHA-512 Certificate expired Create a new certificate with the Create Certificate action (certificates are valid for one year) Valid but "not trusted" The certificate is self-signed or its issuer is not in the trust store - pick a trust store that contains it in Expert Mode Detached signature does not verify The .sig.xml references the original by file name - keep both files in the same folder

docs.title: Supported Formats
docs.text: Type Formats Input XML files (.xml) Keystores / trust stores .jks, .p12, .pfx, .keystore (Create Certificate always produces a .jks) Output Enveloped/enveloping: <name>.signed.xml; detached: <name>.sig.xml

docs.title: What if I lose my password?
docs.text: Unfortunately, passwords cannot be recovered. You'll need to create a new certificate.

docs.title: Can I sign multiple files at once?
docs.text: Currently, files must be signed one at a time.

docs.title: What signature type is used?
docs.text: The tool creates XML signatures (XMLDSig) with RSA-SHA256 (RSA keys) or ECDSA-SHA256 (EC keys) and exclusive canonicalization unless you choose other algorithms in the Sign form. You choose the structure in the Sign form: enveloped (default - the signature is embedded within the XML document), enveloping (the content is wrapped inside the signature document) or detached (a separate .sig.xml file referencing the original).

docs.title: Can I sign PDFs?
docs.text: No, this tool is specifically for XML documents. Use the PDF Generator for PDF-related tasks.

docs.title: Execution Statistics
docs.text:
Optional developer feature | Off by default

FreeXmlToolkit can record resource statistics for every technical operation it runs — XSLT transformations, XQuery and XPath evaluations, XSD and Schematron validations, XProc pipelines, and PDF (XSL-FO) rendering. For each run it captures:

  • Wall-clock duration and — where measurable — a phase breakdown (XSLT: compile vs. transform; validation: XSD vs. Schematron stage),
  • CPU time of the executing thread,
  • Heap usage before the run and the heap delta it caused,
  • GC activity (collections and GC time observed during the run),
  • Input and output sizes,
  • success/error state with the error's first line.

This is aimed at technical users: inside the desktop app it rarely matters how long a transformation takes — but when the same stylesheets, queries or validation rules are later moved to a server or cloud environment billed by resources (for example mass transformations of large deliveries), these numbers tell you what one work step costs and where optimizing the script pays off.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text: Open Settings → Extensions → DEVELOPER and tick Record execution statistics, then click Save Settings. The flag is persisted; regular users who leave it off see no change anywhere in the UI and no measurements are taken (zero overhead).

docs.title: Where the numbers appear
docs.text:
• Inline — panels append the run duration to their status lines: the OUTPUT panel already shows Transformed · 42 ms · 1234 chars; with the feature enabled the Query Console's RESULTS header, the Validation panel's status (Valid · 128 ms) and the PDF panel's success message gain the same information.
  • Status bar — a last run item (e.g. XSLT · 42 ms) appears next to the memory meter. Click it to open the full history.
  • Execution Statistics tool tab — the complete history (last 200 runs): a table with time, operation, target, duration, CPU, memory delta, GC, sizes and status; selecting a row shows the detail report with the phase breakdown and throughput. Also reachable via Execution Statistics in the Transform panel's OPTIONS & TOOLS section.

The screenshot shows two recorded runs: the validation of a FundsXML document (917 ms — also visible inline as Valid · 917 ms in the Validation panel and as VALIDATION · 917 ms in the status bar) and an XSLT check stylesheet (2.0 s, with its compile/transform phases in the detail report below the table).

Batch runs (multi-file transforms and batch validation) record one entry per file, so a mass run over a folder yields a per-file cost profile.

docs.title: Export
docs.text: The tool tab exports the recorded history as CSV or JSON — ready for a spreadsheet or your own analysis tooling when sizing server workloads or comparing script revisions.

docs.title: Interpreting the numbers
docs.text:
• Memory deltas are approximate. All operations share one JVM heap, and a garbage collection during a run can even make the delta negative. Use the values to compare runs of the same kind, not as absolute costs.
  • Compile 0 ms on an XSLT run means the compiled stylesheet came from the engine's cache — a server executing the stylesheet once per process will pay the compile cost on the first run only.
  • CPU vs. wall time: a large gap usually indicates I/O or waiting, not computation.

docs.title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
docs.text: Answers to common questions and fixes for typical problems. If your problem is not listed, send a report from inside the app with Help → Report a Problem… or open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: How does FreeXmlToolkit compare to Oxygen XML Editor, XMLSpy or XMLBlueprint?
docs.text: See Comparison with Other Editors: a feature table with sources, including the areas where the other editors offer more.

docs.title: Application Does Not Start (Windows)
docs.text:
On some Windows computers, the application may fail to start or crash immediately after launch. This is typically caused by incompatible graphics drivers.

What to try:

  1. Update your graphics drivers -- Visit your GPU manufacturer's website (NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel) and install the latest driver for your graphics card.
  2. Try the portable version -- If you used the installer (.exe or .msi), try the portable (.zip) version instead.
  3. Report the issue -- If the problem persists, please report it on the project's GitHub Issues page with your Windows version and graphics card model.

Note: FreeXmlToolkit picks a safe renderer automatically (software rendering on graphics adapters it does not recognise). You can force hardware or software rendering under Settings → Appearance → RENDERING; the change takes effect after a restart.

docs.title: Application Looks Blurry or Slow
docs.text: If the interface appears blurry or animations are slow, your system may be using software rendering instead of hardware acceleration. Updating your graphics drivers usually resolves this.

docs.title: A large file does not open or the app runs out of memory
docs.text: The editor keeps a document in memory several times over (text, highlighting, structured views). Raise the limit under Settings → Appearance → MEMORY (Automatic uses half of the installed memory) and restart the application. The Memory and large files section lists how large a file each limit allows. To look at, search or copy from a file of any size without raising the limit, open it in the Large File Viewer.

docs.title: Downloads fail behind a corporate proxy (e.g. HTTP 407)
docs.text: Configure the proxy under Settings → Network & Security → HTTP PROXY: System proxy (default, includes PAC/WPAD), Manual proxy or No proxy, hosts to reach directly, and proxy authentication (user and password, or the Windows account via NTLM/Kerberos). Test Connection checks an address with the values shown. Every connection of the application uses these settings - schema and catalog downloads, updates, FundsXML, telemetry, JSON Schema $refs, XProc and HTML previews. See Settings.

docs.title: Can I use FreeXmlToolkit offline?
docs.text: Yes. Editing, validation against local schemas, transformations, debugging and PDF output run locally. What goes online is optional or comes from your documents: the update check, the anonymous telemetry, the FundsXML extension, and schemas a document or import refers to by an http(s) URL that is neither cached nor mapped to a local file. Operation without internet lists every connection, how to switch it off and how to prepare schemas for an offline machine.

docs.title: My XML document is not bound to its schema
docs.text:
• Bind one by hand: click the No XSD indicator in the status bar or use Schema ▾ → Set XSD Schema… - see Binding an XSD Schema.
  • Documents without xsi:schemaLocation are bound through the Schema Library (namespace mappings and XML catalogs) - its troubleshooting section explains why a mapping may not match.

docs.title: Imported schemas are not found
docs.text: Imports and includes are resolved from local files, from the schema cache, via HTTP and through the Schema Library's catalogs. When a server is unreachable, check the proxy settings above; a stale download can be removed with Settings → Files & Cache → TEMP & CACHE → Clear Cache Folder (it is fetched again when needed).

docs.title: Are DTD and RELAX NG supported?
docs.text: Yes, for validation and IntelliSense: a document is checked against the DTD of its <!DOCTYPE> or the RELAX NG schema of its <?xml-model?> (XML syntax .rng and compact syntax .rnc), or against one you bind. There is no graphical editor or documentation generator for DTDs and RELAX NG schemas (those are for XSD). See Schema Support.

docs.title: Where are my settings stored?
docs.text: In ~/.freeXmlToolkit/FreeXmlToolkit.properties in your home folder, next to the cache and other application data. Settings → Reset to Defaults… restores the default values.

docs.title: Where are the log files?
docs.text: Settings → Files & Cache → LOG FILES → Open log folder opens the folder; the card also shows how many log files there are and how much space they use. Old logs are deleted automatically (by default after 14 days or above 100 MB).

docs.title: How do I switch off the anonymous usage statistics?
docs.text: Clear Send anonymous usage statistics and Send anonymous error reports under Settings → Privacy → USAGE STATISTICS and click Save Settings. Administrators can disable both centrally - see Privacy & Telemetry.

docs.title: How do I update?
docs.text: Help → Check for Updates… (on macOS in the application menu) looks for a newer version; the update check at startup can be switched off under Settings → Network & Security → UPDATES. Installations from Scoop or Homebrew are updated with the package manager - see Installation.

docs.title: Which version am I running, and what changed?
docs.text: Help → About FreeXmlToolkit shows the version. The What's New page lists the highlights of every release.

docs.title: Where did the XSD Editor / XSLT Viewer / … tabs go?
docs.text: The former per-tool tabs were replaced by the Unified Shell - see Where the former tabs went.

docs.title: Ctrl+Shift+F no longer formats my document
docs.text: Following the VS Code convention, Ctrl+Shift+F opens Find in Files; Format Document is now Shift+Alt+F. See Keyboard Shortcuts.

docs.title: Favorites System
docs.text: Save your frequently used files for quick access. The favorites system works across all editors in FreeXmlToolkit.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Favorites panel with its Add current and Manage… buttons, the search field, and favorites grouped by file type

The favorites system helps you quickly access the files you use most often. Save any file as a favorite and open it with one click from any editor.

docs.title: Quick Access
docs.text: Feature Description Works Everywhere Open favorites from the header star, the Explorer (star + FAVORITES tab) and File → Open Favorite File Recognition Automatically detects file types (XML, XSD, etc.) One-Click Loading Open files instantly

docs.title: Organization
docs.text: Feature Description Folders Move favorites into folders like "Project Files", "Templates", "Schemas" (context menu Move to folder) Easy Management Rename or remove favorites from the panel; the Manage… view offers smart collections and clean-up Mixed Files Store different file types in the same folder

docs.title: File Information
docs.text: Feature Description Custom Names Give favorites easy-to-remember names Descriptions Add notes about what each file is for File Icons Quickly see file types at a glance

docs.title: Grouped by Folder or File Type (Unified Shell)
docs.text:
The Favorites panel in the Unified Shell (star icon in the activity bar, or Ctrl+Shift+D) groups your favorites by folder as soon as at least one favorite has been moved into a folder; favorites without a folder are listed under Uncategorized at the end. While no folder is in use, the panel groups by file type instead - for example XML Document, JSON Document, XSD Schema, Schematron Rules, and XSLT Stylesheet. Each entry shows a colored type icon, so you can tell the file kinds apart at a glance. Click an entry to open it as an editor tab; the search field filters by name or path.

Keystore and trust store files (.jks, .p12, .pfx, .keystore) are recognized as their own Keystore type with a lock icon - they form their own group in the Favorites panel and feed the keystore star menus on the Signature page (see below).

docs.title: Star Menus in the Side Panels
docs.text:
Wherever a side panel asks you to pick a file, a star button next to the row's Change link opens a quick-select menu of your matching favorites - pick one to use it in a single click, without browsing the file system:

Panel Row Favorites Listed Validation XSD schema XSD favorites Validation Schematron rules Schematron favorites Validation JSON Schema (shown for JSON documents) JSON favorites Transform STYLESHEET / INPUT XSLT / XML favorites PDF / FOP XML input / XSL-FO stylesheet XML / XSLT favorites Sign & Encrypt Keystore (KEYSTORE section) Keystore favorites Sign & Encrypt Trust store (Expert Mode) Keystore favorites

The menu is rebuilt each time you open it, so newly added favorites appear immediately. When you use more than one favorites folder, the entries are grouped by folder as submenus. While you have no matching favorites, the star button is grayed out.

Picking a favorite from a star menu (or dropping a file on the same row) also loads the file into the editor: a Transform or PDF/FOP input becomes the active tab; a stylesheet, schema or Schematron opens behind the active tab, because those panels work on the active document and must not lose it. The same holds for every other way of picking a file on a page - file dialogs and recent menus included (see Every Picked File Opens in the Editor).

docs.title: Open Favorites From Anywhere
docs.text:
You do not need to switch to the Favorites activity to open a favorite:

  • Header star - the star next to ? in the header bar lists every favorite, in every activity and on the Settings / Schema Library / Signature pages.
  • Explorer - the star in the Explorer header opens the same menu, and the FAVORITES tab at the bottom of the Explorer (next to RECENT) lists all favorites; click one to open it.
  • File → Open Favorite in the menu bar.

These menus list all favorites regardless of type (grouped by folder once you use folders) and end with Add Active Document (Ctrl+D) and Manage Favorites….

docs.title: Adding Files to Favorites
docs.text:
1. Open a file (it must be saved to disk - unsaved buffers cannot be added)
  2. Press Ctrl+D or click Add current in the Favorites panel - the file is added immediately under its file name, without a dialog
  3. Optionally, right-click the new entry to give it a different name (Rename…) or to put it into a folder (Move to folder)

docs.title: Opening Favorites
docs.text:
1. Open the "Favorites" activity from the activity bar on the left (or press Ctrl+Shift+D)
  2. Browse the folder or file-type groups, or type in the search field
  3. Click any file to open it immediately

docs.title: Managing Favorites
docs.text:
Right-click an entry in the Favorites panel for its context menu: - Open - Open the file as an editor tab - Rename… - Change the display name - Move to folder - Put the favorite into an existing folder or a new one - Remove - Delete the favorite (the file itself is untouched)

Click Manage… for the full-size Favorites Manager view: it adds smart collections (recently used, most used) and a Clean up button that removes favorites whose files no longer exist.

docs.title: Organization Ideas
