docs.text: Strategy Description By Project Create a category for each project By Type Organize by file type ("Schemas", "Templates") By Frequency "Daily Use", "Archive"

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use descriptive names that make sense to you
  • Add descriptions for complex files
  • Clean up favorites regularly when files are moved or deleted

docs.title: Supported File Types
docs.text: Type Extension XML documents .xml JSON documents (incl. JSON Schemas) .json, .jsonc, .json5 XSD schemas .xsd Schematron rules .sch XSLT stylesheets .xsl, .xslt Keystores / trust stores .jks, .p12, .pfx, .keystore

docs.title: Auto-Populated Categories
docs.text:
Some optional features add their own files to your Favorites automatically:

Category Source FundsXML Examples Sample XML documents (and the examples folder) downloaded by the FundsXML Extensions feature FundsXML Schema The active FundsXML XSD schema FundsXML Schematron Schematron rule files downloaded by the FundsXML Extensions feature FundsXML XSLT XSLT stylesheets shipped with the FundsXML examples

These categories are created automatically: right after you enable the FundsXML feature (the content downloads in the background - no manual download step needed) and again on every application start, when they are re-registered from the on-disk cache.

docs.title: File Associations
docs.text:
FreeXmlToolkit can register itself as the default application for the file types it edits — XML, XSD, XSLT, Schematron and JSON — so that double-clicking a file in your file manager opens it directly in the toolkit.

Registration is always per user and requires no administrator rights on any platform.

docs.title: Registering from the app
docs.text:
1. Open Settings (Activity Bar → gear icon).
  2. Find the FILE ASSOCIATIONS card (group Files & Cache in the side panel).
  3. Tick the file types you want (XML, XSD Schema, XSLT Stylesheet, Schematron, JSON).
  4. Click Register.

To undo, select the types and click Unregister — FreeXmlToolkit restores the previously configured default application where it recorded one.

Note: The card is only active when you run the installed application. When the app is started from an IDE or a build directory there is no native launcher to register, and the card is disabled.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows does not allow any application to make itself the default silently — the actual default choice is protected by the operating system. FreeXmlToolkit therefore:

  1. Registers itself (ProgIds and application capabilities) under HKCU\Software\Classes — visible in every "Open with" menu, no admin rights needed.
  2. Opens the Windows Settings → Default apps page pre-filtered to FreeXmlToolkit, where you confirm the file types with one click.

Unregister removes all registry entries FreeXmlToolkit created.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
The default handler is set directly through Launch Services (the same mechanism as Finder's Get Info → Open with → Change All…) — silent and per user.

Unregister restores the previous default application where one was recorded. If no previous handler is known, use Finder's Change All… to pick another application — macOS offers no way to "clear" a default.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
FreeXmlToolkit writes a desktop entry to ~/.local/share/applications/ and sets the defaults via xdg-mime default (stored in ~/.config/mimeapps.list). Since Schematron files have no MIME type in the shared MIME database, a small per-user MIME definition (application/x-schematron+xml for *.sch / *.schematron) is installed as well.

Unregister restores the recorded previous defaults, or removes FreeXmlToolkit's entries from mimeapps.list.

docs.title: Installer registration
docs.text: The native installers (MSI/EXE, DMG/PKG, DEB/RPM) additionally declare the file types at install time, so FreeXmlToolkit appears in "Open with" menus right after installation. This does not make it the default — use the Settings card for that.

docs.title: Opening files while FreeXmlToolkit is running
docs.text:
FreeXmlToolkit runs as a single instance: if it is already open, a file opened via "Open with", a double-click or the command line opens as a new tab in the running window, which comes to the front — no second window or splash screen. On macOS, dropping files on the Dock icon works the same way.

To start an independent second instance anyway, set the Java option -Dfxt.multiInstance=true (for example via the environment variable JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Dfxt.multiInstance=true). Development runs (./gradlew run) are never single-instance.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Register also repairs: after moving or updating the installation, click Register again — it rewrites all entries with the current installation path.
  • Opening files from the command line works too: FreeXmlToolkit myfile.xml opens the file on startup (and in a running IDE session, ./gradlew run --args="myfile.xml").

docs.title: FundsXML Extensions
docs.text:
Optional integration with the FundsXML standard for the fund management industry. When enabled, FreeXmlToolkit automatically downloads and keeps up to date the official FundsXML schemas, sample documents, Schematron rules, and XPath/XQuery snippets - and uses them for quick validation of your own files.

This feature is off by default. Enable it only if you work with FundsXML documents.

The FundsXML integration is a built-in plugin: Settings → Extensions → PLUGINS can switch it off completely (no FundsXML activity, Help links, update check or hint), and administrators can do the same with plugin.fundsxml.enabled=false.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
FundsXML is an open XML standard used to exchange fund data between asset managers, fund administrators, depositaries, and regulators. The FundsXML community publishes:

  • Schemas (XSD) - the official FundsXML4.xsd and its include files
  • Examples - real-world sample XML documents
  • Schematron rules - additional business-rule checks beyond what XSD covers
  • Query snippets - useful XPath and XQuery expressions for common tasks

The FundsXML Extensions feature downloads all of this from the official GitHub repositories and integrates the content into FreeXmlToolkit so you can use it directly from the FundsXML side panel, the Welcome page, the Query Console, and Favorites.

Note: No FundsXML content is bundled with FreeXmlToolkit. Everything is fetched at runtime from the official GitHub repositories (fundsxml/schema, MIT License, and fundsxml/examples, Apache-2.0 License).

docs.title: Enabling the Feature
docs.text:
The feature is opt-in. Until you enable it, nothing in the application changes - apart from a one-time hint when you open a FundsXML document (see The FundsXML hint bar).

  1. Open Settings (the gear icon at the bottom of the activity bar).
  2. Select the Extensions group in the side panel (or type FundsXML into the settings search field) to reach the FUNDSXML card.
  3. Check Enable FundsXML extensions.
  4. Click Save Settings in the save bar at the bottom of the page.

Enabling the feature is all you need to do: the FundsXML content starts downloading automatically in the background, and a small toast notification tells you when it is ready. There is no separate download step.

Once enabled, the FundsXML integration appears in several places:

Where What appears Activity bar A new FundsXML activity with its own side panel Welcome page A FUNDSXML quick-access row with Open Example, Open Schema, and Browse Examples cards (shown as soon as content is cached) Query Console A FUNDSXML section in the Snippets menu with the community's example queries Help menu The FundsXML Website and FundsXML Schema Docs links

You can turn the feature off again at any time from the same Settings card. Disabling it hides these entries, but leaves the downloaded content on disk intact.

docs.title: Recognised documents: the FundsXML mark
docs.text: While the extension is on, a FundsXML document (root element FundsXML4, FundsXML …) shows a small green FundsXML mark in the status bar, next to the encoding. It tells you that the document was recognised and that the FundsXML data-quality checks run with every validation of it. A click opens the FundsXML panel. Other documents, or a FundsXML document while the extension is off, show no mark.

docs.title: The FundsXML hint bar
docs.text:
You do not have to know about the extension in advance. When you open a document whose root element is a FundsXML root (for example FundsXML4) while the extension is off, a hint bar appears above the editor:

This looks like a FundsXML document. The FundsXML extension adds its schemas, examples and quality checks.

  • Enable FundsXML extensions - does the same as checking the box on the FUNDSXML Settings card and saving: the FundsXML activity appears in the activity bar and the content is downloaded in the background (or, if it was downloaded before, the cached content is used right away).
  • Not now - closes the bar.

The hint is shown only once. If you dismiss it and change your mind later, enable the feature in Settings as described above.

docs.title: Downloading FundsXML Content
docs.text:
Downloads are fully automatic. Content is fetched in the background right after you enable the feature, and on every application start any missing content is downloaded again. When a background download finishes, a non-blocking toast notification appears - no dialogs interrupt your work.

You normally never need to trigger a download yourself. To force a manual refresh, open the FundsXML side panel and click Download / Update Content. The panel shows a progress bar with a stage description while a download is running - for manual and automatic background downloads alike.

Whenever content is downloaded (automatically or manually), the application will:

  • Download the latest schema release from fundsxml/schema (the official FundsXML4.xsd and its included files).
  • Download example documents, XSLT stylesheets, Schematron rule files, and XPath/XQuery snippets from fundsxml/examples.
  • Register the active XSD schema as a Favorite under the category FundsXML Schema (XSD type), so it shows up alongside your other schema favorites.
  • Register the examples folder as a Favorite under FundsXML Examples, plus the most compact sample XMLs (up to 10) as individual file favorites for one-click access.
  • Register each XSLT stylesheet found in the examples as an XSLT Favorite under FundsXML XSLT.
  • Register the Schematron files as Favorites under the category FundsXML Schematron.
  • Register the most compact sample XMLs as new-document templates under the FundsXML category, so you can start a fresh document from a real sample via the toolbar's New button (Ctrl+N) → Template list.
  • Seed the XPath/XQuery snippets into your Saved Queries, tagged fundsxml - they show up in the Query Console's Snippets menu under a FUNDSXML section (for example fund-summary, top-holdings, look-through, aggregate-by-assettype).
  • Select the newly downloaded schema version as the active version.
  • Make a compact starter sample available from the Welcome page's Open Example card, so you can immediately try Validate active document in the FundsXML panel.

Tip

Independently of this downloaded content, your FreeXmlToolkit installation itself ships FundsXML4-based query collections in its examples folder: 32 XPath 3.1 examples (examples/xpath/) and 17 XQuery 3.1 scripts (examples/xquery/), including a reporting series that produces CSV, ASCII tables/charts, Markdown and JSON output. Each folder has a README.md describing every example.

Existing versions are kept on disk - downloads are additive, not replacements. Downloads are idempotent — favorites, snippets, and templates that already exist are not duplicated. On every application start, favorites and query snippets are also re-registered from the on-disk cache, so they stay available even without a network connection.

docs.title: Choosing an Active Schema Version
docs.text:
If you have downloaded more than one version of the FundsXML schema, you can switch between them.

Open the FundsXML side panel and pick the version from the Active version drop-down in the MANAGEMENT section.

The active version is the schema used by the Quick-validate action (see below) and by the Open Schema in Editor button. Switching does not delete any files - you can change versions back and forth freely.

docs.title: Quick-Validate Your XML
docs.text:
The fastest way to check an XML file against the FundsXML schema:

  1. Open your XML document in the editor.
  2. Click Validate active document in the FundsXML side panel (FundsXML validation lives only there).
  3. If the document is valid, you get a confirmation message.
  4. If there are errors, they are listed line-by-line in an alert dialog so you can locate and fix each one.

The validation uses whichever FundsXML schema version is currently marked as active.

Tip: Use the Schematron Favorites under FundsXML Schematron to run additional business-rule checks. Open a Schematron file from Favorites, then validate your XML against it as you would with any other Schematron file.

docs.title: Data-Quality Checks
docs.text:
Run Data Quality Checks in the FundsXML side panel checks the active FundsXML document with 17 XQuery checks and opens a report (passed / findings / not run, with every finding):

Check What it looks at Control data complete UniqueDocumentID, DocumentGenerated, ContentDate, data supplier name Content date not in the future ControlData/ContentDate ISIN / LEI check digits every ISIN (ISO 6166) and LEI (ISO 17442) Currency codes currency elements and ccy attributes are ISO 4217 codes Position weights add up to 100 % TotalPercentage of the positions per date (± 0.5), for each node with its own portfolios: fund, subfund, segment and share class — a share-class portfolio is weighted against its share class, not the fund Positions vs. net asset value market values against the TotalNetAssetValue of the same node and date, in that node's currency (± 1 %) No duplicate positions one UniqueID per portfolio Positions have master data / unused master data positions without an Asset, assets nobody refers to No negative values of securities equities, bonds, fund shares, certificates, warrants Securities have an identifier the same positions without Identifiers Portfolio dates have a net asset value each Portfolio/NavDate has a TotalAssetValue of the same node (fund, share class …) Share classes add up to the fund share class net asset values against the fund's (± 0.5 %) Price × shares = share class value NavPrice × SharesOutstanding against the share class's net asset value (± 1 %) Transactions settle after entry ValutaDate not before EntryDate No matured instruments held maturity dates before the content date of held assets

The checks also run with every validation of a FundsXML document while the extension is on; their findings appear as warnings with the source FundsXML DQ. Each finding carries the line of the element it is about (the position, the ISIN, the transaction …): a click in the PROBLEMS pane shows it in the current view — Text, Tree or the Graphic grid, where the row or table cell is highlighted. In the Query Console they are available as snippets (FUNDSXML section) together with analysis queries — all funds, top 10 positions, exposure by asset type and by currency, positions over 5 %, positions without ISIN, derivatives, share class prices — so each can be run, adapted and saved on its own. The checks were developed against the documents of the official fundsxml/examples repository.

docs.title: Grid Formulas and Filters
docs.text:
Add Grid Formulas & Filters in the side panel opens a copy of the active document in the Grid view with named formulas and saved filters added:

Element Formulas Saved filter (off until clicked) root Funds, Positions, Assets – Fund Net asset value, Positions value, Weights %, Share classes – Positions Count, Value (per currency), Weight %, Largest, Without ISIN positions over 5 % AssetMasterData Assets, By asset type, By country assets without ISIN Transactions Count, Market value (per currency), By kind transactions settling before their entry ShareClasses Share classes, Net asset value (per currency) –

Formulas show their live result as the first rows of their element; a saved filter appears as a grey funnel line and filters the rows when you click it. Running the action again adds nothing twice. The stylesheet behind it, plugins/fundsxml/fundsxml-grid-setup.xsl, can be used in the Transform panel on any FundsXML file as well. For a signed document you are asked first: the copy no longer matches the signature.

docs.title: The FundsXML Side Panel
docs.text:
Select the FundsXML activity in the activity bar to open its side panel.

It has three sections:

Section What you can do MANAGEMENT Pick the Active version and force a manual Download / Update Content. A progress bar with stage text at the bottom of the panel tracks running downloads - including automatic background downloads. VALIDATE Validate active document - check the open XML against the active FundsXML schema. DOCS & RESOURCES Open the schema and browse the downloaded content (see below).

The DOCS & RESOURCES buttons:

Button What it does Open Schema in Editor Opens the active version's FundsXML4.xsd directly as an editor tab - explore it in the Text view or as a diagram in the Graphic view Generate Documentation… Generates browsable HTML documentation for the active schema into ~/.freeXmlToolkit/fundsxml/docs/<version>/ Open Examples Folder The folder with downloaded sample XML documents Open Schema Folder The folder containing the active schema and its include files Open Schematron Folder The folder with downloaded .sch rule files Open Online Docs Opens https://fundsxml.org/ in your default browser

You can also reach the downloaded files directly through Favorites: example documents under FundsXML Examples, the active schema under FundsXML Schema, Schematron rules under FundsXML Schematron, and stylesheets under FundsXML XSLT (handy in the Transform panel's star menus).

docs.title: Welcome Page Quick Access
docs.text:
When the feature is enabled and content is cached, the Welcome/Dashboard page shows a FUNDSXML quick-access row with three cards:

  • Open Example - opens a compact starter sample document.
  • Open Schema - opens FundsXML4.xsd in the editor.
  • Browse Examples - opens the cached examples folder in your file manager.

The row appears automatically; if a background download is still running, it shows up live the moment the download finishes.

docs.title: Where the Files Are Stored
docs.text:
All FundsXML content is stored under your user home directory:

~/.freeXmlToolkit/fundsxml/
├── schema/
│   └── <version>/
│       ├── FundsXML4.xsd
│       └── include_files/
├── examples/        (downloaded XML sample documents)
├── schematron/      (downloaded .sch rule files)
├── queries/         (downloaded XPath/XQuery snippets)
└── metadata.json    (tracks installed versions and timestamps)

You can have multiple schema versions installed side by side; each lives in its own schema/<version>/ subfolder.

On Windows the path is typically C:\Users\<you>\.freeXmlToolkit\fundsxml\. On macOS and Linux it is /Users/<you>/.freeXmlToolkit/fundsxml/ or /home/<you>/.freeXmlToolkit/fundsxml/.

docs.title: Automatic Update Checks
docs.text:
Updates are installed automatically instead of showing a dialog.

By default, FreeXmlToolkit checks once per day whether a newer FundsXML schema release is available on GitHub. If a new release is found, it is downloaded and installed automatically in the background - a toast notification confirms when the new content is in place, and the new version becomes the active one. There is no update dialog to answer.

The check is throttled to at most once every 24 hours and runs quietly in the background. Missing content (for example after clearing the cache folder) is also re-downloaded automatically on the next application start. To turn the daily check off, set fundsxml.update.check.enabled=false in your ~/.freeXmlToolkit/FreeXmlToolkit.properties file.

docs.title: Contributing Snippets Upstream
docs.text:
The XPath/XQuery snippets in the queries/ folder follow a simple convention so the community can grow them.

If a queries/index.json manifest is present, it tells FreeXmlToolkit how to label and tag each snippet:

{
  "snippets": [
    {
      "file": "list-portfolios.xq",
      "name": "List all Portfolio IDs",
      "type": "xquery",
      "description": "Returns the unique identifier of every Portfolio in the document.",
      "tags": ["fundsxml", "portfolio"]
    },
    {
      "file": "total-nav.xpath",
      "name": "Total Net Asset Value",
      "type": "xpath",
      "description": "Sum of all NAV values across funds.",
      "tags": ["fundsxml", "nav"]
    }
  ]
}

Field reference:

Field Description file Path of the snippet file relative to the queries/ folder name Short title shown in the Saved Queries list type Either xpath or xquery description Human-readable explanation (optional but recommended) tags List of tags used for filtering; include fundsxml for FundsXML snippets

If no index.json is present, snippets are still loaded - file names are used as titles and the snippet type is inferred from the file extension.

To propose a snippet for everyone, submit a pull request to the fundsxml/examples repository.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text:
The feature's options and where to find them:

Setting Where Description Default Enable FundsXML extensions Settings page, FUNDSXML card Master switch; enabling it starts the initial background download Off Active version FundsXML side panel Which downloaded schema version is used for Quick-validate and Open Schema in Editor Latest installed Download / Update Content FundsXML side panel Force a manual refresh from GitHub - Daily update check fundsxml.update.check.enabled property Once-per-day background check that installs newer schema releases automatically On

These preferences are stored in ~/.freeXmlToolkit/FreeXmlToolkit.properties in your user home directory.

docs.title: A download fails
docs.text:
• Check your internet connection.
  • If you are behind a corporate proxy, configure proxy settings in the HTTP PROXY card of Settings.
  • Verify that github.com is reachable from your network.
  • Retry with Download / Update Content in the FundsXML side panel; the panel's status line shows the reason for the failure.

docs.title: Quick-validate reports "No active schema"
docs.text: The automatic background download has not finished yet (or it failed - for example without a network connection). Watch the progress bar in the FundsXML side panel and wait for the completion toast, or click Download / Update Content there to retry.

docs.title: The FundsXML activity disappeared
docs.text: The feature was disabled. Re-enable it under Settings → Extensions → FUNDSXML → Enable FundsXML extensions. Your downloaded content is still on disk and will reappear immediately.

docs.title: I want to remove everything
docs.text:
1. Disable the feature in Settings (otherwise the content is re-downloaded automatically on the next start).
  2. Delete the folder ~/.freeXmlToolkit/fundsxml/.
  3. Optionally remove the Favorites entries under FundsXML Examples, FundsXML Schema, FundsXML Schematron, and FundsXML XSLT.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text:
The FundsXML content downloaded by this feature is published by the FundsXML community:

  • Schemas (fundsxml/schema): MIT License
  • Examples, Schematron, Queries (fundsxml/examples): Apache License 2.0

FreeXmlToolkit itself does not bundle any of this content - it is fetched from the public GitHub repositories only after you enable the feature.

docs.title: Grid View
docs.text:
The Graphic view of an XML or JSON document is an editable grid: nested blocks for containers, repeating elements as tables, inline editing, drag & drop and search. Switch to it with the Graphic button of the view switch in the editor toolbar.

The grid can be exported as PNG, SVG or PDF, or copied as an image, with all its rows as currently expanded (File → Export View…, Edit → Copy View as Image, or the grid's context menu) - see Exporting a Graphical View.

docs.title: The Grid (Graphic view for XML)
docs.text:
When an XML-instance document (XML, XSLT, or Schematron) is in the Graphic view, the editor shows the editable grid, laid out as follows:

  • A header strip at the top reads "Grid view · nested · repeating elements as embedded grids" and offers the zoom pill (− 100% +), Optimal widths, the Wrap toggle, Expand all / Collapse all, and a ⋯ menu with the cell-height limit. In a narrow editor column the strip first drops its subtitle and shows the tool buttons as icons only (hover for their names); narrower still, only the title icon, the zoom pill and ⋯ remain, and Optimal widths, Wrap, Expand all / Collapse all and the entry helpers toggle become entries of the ⋯ menu, so every action stays reachable.
  • Nested containers. Every element is a row with a name cell (expand arrow, type icon, bold name) and, to its right, either its value cell or the block of its children. A child block is docked at the parent's value column, so the structure reads as nested boxes; an expanded container's name cell spans its whole child block. Each block has its own name-column width (the widest name in it).
  • Type icons: <> element, = attribute, Abc text, [ ] CDATA, <! comment, <? processing instruction. Colours come from the application theme (light/dark).
  • Attributes always show as = rows directly beneath their element - also while the element itself is collapsed.
  • Collapsed containers show a grey one-line preview of their content (the markup without whitespace, cut off with "…"); hovering the preview shows a longer excerpt as a tooltip.
  • Counts. A container's name is followed by its child count (n); a repeating group shows the number of its members and a small table glyph.
  • Nothing is cut off. Values take the width their content needs; long values wrap onto further lines (the row grows). Very wide content is reached with the horizontal scrollbar (Shift+wheel).
  • Zoom the whole grid - text, rows, icons and embedded tables - with Ctrl+mouse wheel, Ctrl + / Ctrl − (10 % steps, 50-300 %) or the −/+ buttons; Ctrl 0 or a click on the percentage resets to 100 %. The zoom factor is remembered across files, XML and JSON grids and restarts.
  • Repeating elements (two or more siblings with the same name) are rendered as an embedded table beside the group's name cell: one row per element (numbered in the first column), one column per attribute (=) and child element (<>). Click the small arrow at the right of a column header to sort the group (also: Sort Column in the context menu); numbers, dates and text are recognised, and one Undo restores the order. A table of 20,000 rows or more is sorted in the background: the grid stays usable (wait cursor), and an edit made meanwhile makes the sort start again from the new state. Cells with nested structure expand inline. Right-click a cell that is an element of its own (e.g. Identifiers of an Asset row): the node actions of the context menu (Add Child Element / Attribute, Rename, Copy, Delete, Move, …) act on that element; whole-row actions are in the Table submenu (Insert Row Before/After, Append Row, Delete Row).
  • Every node looks like a root node, at any depth. An opened table cell shows its content as a grid of its own: expandable rows, blocks and - for repeating children - a table again (or numbered rows <1>, <2>, … after a click on the table glyph), whose cells open the same way, however deep tables and rows are nested. A column with several children of one name (e.g. four Positions of a Waehrung) is one cell (4 × <Position>) holding them all. Rows inside cells are selected, edited (double-click), expanded and navigated with the arrow keys like any other row (Left at the top of a cell's grid returns to the cell); tables inside cells sort, flip and edit like the outer ones. Hover, the name-column separators of blocks, column handles and column drags of tables, Optimal widths and drag & drop of rows (with auto-scroll at the top and bottom edge) work at every depth too. Open cells, expanded rows, dragged widths and table/flip choices at every depth survive edits.
  • Open whole rows and columns. Click a row number to select the whole row, click a column header (its name, not the arrow) to select the whole column; Shift+click extends to more rows or columns. Then press + to open the nested cells of the selection one level, and again for the next level inside them; − closes the deepest open level first, then the cells. The same entries are in the Table submenu (Expand / Collapse Selected Cells). Without a table selection, + / − open and close the selected grid rows one level. Open cells stay open after edits.
  • Table or rows. The small table glyph after the group's name (or the context menu's Display as Table) switches the group between the table and the standard display, where every member is its own row numbered <1>, <2>, … The choice is kept per group while the document is open.
  • Flip Rows/Columns. The corner cell of a table (or the context menu entry) transposes it: the columns become rows and the numbered members become columns - handy for wide tables with few rows. Sorting, editing and the inline sub-trees keep working.
  • Whole rows and columns. Right-click inside a table for the Table submenu: Insert Row Before / After and Append Row add a member with every column present but empty; Insert Column Before / After… adds an attribute (type @name) or a child element (name) to every member; Rename Column… (also: double-click a column header) renames it in every member. Each of these is one undo step. Typing into an empty cell whose member lacks that child element creates the element. Drag a column header onto another header to move that column - a blue line shows where it lands; the child element (or attribute) moves in every member, one undo step. Attributes move only among attributes.
  • Cell colours. Settings → Editor → GRID TABLE COLOURS sets your own colours for table headers, missing cells, the selection and the focus frame - separately for the light and the dark theme (switch the theme to set the other one). Open grids repaint at once; switching the option off returns to the theme colours.
  • Spreadsheet exchange. Click a table cell to select it, Shift+click another cell (or a row number) to select a range, Ctrl+A selects the whole table. Ctrl+C copies the selection as tab-separated text (the whole table with a header line); the context menu offers Copy Table as Tab-separated Text. Values arrive in the spreadsheet unchanged and each in its own cell, even when they contain tabs, line breaks or quotes (the clipboard holds quoted text plus an HTML table; values such as 00123 stay text). Copy a range in Excel or LibreOffice, select a table cell and press Ctrl+V: the values fill the table from that cell to the right and down, overwriting existing cells; extra rows become new elements. One undo step.
  • Column widths. Name columns and table columns size themselves to their content. Drag the hairline between a name column and its values (or a column separator in a table's header row) to resize it - text re-wraps to the new width - and double-click the line to return to automatic sizing. Each nested block has its own name-column width. Optimal widths in the header resets every column at once. Dragged widths survive edits and undo.
  • Wrap (header toggle, remembered across restarts) switches word wrap off: every value stays on one line and the grid grows to the right instead. The ⋯ menu limits the cell height to 3, 6 or 12 lines (longer values end with "…"), also remembered.
  • Keyboard navigation works as soon as the view opens (no click needed): ↑/↓ walk the rows, → expands a collapsed element, ← collapses it (or jumps to the parent), Space or Enter toggles a container (on a leaf row Enter starts renaming it), Home/End jump to the first/last row, F2 renames, and the usual Ctrl+C/X/V, Ctrl+D (duplicate) and Delete act on the selected node.
  • Several rows at once. Ctrl+click adds or removes a row from the selection, Shift+click selects every sibling between the selected row and the clicked one. Shift+click on the arrow of a selected row expands or collapses all selected rows.
  • Expand Fully (Ctrl+Shift++) opens the selected container with everything below it; Collapse Unselected (Ctrl+Shift+−) folds every container except the path to the selection. Both, plus Expand All / Collapse All, are in the context menu. The expanded state and the selection survive edits, undo and sorting (rows are tracked by their XPath).
  • Editing every node kind. Double-click a value to edit it - with a bound schema the editor follows the declared type: a dropdown for enumerations (elements and attributes, in tree rows, table columns and opened cells), date pickers, number spinners, length/pattern checks - also comments, CDATA sections and processing instructions; double-click the name of an attribute or a processing instruction to rename it. Enter or a click anywhere else keeps the new value, Esc discards it. A context menu closes as soon as you click somewhere else. Click the type icon of a row (or press Ctrl+Alt+T) to change the node's type - element, attribute, text, CDATA, comment or processing instruction; name and value are kept, attributes move into their element's attribute list. Containers with child elements keep their type. Wrap in Element… (Ctrl+Alt+W, context menu) puts a new parent element around the selected node. Edit as Raw Text… (Ctrl+Alt+R) opens the selected element's content as markup (entities unresolved) and parses it back; not well-formed markup is reported and the editor reopens. All of these are undoable.
  • Sibling groups for very large files (⋯ menu → Sibling groups: 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 nodes, remembered): an element with more children than that shows them in collapsed groups such as record <1001..2000>; opening a group closes the other groups of the same element.
  • Large files (from 8 MB of text). Grid edits are not written into the text after every change: the text follows when you switch to the Text view, save, validate or transform. While it is written back, a loading indicator shows and the text is read-only for a moment.
  • Validation markers. After a validation (Validation panel), rows whose element has a problem show a red ! at the end of the name cell and a red value; hover the row for the message. Problems inside a repeating group mark the member's row number. The markers clear on the next grid edit and come back with the next validation. Selecting a problem in the PROBLEMS panel keeps the grid open and reveals it: the row or table cell is selected, opened on the way and briefly highlighted.
  • Split view. The header's ⋯ menu splits the grid top / bottom or side by side into two views of the same document; each scrolls, expands and selects on its own, and an edit in one appears in the other at once. Single view closes the second one.
  • Entry helpers. The header's panel button (right of Collapse all) opens the entry helpers beside the grid. They need an XSD bound to the document and follow the selected row. Siblings lists the attributes and elements the schema allows next to the selected node, Children lists those allowed inside the selected element, and Values lists the enumeration values of the selected element or attribute. Entries that are already there and cannot occur again are greyed out. Required ones (use="required", minOccurs ≥ 1 outside an optional or choice group) carry a red !. A double-click inserts:
  • Siblings: after the selected node; the buttons insert before it or append at the end.
  • Children: as the last child of the selected element. An attribute starts with its schema default.
  • Values: sets the value.

Every insertion is one undo step. The panel stays open or closed across sessions. - Scroll header. While you scroll through a long element, a bar at the top shows the path of containers you are inside (root › section › body); click one to select it and scroll back to its start. - Drag & drop. Drag a node by its name cell: drop it on the upper or lower third of another name cell to place it before / after that node, on the middle (or anywhere in an expanded element's cell) to append it as a child. A blue line or frame shows the target; hold Ctrl to copy instead of move. Text dragged in from other applications replaces a value when dropped on a value cell; dropped on a name cell, an XML fragment becomes new nodes and plain text a text node. A node is never dropped into its own subtree; every drop is one undo step. - Filters. Right-click an element → Filter… and enter an XQuery 3.1 expression evaluated with that element as context, e.g. Month[number(Min) > 10]: below the element only the matching nodes (with their ancestors and subtrees) stay visible, repeating groups shrink to their matching members. A blue funnel line under the element shows the expression - click the funnel to switch the filter off and on, double-click the line to edit it. To remove a filter, right-click its funnel line (or the element / the table cell it was set on) → Remove Filter; Remove All Filters clears every filter of the view. Filter to Focus filters the root down to the selected node - on a row of an embedded table, the table keeps only that row. Right-clicked inside a table, Filter… filters the element that holds the table (on a group row too). On a cell with nested content (e.g. 22 × <Datenpunkt>) it filters that cell's content only: the cell opens and the filter goes to its record, every other node stays complete. Inside an opened cell the target is the cell's record: in the Datenpunkt table of a PK.006… row, Filter… with Datenpunkt[starts-with(Wert_C0010PK, 'AT')] leaves only those Datenpunkte in that cell; the funnel line is the cell's first row and the record's formulas still sum all of its data. A filter higher up reduces the opened cells below it as well, e.g. on the root */Datenpunkt[starts-with(Wert_C0010PK, 'AT')] for every record at once. Filters only change the display; an invalid expression is reported and filters nothing. A filter lives while the document is open unless you save it: right-click it → Save Filter in Document stores it in the file as <?fxt-filter expression="…"?> in the filtered element (one undoable edit; its funnel line then starts with saved ·). A saved filter always comes back switched off when the file is opened, so nobody sees a filtered grid without knowing it: the grey funnel line shows it, and a click on the funnel or right-click → Filter Active switches it on. Editing a saved filter updates the file; Remove Filter / Remove All Filters also remove it from the file, unticking Save Filter in Document only from the file. A filter on an element with more than 20,000 nodes below it is evaluated in the background: its funnel line ends with (evaluating…) and the grid stays usable. Until the result is in, the grid keeps the filter's previous result (after an edit) or shows all rows (when it is new), then filters once the result arrives.

  • Formulas. Right-click an element → Add Formula…: a name and an XQuery 3.1 expression evaluated with that element as context (e.g. avg(Month/Min)). The formula row (icon ƒ) shows the expression and, below it, the live result - or the error in red; double-click the expression or the name to edit it. Formula rows are listed first under their element, above its tables and other children (in the file they stay where they are). A new formula is selected and its element expanded. Right-clicked inside a table, the formula goes to the element that holds the table (e.g. avg(Month/Min) on the parent of the Month rows), since a table cell cannot show it. When that element is itself a row of an outer table, its formulas are listed first in its opened cell — in the cell of the group the expression names (sum(Datenpunkt/Wert) → the Datenpunkt cell), otherwise in its first cell. An element can hold several named formulas, e.g. one sum per numeric column; format-number(sum(Datenpunkt/Wert ! xs:decimal(.)), '#,##0.00') gives an exact sum with two decimals and thousands separators (12,005,649.85). The German number format is predeclared as de: format-number(…, '#.##0,00', 'de') gives 12.005.649,85. Formulas are saved in the file as <?fxt-formula name="…" expression="…"?> instructions. Formulas and filters see only their own element and what is inside it — not the rest of the document: //Position in a formula on AssetMasterData finds nothing. Put the formula on a common ancestor instead (e.g. the root). A formula over more than 20,000 nodes is computed in the background: it shows … until its result arrives, and is computed again only after the data changed. Store Formula Result in Document also writes the result into an element named after the formula, right after it; Recalculate Stored Formula Results refreshes all of them in one undo step.

  • Search (Ctrl+F) finds names and values in the rows and in the cells of embedded tables, including the content of cells that are still closed (nested elements, attributes such as ccy="EUR") at any depth; a hit opens the cells and expands what hides it, then selects it. Enter / Shift+Enter walk through all hits.
  • Copy XPath / Copy Node: the grid's context menu offers Copy XPath (Ctrl+Alt+X), Copy Cell Content (Ctrl+Shift+C) and Copy Node (XML) (Ctrl+Alt+C); all three shortcuts also work directly on the selected node. Ctrl+Shift+X toggles the Query Console everywhere, including while the grid has focus.
  • Go to Definition: right-click an element → Go to Definition opens the bound XSD in the Graphic view, expanded along the element's path, with the card of its declaration selected - see Go to Definition. The entry is disabled while no schema is bound.

docs.title: The Grid (Graphic view for JSON)
docs.text:
JSON documents (.json, .jsonc, .json5) get the same grid in the Graphic view - same header strip, same rows, same keyboard shortcuts and context menu - so a JSON file looks and feels exactly like an XML file in the grid:

  • The root value is the $ row; object properties and array items ([0], [1], …) are the rows beneath it. Objects and arrays are collapsible containers showing their child count; scalar properties show as key = value rows.
  • Every row carries a type glyph in its own colour: {} object, [] array, " string, # number, T/F boolean and ∅ null. Strings are shown quoted (= "Alice") - like XML leaf values - so "42" and 42 are never confused.
  • Arrays of objects are rendered as embedded grids (a table with one column per key, merged across all items), exactly like repeating elements in XML. The arrow in a column header sorts the array (numbers, dates and strings are recognised), nested objects expand inline; a click on the header's name selects the column, + / − open and close its nested objects level by level, as in XML.
  • Inline editing keeps the value's type: double-click a number and type a number (anything else is rejected with a hint and the editor stays open), booleans toggle between true/false, null stays null unless you type text. Double-click a key to rename it (duplicate keys are refused).
  • The context menu mirrors the XML one: Add (Property / Array Item / Sibling Before / After), Rename Key (F2), Duplicate (Ctrl+D), Copy / Cut / Paste as Sibling / Paste as Child, Copy Cell Content, Copy JSONPath (Ctrl+Alt+X - e.g. $.items[1].name), Copy Node (JSON) (Ctrl+Alt+C), Change Type (String / Number / Boolean / Null / Object / Array), Move Up / Down (Alt+↑/↓), Expand Fully / Collapse Unselected, Display as Table, Flip Rows/Columns, Copy Table as Tab-separated Text, Expand All / Collapse All, Sort Column and Delete. Copy Cell Content is Ctrl+Shift+C, as in the XML grid.
  • All edits go through the document's undo history (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) and are written back into the text - the Text, Tree and Graphic views share one model, and the Properties inspector edits keys and values from any of them.
  • Same layout and controls as the XML grid. Objects and arrays are nested blocks with one-line previews when collapsed; the header strip offers the zoom pill, Optimal widths, Wrap, Expand all / Collapse all and the ⋯ menu (cell-height limit, sibling groups); name and table columns can be dragged to a new width (double-click to auto-fit). Expand Fully (Ctrl+Shift++) and Collapse Unselected (Ctrl+Shift+−), Display as Table / Flip Rows/Columns for arrays of objects, the scroll header and the search in table cells all work as described above. Table cells can be selected and copied as tab-separated text (Ctrl+C or Copy Table as Tab-separated Text); Ctrl+V overwrites existing cells only. The zoom factor is shared with the XML grid.
  • Change a value's type by clicking its type glyph (or Ctrl+Alt+T on the selected row): a popup lists the other types. Number ↔ String ↔ Boolean ↔ Null convert the value ("42" → 42); Object and Array start empty. One undo step.
  • Drag & drop: drag a row by its name cell onto another row - the upper part of the name cell inserts before it, the lower part after it, the middle of an object or array into it; hold Ctrl to copy instead of move. A property moved into another object keeps its key (made unique with _copy if it is taken); an item moved into an object gets the key item. JSON text dragged in from another application becomes a new value (an object dropped into an object adds its properties), plain text a string; dropped on a value cell it replaces the value. A node can never be dropped into itself.
  • Table submenu (right-click a cell of an array-of-objects table): Insert Row Before / After, Append Row (a new object with every column as an empty string), Insert Column Before / After… (the key in every object, next to the clicked column) and Rename Column… (also a double-click on the column header; refused as a whole when an object already uses the new key). Each is one undo step.
  • XML only: Wrap in Element, Edit as Raw Text, filters, formulas and validation markers.

Comments and JSON5 syntax are not preserved

The grid edits the parsed model. Comments (JSONC) and JSON5 syntax (unquoted keys, single quotes, trailing commas) are not part of it, so the first grid edit rewrites the file as standard JSON. The grid shows a warning the first time it opens such a file; if you need to keep the comments, edit in the Text view instead.

docs.title: Industry Plugins
docs.text:
FreeXmlToolkit ships optional plugins for industry standards. Each one has its own page that explains its functions in detail:

Plugin For Page ISO 20022 Payments (SEPA) pain, pacs and camt payment messages; control sums and the EPC SEPA rules ISO 20022 Payments ebInterface Austrian XML e-invoices 4.1–6.1; line, tax and total calculations ebInterface FinDatEx Templates EMT, EET, EPT and TPT (V7/V8) files as CSV or Excel FinDatEx Templates XBRL (with Arelle) XBRL instances and inline XBRL reports, validated with Arelle XBRL

The FundsXML extension is a plugin as well, with its own page.

docs.title: Switching them on
docs.text: The industry plugins are off by default: switch them on in Settings → Extensions → PLUGINS and restart. Administrators can keep a plugin off for everyone with plugin.<id>.enabled=false (iso20022, ebinterface, findatex, xbrl), see Administration.

docs.title: What every industry plugin adds
docs.text:
• an activity in the Activity Bar with a side panel:
    • ABOUT — what the plugin checks;
    • ACTIVE DOCUMENT — what the open document is (message type, invoice number, template, number of facts …), updated when you switch tabs;
    • Check Active Document — runs the plugin's checks; the first ten problems are shown, Show All Problems opens the full list;
    • the plugin's own actions (sample documents, new template files, Excel import, Arelle command);
    • CHECK AN IDENTIFIER — checks a pasted IBAN (ISO 13616: country length and check digits), BIC (ISO 9362), LEI (ISO 17442), ISIN (ISO 6166) or Austrian VAT id (UID), depending on the plugin;
  • checks that run with every validation (Validation panel, F8, fxt-cli validate) and appear with the plugin's name as source — ISO 20022 and ebInterface; FinDatEx and XBRL files are checked from their side panel;
  • where the standard has official XML Schemas, Schema Library entries (source Plugin), so documents get their schema bound automatically. Remote schemas are downloaded once and cached.
Schemas Checks with every validation Sample / new documents Identifier checker ISO 20022 19 message versions yes SEPA credit transfer, SEPA direct debit IBAN, BIC, LEI ebInterface versions 4.1–6.1 yes ebInterface 6.1 invoice UID, IBAN, BIC FinDatEx — (field definitions bundled) no, side panel new EMT / EET / EPT / TPT files, Excel import ISIN, LEI XBRL taxonomies via Arelle no, side panel — —

docs.title: Properties Inspector
docs.text:
Property editing works in all views - for XML files in Text, Tree, and Graphic, and for XSD files in the Text view as well as the Tree and Graphic views (see XSD Files below). For JSON files the inspector edits keys and values from the Tree and Graphic views (see JSON Files below).

The inspector is not fixed-width: drag the divider line between the editor and the inspector to make it wider (handy for long XPaths, attribute values, or documentation). The width is remembered across restarts - see Resizing and collapsing the side panels.

The Properties inspector for an XML element with a bound schema: node header with validation pill, NODE & XPATH, schema facts, and documentation with example values and valid children.

While nothing is selected, the inspector shows a short hint instead of empty sections: "Open a document to see the properties of its nodes here." when no document is open, and "Select a node in the Tree or Graphic view to see and edit its properties." (or, in the Text view, a hint to place the caret on an element) when no node is selected.

docs.title: Layout of the inspector
docs.text:
From top to bottom:

  • Top bar - the title PROPERTIES, a star button and a ⋮ menu.
  • The star adds the active file to Favorites (or removes it, when it is already a favorite). It is greyed out for a document that has never been saved.
  • The ⋮ menu offers Copy XPath, Copy Node (XML), Expand All Sections and Collapse All Sections (the two copy actions are also buttons in NODE & XPATH).
  • Node header - an icon for the kind of node, the node's name, a subtitle such as Element · xs:string (kind · type), and the validation pill: Valid, the number of errors, or Well-formed · no schema bound. Click the name to rename the node in place (only for nodes that have a name).
  • Sections - collapsible sections with a full-width title bar. Each row shows the property name on the left and its value on the right.

Editing in place: editable values (type, minOccurs/maxOccurs, use, form, fixed, default, …) look like plain text until you point at them or click them - then the field frame, the drop-down arrow or the spinner buttons appear. Values without that hover effect are read-only.

The sections appear in this order. A section is shown only when it has content for the selected node - empty sections are left out:

Section Content NODE & XPATH Kind, Namespace, Depth (the nesting level; the root element is 0), Position Ln x · Col y (Text view only), and the XPath in a code box with the Copy XPath and Copy Node (XML) buttons NAMESPACE Edit the element's namespace prefix and URI (expanded by default) TYPE & FACETS Type, Base type, Derivation (restriction / extension / list / union) and the list of facets; for an XML element with a bound schema it starts with the declaration box (see Editing the bound schema from the XML document) CARDINALITY & USE minOccurs / maxOccurs, Use, and Order - the node's position in its parent compositor, e.g. 3 of 3 · sequence VALUE & ATTRIBUTES The element text and the list of attributes CONTENT / PROCESSING INSTRUCTION / XML DECLARATION The text of comments, CDATA sections, processing instructions and the XML declaration DOCUMENTATION & REFS Documentation, value check, example values, valid children and USED IN (see below) ADVANCED, SCHEMA, CONSTRAINTS Further schema-node properties (fixed/default, nillable, form, final, appinfo, identity constraints, assertions, …)

The Namespace row in NODE & XPATH shows the URI, marked (default) for an unprefixed namespace, otherwise prefix → URI. An undeclared prefix shows as prefix → (unbound), an element without a namespace as (no namespace). For an XSD declaration the row shows the target namespace for global and qualified declarations, and (no namespace) for unqualified local ones.

docs.title: Copying the XPath or the node
docs.text:
The NODE & XPATH section shows the selected node's XPath in a code box:

  • Copy XPath - click the Copy XPath button next to the code box, or click the XPath itself, to copy the positional XPath (e.g. /root/item[2]) to the clipboard.
  • Copy Node (XML) - the second button next to the code box; copies the selected node's XML serialization.

Both actions are also in the ⋮ menu of the top bar. In the Text view they act on the element enclosing the caret; in the Tree/Graphic views they act on the selected node. For an XSD node selected in the Tree or Graphic view, Copy XPath copies the schema XPath and Copy Node copies the XSD source of that node; for JSON they copy the JSONPath and the JSON source.

docs.title: Facets and attributes lists
docs.text:
Facets (in TYPE & FACETS) and attributes (in VALUE & ATTRIBUTES) are shown as framed lists that you edit directly:

  • Click a value to edit it. Enter saves the change, Esc cancels it.
  • For attributes, click the name to rename the attribute.
  • Point at a row to show its trash icon; click it to delete the facet or attribute.
  • Add a new entry with the row below the list (facet kind or attribute name, value, Add).
  • Inherited facets (from a base type) are shown in italics and cannot be edited here.
  • Nodes of a named type selected inside a type frame of the Graphic view are read-only: a note above the sections names the type, and Edit type opens it in the type editor (see Named Types in Frames).
  • Long values wrap onto several lines instead of being cut off. The row's tooltip shows the full value, plus where it comes from (inherited from the referenced named type or defined by the schema).
  • Keyboard: press Tab to move to a row; Enter edits its value and Delete removes the row.

docs.title: XML Files
docs.text:
When an XML file is open, the Properties sidebar (Ctrl+Shift+P) shows the selected node and lets you edit it from whichever view you are in:

  • Text view - Move the text caret into an element to select it. The inspector shows the element's name, namespace, attributes, and text as editable fields. Edits round-trip into the source as a minimal change that preserves your caret and scroll position. If the caret is not inside a well-formed element, the inspector falls back to a read-only name/XPath view. When you switch back to the Text view, the inspector shows the node at the caret again right away.
  • Tree view - Click any node (element, text, comment, CDATA, or processing instruction) to edit its properties.
  • Graphic view (the grid) - Select a row to edit its properties. The grid also handles structural editing (adding, deleting, and moving nodes) through its right-click context menu.

All three views share one in-memory model per open document, so your edits and Undo/Redo history are preserved when you switch between Text, Tree, and Graphic.

With a bound XSD schema, the inspector also shows what the schema says about the selected element: Type, Base type, Derivation (including the list item type or the union member types), the facets (including the enumeration values), minOccurs/maxOccurs/Use, Order, nillable, default and fixed values, Since … / Deprecated: … from the schema's documentation tags, the schema's appinfo, and in CONSTRAINTS the identity constraints, assertions and type alternatives. Where the declaration is editable you can change many of these right here - see Editing the bound schema from the XML document. The DOCUMENTATION & REFS section adds:

  • the element's documentation from the schema, or "No documentation in the schema" when the schema has none;
  • a value check - "Value matches the schema facets" in green, or an amber warning such as "Value should be one of: …" when the current text breaks a facet;
  • EXAMPLE VALUES as chips - click one to set it as the element's text;
  • VALID CHILDREN as chips - click one to add that child element (None for a container element that allows no children);
  • USED IN - the containing element and its type.

Attributes with a bound schema: each attribute row shows its declared type as a small badge (* marks a required attribute). Attributes the schema does not declare are marked undeclared. For an attribute with enumerated values, the value editor is a drop-down. Below the list, DECLARED, NOT SET shows chips such as + id * for declared attributes that are missing - click one to add the attribute. Required ones are highlighted, and a default or fixed value is filled in for you.

docs.title: Editing the bound schema from the XML document
docs.text:
For an XML element with a bound XSD, TYPE & FACETS starts with a box such as Declared in order.xsd · local element · type AmountType and an Open in schema link. The link opens the XSD in the Graphic view, expanded along the element's path in the document (root element › … › element), and selects exactly this card - also when the schema has several local elements with the same name or the element sits in a named type used in several places.

When the declaration is editable, these inspector fields change the declaration in the XSD (not the XML): Type, minOccurs/maxOccurs, Nillable, Fixed, Default (in ADVANCED), the facets (add, edit, delete) and the documentation/appinfo. What happens:

  1. The XSD opens as a background tab - your XML document stays in front.
  2. The change is one undo step in the XSD tab, and the XSD tab shows as unsaved.
  3. Save the XSD. The XML document's schema facts (value check, example values, attribute information) are then reloaded.

Things to know:

  • The Type field here is the same type picker as in the XSD inspector: it lists the schema's own types and the XSD built-in datatypes and explains the highlighted one.
  • If the element uses a named simple type, its facets are the facets of that type. The list says so: "Facets of the named type T – a change applies to every element of that type".
  • Before you change a type or a global declaration that is used in several places, the inspector asks once for confirmation (Change T).
  • Some declarations are read-only, with a note:
  • "Read-only: declared in an included or imported schema."
  • "Read-only: a cached copy from the Schema Library." (also for read-only files)

docs.title: XSD Files
docs.text:
When an XSD (schema) file is open, the Properties sidebar shows the selected schema node and lets you edit it from whichever view you are in. XSD files have the same three views - Text, Tree, and Graphic (for XSD, the Graphic view shows the schema diagram):

  • Tree and Graphic views - Select a schema node to edit its name, type, cardinality/occurrence, use, form, constraints, documentation, and facets. Compositors (xs:sequence, xs:choice, xs:all), group references and xs:any show editable minOccurs/maxOccurs and their Order in CARDINALITY & USE. A simple type shows its final value (read-only) in ADVANCED. When all facets of an element or attribute come from a named type, the add row is replaced by the hint "Facets come from T – click to edit them there."; clicking it selects that type.
  • Text view - Move the text caret into an XSD construct (such as an xs:element, xs:complexType, xs:simpleType, xs:attribute, a compositor, or a facet) to select the matching schema node and edit the same properties you would in the Tree and Graphic views - without leaving the source editor. Edits round-trip into the schema text as a minimal change that preserves your caret and scroll position. If the caret is not inside a recognizable construct (for example inside an xs:annotation, a comment, or blank space), the pane falls back to a read-only caret/XPath view.

docs.title: Choosing a type with the type picker
docs.text:
The Type row of an element or attribute is a text field with a chevron button that opens a list of every type you can reference - in the Text, Tree and Graphic view alike. The same field sits in the small dialog behind Change Type… in the right-click menu of the Graphic view (the schema diagram) and of the Tree view, pre-filled with the current type, and in the SimpleType Editor for the base type, the list item type and new union member types - there it offers simple types only.

The list is grouped under section headers:

  • Simple types and Complex types defined in the schema itself, in included schemas and in imported schemas. Imported types carry the namespace prefix your schema declares for their namespace (for example cmn:Money). If the schema declares no prefix for that namespace, the bare name is shown and the detail pane reminds you to add an xmlns prefix for it before referencing the type.
  • Built-in XSD datatypes - all of them, grouped by category: Any, String, Numeric, Date & Time, Binary, Boolean, URI & Names, IDs & References. They use the prefix your schema actually uses (xs: or xsd:). The XSD 1.1 additions (dateTimeStamp, dayTimeDuration, yearMonthDuration, precisionDecimal) are included and marked as XSD 1.1 only.

Each row shows the type's name and a one-line summary - a short description for a built-in type, otherwise its make-up such as restriction of xs:string, extension of BaseType or sequence. The detail pane on the right explains the highlighted type: what kind of type it is (built-in with its category, simple or complex), its description or xs:documentation (English preferred), base type and derivation (restriction / extension / list / union), facts such as enumeration values, patterns, length limits, abstract, mixed content, the content model and the number of attributes, where it comes from (Imported from common.xsd, Included from …), an example value for built-in types, and notes such as XSD 1.1 only or not supported by Xerces (for precisionDecimal). Point at a row to read its explanation; click it or press Enter to pick it.

Working with the field:

  • Type to filter. The list opens as you type and narrows to matching names. Exact matches come first, so typing xs:int highlights xs:int, not xs:integer.
  • Open the full list with the chevron button, ↓ or Ctrl+Space - the current type is highlighted.
  • ↑ / ↓ move through the list, PageUp / PageDown jump eight rows at a time, Enter picks the highlighted type, Esc closes the list; a second Esc reverts an edit you have not committed yet.
  • Free text still works. When nothing in the list matches, Enter commits exactly what you typed - useful for a type reference the picker does not know.

A picked type is applied like every other inspector edit: one undo step (Ctrl+Z), written into the schema text right away. If the element defines its own content (for example a sequence of child elements), a dialog asks before the type replaces it, and Cancel shows the previous type again. For an element or attribute reference the field is locked. See Only Valid Changes.

The type picker arrived in version 2.6.0; earlier versions took the type as plain text.

USED IN (in DOCUMENTATION & REFS) shows where a node is used:

  • For a global type, element or group, it lists every place that references it. Click an entry to select the referring node in the Tree or Graphic view.
  • For a local declaration, it shows the global component that contains it.

All three XSD views share one in-memory schema model, so your edits and Undo/Redo history are preserved when you switch between Text, Tree, and Graphic. Structural editing (adding, deleting, and moving nodes) remains a Tree/Graphic capability through the right-click context menu.

docs.title: JSON Files
docs.text:
When a JSON file is open, select a node in the Tree or Graphic (grid) view and the Properties sidebar shows it:

  • NODE & XPATH shows the node's JSONPath (e.g. $.items[1]) instead of an XPath; click the value to copy it.
  • The key is editable for object properties - click the name in the node header to rename the key (duplicate keys are refused). Array items ([0], [1], …) and the root $ have no key.
  • The Value field is editable for scalars (strings, numbers, booleans, null); the type is kept, so a number must stay a number. Objects and arrays show a summary instead.
  • The node kind (object, array, string, …) is shown for information.

The inspector shares the document model with the grid, the tree and the text, so an edit here is one undo step (Ctrl+Z) and is written back into the text immediately. Structural editing (adding, deleting, moving or duplicating nodes, changing a value's type) is done in the grid's right-click context menu - see The Grid for JSON. In the Text view the inspector shows only the document type for JSON files.

docs.title: More XSD editing in the inspector
docs.text:
When an XSD file is open, the Properties inspector (Ctrl+Shift+P) shows the selected schema node. In addition to name, type, cardinality, facets, and constraints, you can now:

  • Pick the type from a list - The Type field opens a dropdown of the schema's own simple and complex types and all XSD built-in datatypes, each explained in a side pane as you move through the list. See Choosing a type with the type picker.
  • Edit the node's xs:appinfo - The machine-readable metadata attached to the node. Structured fields cover @since, @version, @see, @deprecated, a Markdown choice (Not set / Markdown / Plain text, written as @markdown) and the node's example values. Everything the fields do not cover - other tags and custom XML inside the appinfo - is preserved untouched. See Adding Technical Notes to Your Schema.
  • Edit multi-language xs:documentation - One row per language. Use Add language to add a translation and the ✕ button to remove one.
  • Edit comments - Select an XSD comment in the tree to edit its text. To add a new comment, use Add Comment… in a node's right-click context menu.
  • Delete a constraint - In the CONSTRAINTS section, select a key, keyref, unique, or assert constraint and click Delete constraint to remove it.
  • See where a component is used - USED IN (in DOCUMENTATION & REFS) lists every reference to a global type, element or group; click one to select the referring node.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: FreeXmlToolkit is free and needs no registration. All files are published on the GitHub Releases page; the download buttons on the home page always point to the latest release.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
1. Download the package for your operating system using the download buttons on the home page (or from the GitHub Releases page)
  2. Install it:
    • Windows: run the .exe installer (no administrator rights required) or the .msi; the portable .zip only needs to be extracted
    • macOS: open the .dmg and drag FreeXmlToolkit to Applications, or run the .pkg installer
    • Linux: sudo dpkg -i freexmltoolkit-*.deb (Debian/Ubuntu) or sudo rpm -i freexmltoolkit-*.rpm (Fedora/RHEL/openSUSE); the portable .zip only needs to be extracted
  3. Launch FreeXmlToolkit from your applications menu (portable: run FreeXmlToolkit / FreeXmlToolkit.exe in the extracted folder)

On first start the app opens on the Welcome page - continue with Your First Steps or the Unified Shell guide.

docs.title: Download Formats
docs.text: FreeXmlToolkit is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux in multiple formats. Choose the one that works best for you - all files are published on the GitHub Releases page (see the download buttons on the home page).

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Format Architecture Description .exe x64 Installer - Standard setup wizard. No admin rights required. Recommended for most users. .msi x64 MSI Package - For enterprise deployment and silent installation via Group Policy. .zip x64 Portable - No installation needed. Extract and run. Good for USB drives or restricted systems.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Format Architecture Description .dmg Intel (x64), Apple Silicon (ARM64) Disk Image - Standard macOS installation. Drag to Applications folder. .pkg Intel (x64), Apple Silicon (ARM64) Package Installer - Guided installation wizard. Useful for managed deployments. .zip Intel (x64), Apple Silicon (ARM64) Portable - No installation needed. Extract and run the app directly.

The macOS packages are signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so they open without a Gatekeeper warning.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Format Architecture Description .deb x64 Debian Package - For Ubuntu, Debian, Linux Mint. Install with sudo dpkg -i or double-click. .rpm x64 RPM Package - For Fedora, Red Hat, openSUSE. Install with sudo rpm -i or dnf install. .zip x64 Portable - No installation needed. Extract and run. Works on any Linux distribution.

Note: On macOS, pick the build that matches your Mac: Apple Silicon (ARM64) for M-series Macs, Intel (x64) for older Macs (Apple menu → About This Mac shows the chip). Windows and Linux builds are provided for x64 (Intel/AMD) only.

docs.title: Install with a Package Manager
docs.text: If you already use a package manager, it can install FreeXmlToolkit for you and keep it up to date. The packages are published with every release and contain the same builds as the download buttons on the home page.

docs.title: Windows – Scoop
docs.text:
Scoop installs the portable build into your user profile – no installer, no admin rights. Add the FreeXmlToolkit bucket once, then install:

scoop bucket add karlkauc https://github.com/karlkauc/scoop-bucket
scoop install karlkauc/freexmltoolkit

Scoop adds FreeXmlToolkit to the Start menu. Update and remove it with:

scoop update freexmltoolkit
scoop uninstall freexmltoolkit

docs.title: macOS – Homebrew
docs.text:
Homebrew installs the signed and notarized app into Applications and picks the Apple Silicon or Intel build automatically (macOS 11 Big Sur or newer):

brew install --cask karlkauc/tap/freexmltoolkit

Update and remove it with:

brew upgrade --cask freexmltoolkit
brew uninstall --cask freexmltoolkit

brew uninstall --zap --cask freexmltoolkit also removes your settings (~/.freeXmlToolkit).

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
A copy installed by Scoop or Homebrew is updated by the package manager: when a new version is out, the update notice in FreeXmlToolkit shows the command to run instead of downloading the new version itself.

On Linux, use the .deb / .rpm packages or the portable ZIP.

docs.title: JSON Editor
docs.text:
The JSON Editor provides a powerful environment for editing, validating, and querying JSON files with support for multiple JSON formats.

Note: The standalone JSON Editor tab has been retired. JSON editing — text editing, the tree and grid views, and validation — now lives in the Unified Shell: open a .json file and the Text, Tree and Graphic (grid) views are available there. The capabilities below are unchanged; they are now part of the shell rather than a dedicated sidebar tab.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
FreeXmlToolkit includes a full-featured JSON Editor that supports: - Standard JSON - RFC 8259 compliant - JSONC syntax - JSON with Comments (single-line // and block /* */) - JSON5 syntax - trailing commas, unquoted keys, single-quoted strings, and comments

File extensions: .json, .jsonc and .json5 all open in the JSON editor (tree view, grid view, JSONPath, schema binding). The flavor is detected from the content, not from the extension - a .json file with comments is treated as JSONC just like a .jsonc file. Only .json is offered for operating-system file associations (.jsonc/.json5 have no MIME type in the shared databases).

The Tree view of a JSON document in the Unified Shell

The same document in the Graphic (grid) view - the grid the shell also uses for XML

docs.title: Text Editor
docs.text: Feature Description Syntax Highlighting Color-coded JSON for easy reading Auto Format Beautify JSON with proper indentation Minify Compress JSON by removing whitespace Undo/Redo Full undo/redo support Line Numbers Numbered lines for easy navigation Drag & Drop Drop JSON files directly into the editor

docs.title: Tree View
docs.text:
The tree view provides a hierarchical view of your JSON structure:

Feature Description Interactive Navigation Click on nodes to jump to that location in the text Expand/Collapse Expand or collapse nodes to focus on specific areas Search Search for keys or values within the tree Sync with Editor Synchronize selection between tree and text Type Icons Visual icons for objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null

The tree shares the document model with the grid view and the Properties inspector, so an edit made there shows up in the tree immediately, and Ctrl+F searches keys and values.

docs.title: Grid View
docs.text:
The Graphic view mode shows the document as the editable grid - the very same grid the shell uses for XML files, so it is instantly familiar:

Feature Description Rows The root $, object properties (key = value) and array items ([0], [1], …); objects and arrays collapse/expand Type glyphs {} object, [] array, " string, # number, T/F boolean, ∅ null - each in its own colour; strings are shown quoted Arrays of objects Rendered as embedded tables (one column per key); click a column header to sort, expand nested objects inline Inline editing Double-click a value; the type is kept (numbers must stay numbers, booleans toggle, null stays null unless you type text). Double-click a key to rename it Context menu Add Property / Array Item / Sibling Before / After, Rename Key (F2), Duplicate (Ctrl+D), Copy / Cut / Paste as Sibling / Paste as Child, Copy Cell Content (Ctrl+Shift+C), Copy JSONPath (Ctrl+Alt+X), Copy Node (JSON) (Ctrl+Alt+C), Change Type, Move Up/Down (Alt+↑/↓), Expand All / Collapse All, Sort Column, Delete Undo/Redo Every grid edit is one undo step (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) and is written back into the text Search Ctrl+F finds keys and values, revealing matches inside collapsed nodes Zoom & layout Zoom the whole grid with Ctrl+mouse wheel, Ctrl + / Ctrl − or the header's zoom pill (Ctrl 0 resets; the factor is shared with the XML grid). Nothing is cut off - long strings wrap onto further lines - and the columns of an array table can be dragged to a new width (double-click the separator to auto-fit). Expand all / Collapse all buttons sit in the header

See Grid View - JSON for details.

docs.title: Properties Inspector
docs.text:
The Properties inspector on the right (Ctrl+Shift+P) works for JSON documents too. Select a node in the Tree or Graphic (grid) view and the inspector shows:

  • the key - editable for object properties (renaming a key here is the same as Rename Key in the grid; duplicate keys are refused),
  • the node type (object, array, string, number, boolean, null) and its depth,
  • the JSONPath of the node in the NODE & XPATH line (e.g. $.items[1]) - click it to copy the path,
  • the value - editable for strings, numbers, booleans and null; the type is kept, so a number stays a number.

Edits made in the inspector are undoable (Ctrl+Z) and written back into the text just like grid edits. See Properties Inspector - JSON Files for details.

docs.title: Hover Information
docs.text: When you hover over any element in the JSON editor, you'll see: - JSONPath - The full path to the current element (e.g., $.store.book[0].title) - Type - The JSON type (object, array, string, number, boolean, null) - Key - The property key name - Value - A preview of the value (truncated for long values)

docs.title: JSONPath Queries
docs.text:
Execute JSONPath queries to extract data from your JSON documents:

Query Example Description $.store.book[*].author All authors in the store $..author All authors anywhere in the document $.store.book[?(@.price < 10)] Books cheaper than 10 $.store.book[0,1] First two books $.store.book[-1:] Last book

To run a query: 1. Open the Query Console (terminal icon in the toolbar, or Ctrl+Shift+X) - with a JSON document active its mode toggle reads JSONPath and it evaluates JSONPath 2. Enter your JSONPath expression 3. Run it to see the results in the console's result pane

docs.title: Syntax Validation
docs.text: Click Validate to check if your JSON is syntactically correct. The editor will report: - Parse errors with line and column numbers - Detected format (JSON, JSONC, or JSON5)

docs.title: JSON Schema Validation
docs.text:
JSON documents bind a JSON Schema the same way XML documents bind an XSD:

  • Automatic: a top-level "$schema" member pointing at a schema file or URL (e.g. "$schema": "./product-schema.json") is detected when the file opens. Relative paths resolve against the document's folder; http(s) URLs are downloaded and cached. (Values pointing at json-schema.org meta-schemas are dialect declarations, not bindings, and are ignored - unless you map that meta-schema URI in the Schema Library yourself; none are bundled.) If the $schema URI isn't directly resolvable, the Schema Library is consulted next - see Schema Library.
  • Manual: click the JSON Schema indicator in the status bar, use the JSON Schema source row in the Validation panel (Change link, favorites star, or drag & drop a .json schema onto the row or the status bar).

Validation runs via Run Validation in the panel, the toolbar's Validate button / F8, or continuously while typing (Validate while typing, on by default). Schema violations appear in the PROBLEMS list with the offending line number — clicking a problem jumps to it. Each problem also carries the failing schema keyword and the JSON pointer of the invalid value.

The validator supports JSON Schema Draft-07, 2019-09, and 2020-12; the dialect is selected by the schema's own $schema declaration (2020-12 is the default for schemas without one). Relative $refs between schema files resolve as expected.

Ready-made examples

The examples/json/ folder shipped with the application contains a complete demo set: a product-catalog schema with a relative $ref, a valid and a deliberately invalid instance (six line-navigable violations), and one dialect demo each for Draft-07 and 2019-09. Open examples/json/products-invalid.json and press F8 to see it in action.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
The complete list is on the Keyboard Shortcuts page (and in the app under Help → Keyboard Shortcuts).

JSON-specific, in the Graphic (grid) view:

Shortcut Action F2 Rename the selected key Ctrl+D Duplicate the selected node (elsewhere Ctrl+D adds the file to favorites) Alt+↑ / Alt+↓ Move the selected node up / down Ctrl+Alt+X / Ctrl+Alt+C Copy JSONPath / Copy Node (JSON) Ctrl+Shift+C Copy Cell Content

docs.title: Supported Formats
docs.text: All three flavors below are recognized in .json, .jsonc and .json5 files; the editor auto-detects the flavor from the content (syntax highlighting and the tree view strip comments and trailing commas before parsing).

docs.title: JSON (Standard)
docs.text:
{
  "name": "John",
  "age": 30,
  "active": true
}

Grid edits rewrite JSONC / JSON5 as standard JSON
