Every row carries a star button next to its Change button: on the XSD row it opens a quick-select menu of your favorited XSD schemas, on the Schematron row a menu of your favorited Schematron files, and on the JSON Schema row a menu of your favorited JSON files - pick one to bind it in a single click, without browsing the file system. The menus group entries by favorites folder when you use more than one, and are grayed out while you have no matching favorites. (See Favorites.)

All source rows are drop targets: drop an .xsd file from your file manager onto the XSD row, a .sch / .schematron file onto the Schematron row, or a .json schema onto the JSON Schema row, to bind it to the active document in one move - the row glows green while a loadable file hovers over it and red for a wrong file type (which is rejected). The dropped file behaves exactly like one picked via Change or a favorite, including appearing in the recent list.

  • The referenced XSD binds automatically. When the XML declares its schema (xsi:schemaLocation / xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation - local or remote), that XSD is bound when the file is opened, so the declared schema is the default. The declaration is also re-checked against the current editor content before every validation run (Run Validation, the toolbar's Validate, and live validation): a schema reference you add or change in the editor is picked up immediately - even in unsaved or untitled documents - and a removed reference downgrades validation to a well-formedness check (the status bar shows "No XSD"). A declared location is first looked up in your XML catalogs and Schema Library mappings; remote https schema URLs that no catalog redirects are downloaded to the schema cache, and if the download fails, a Schema Library mapping for the document's namespace is used instead. The status bar shows how the schema was found - plain "XSD: name" for a declared location, "(catalog)", "(library)" or "(manual)" otherwise (see Status Bar). A schema you picked yourself (via Change, a favorite, or the status bar) is never overridden.
  • JSON documents work the same way: a top-level "$schema" member pointing at a schema file or URL auto-binds that JSON Schema on open, is re-checked before every validation run, and a manual choice always wins. (Values pointing at json-schema.org meta-schemas are dialect declarations, not bindings, and are ignored.) See JSON Editor for details and the supported drafts.
  • Click a bound source name to open the file in the editor - one click on the XSD or Schematron name opens it as a tab for direct editing.

Tip

You can also bind a schema without opening the Validation panel: click the schema indicator in the status bar (for XML it reads "No XSD", "XSD: name", "Detecting XSD…" or "XSD error"; for JSON documents the same states read "No JSON Schema", "JSON Schema: name", and so on; see Status Bar) or click the editor toolbar's Schema button (Set XSD Schema…) and pick a schema file. For XML the binding drives both IntelliSense and schema validation; for JSON it drives validation.

docs.title: Running a Validation
docs.text:
1. Pick a mode with the Single file | Batch toggle.

  2. Click Run Validation.

  3. Single file validates the active document against the bound XSD and/or Schematron.

  4. Batch validates a whole set of XML files. In Batch mode, Run Validation opens a small menu with two ways to pick the files:
    • Select XML files… - a file chooser where you pick one or more XML files.
    • Select folder… - a folder chooser; every *.xml file in the folder and all of its subfolders is validated.

The RESULTS list then shows one row per file with a status icon (red ✕ = errors, orange ⚠ = warnings only, green ✓ = valid) and a badge with the problem count. Select a row to see that file's problems in the panel's PROBLEMS list; double-click to open the file. The plain-text batch report opens from the REPORTS & CHECKS section (Open Last Batch Report).

The status line below the button summarises the run: Valid, 1 problem / N problems, or - when no schema is bound and only the well-formedness check ran - Well-formed · no schema bound (shown neutral, not green - in the panel and in the Inspector's badge: bind an XSD in SOURCES to validate against a schema).

The RESULTS list and the panel's own PROBLEMS list are only shown in Batch mode. In Single file mode the problems are listed in the PROBLEMS panel below the editor, and the side panel shows a single row such as "3 problems — show below the editor" - click it to expand and focus that PROBLEMS panel.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
Problems appear in two places:

  • The PROBLEMS list in the side panel (Batch mode only): the problems of the file selected in RESULTS. Export Problems to Excel in the REPORTS & CHECKS section saves the current list as an .xlsx workbook.
  • The PROBLEMS panel below the editor: it appears automatically when validation finds problems, shows error/warning counts in its header, and can be collapsed to just the header. Drag its top edge to change its height (the height is remembered). Each row shows the message and the file/line in a monospaced label.

Every row in the PROBLEMS panel below the editor carries a source badge - XSD, Schematron, Well-formed, or JSON Schema - so when a run combines several checks you can tell at a glance where each problem comes from. Hovering a Schematron row shows a tooltip with the full message, the failed rule/test expression, and the XPath of the failing node.

Long messages are cut off in the row. Right-click a row in the PROBLEMS panel below the editor to copy it: Copy Message (just the message text), Copy Problem (severity, source, message, file and line/column, plus rule and context for Schematron) or Copy All Problems (one problem per line). Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on macOS) copies the selected row like Copy Problem.

Selecting a problem in either list shows it in the view you are in:

  • Text - the caret jumps to its line and, for XML and XSD errors, to the reported column.
  • Tree - the element of that line is selected and scrolled into view.
  • Graphic - the grid selects the element's row; inside a repeating group it opens the table, selects the cell (the attribute's cell when the message names an attribute) and opens table cells on the way to errors nested deeper. The row or cell flashes briefly, the red problem marker stays. For an XSD the diagram selects the schema node.

The view does not change. This works for Schematron problems too: the failing rule's context node is resolved back to its line in the XML, so a click navigates straight to the offending element.

Schematron problems whose rules define quick fixes (SQF) can be corrected in place: right-click the problem row in either list and pick a fix from the Quick Fix submenu, or use the yellow lightbulb that appears in the editor gutter on lines with fixable problems (click it, or press Alt+Enter / Ctrl+. on the line). See Schematron Quick Fixes.

docs.title: Detailed Schematron Report
docs.text:
A full report of the last Schematron run, opened as a tool tab and saveable as HTML or SVRL.

After validating a document that has a Schematron file bound, open the report in either of two ways:

  • Click the Validation Report row in the Validation panel's REPORTS & CHECKS section (it is enabled once a run with a bound Schematron has finished).

The report opens as a Schematron Report tool tab showing the document name, the Schematron file, a severity summary (errors / warnings), and a table with one row per finding:

Column Content Severity Error or Warning Line Line in the XML document Message The rule's message text Rule / Test The Schematron test expression that failed Context (XPath) The XPath of the failing node Fix A lightbulb button on findings that offer Schematron Quick Fixes — click it to apply a fix directly from the report

Click a row to jump straight to that line in the editor. Two buttons export the report:

  • Save Report (HTML) - a self-contained HTML file you can archive or share.
  • Save SVRL (XML) - the raw SVRL output (Schematron Validation Report Language) of the run, for further processing by other tools.

docs.title: The Tool Sections and the ⋮ Menu
docs.text:
The tools are labelled rows (icon + name) in two collapsible sections at the top of the panel. Both start open; click a header to collapse it.

REPORTS & CHECKS - results and exports of a run:

Row What It Does Validation Report Open the detailed Schematron report of the last validation run (enabled after such a run) Export Problems to Excel Save the current problems as an Excel workbook (enabled while there are problems) Open Last Batch Report Open the plain-text report of the last batch run

FundsXML validation lives in the FundsXML panel (when the FundsXML extension is enabled).

SCHEMATRON AUTHORING - tools for writing Schematron rules (usable without a run):

Row What It Does Rule Templates Insert ready-made Schematron rule patterns Schematron Tester Run the Schematron rules against an XML file Rule Builder Build rules visually Check Rules Run an error detector over the Schematron itself and show a categorised issue table Schematron Documentation Open the Schematron documentation generator

The panel header's ⋮ (overflow) menu keeps only the Validate while typing toggle for continuous (debounced) validation.

Check Rules inspects the Schematron file for problems and lists them by category - XML syntax, structural, XPath, semantic, and best-practice issues - so you can fix mistakes in the rules before you rely on them. See Schematron Validation for details.

docs.title: What's New
docs.text: The highlights of each release. The complete notes and all downloads are on the GitHub Releases page; the version you are running is shown under Help → About FreeXmlToolkit.

Platform and enterprise

  • German user interface: Settings → Appearance → Language (System default, English, Deutsch); all layouts and the shell's messages are translated. See Settings.
  • Command line fxt-cli: validate (XSD, DTD, RELAX NG, Schematron, JSON Schema; text, JSON, JUnit and SARIF reports), transform (XSLT, XQuery, XProc, with profiling), xsd-doc, xspec, scenario, compare, merge, convert, fop. See Command Line.
  • Administrator policies: machine-wide policy.properties (locked) and defaults.properties, telemetry and updates can be switched off centrally, silent installation. See Administration.
  • Plugins: an API for activities with side panels, menu items, validators, startup tasks, document listeners, stylesheets and schemas; jars in ~/.freeXmlToolkit/plugins, managed in Settings → Extensions → PLUGINS. FundsXML is now a plugin. See Plugins and Writing Plugins.
  • Industry plugins (off by default): ISO 20022 payments / SEPA, ebInterface, FinDatEx EMT/EET/EPT/TPT (V7 and V8), XBRL with Arelle. See Industry Plugins.
  • Projects and transformation scenarios: .fxtproj files bind a schema (XSD, DTD, RELAX NG, JSON Schema), a Schematron and a transformation scenario to files by pattern, add catalogs and store named scenarios (XSLT, XQuery, XProc, PDF through FOP).
  • Project Settings edits all of it without touching the JSON.
  • Validate Project checks every bound file.
  • Scenarios run for the chosen files (${file}, ${name}), from the Explorer and with fxt-cli scenario --input.
  • Recent projects are on the menu and the Welcome page.
  • The project reloads when its file changes.

See Projects. - Accessibility: screen-reader names for every button and field, WCAG AA contrast in both themes, documented keyboard alternatives. See Accessibility. - Security: no external entities in Schematron validation, HTML previews without JavaScript or remote content, XProc pipelines run no programs and reach no network, schemas are never fetched from internal addresses, Saxon's parser hardened, SBOM with every release. DTDs and RELAX NG schemas cannot send local files to a server (a parse never mixes local files and downloads), the output of project scenarios stays inside the project folder, YAML alias bombs are stopped, and Jackson, jsoup and AssertJ are past their known vulnerabilities. See Threat Model.

XML work

  • DTD and RELAX NG (XML and compact syntax): validation against the declared or a bound grammar, with IntelliSense. See Schema Support.
  • Compare and merge: XML compared by structure (namespaces, attribute order, whitespace, element order), folder comparison, three-way merge.
  • Conversion: XML ↔ JSON ↔ YAML (Tools menu, fxt-cli convert).
  • Large File Viewer: files of any size (1 GB in seconds, a few MB of memory) with search, structure tree, record table and streaming validation. See Large Files.
  • XSLT profiler: hot spots, call tree, flame graph and line times (Transform panel → Profile run).
  • XSpec: run XSpec tests for XSLT, XQuery and Schematron, with HTML and JUnit reports.
  • FundsXML: 17 data-quality checks with a report and as Query Console snippets, analysis queries, and grid formulas and filters for funds, positions, master data and transactions. See FundsXML Extensions.
  • Grid: filters inside opened table cells, saved filters (off when opened), formulas first under their element, German number format; much faster with very large tables (680,000 records).

Signatures and encryption

  • XML Encryption 1.1: the Signature page is now Sign & Encrypt with Encrypt, Decrypt and Inspect. Encrypt the whole document, the element at the caret or an XPath selection for any number of recipients (certificate, keystore entry, shared key file, password); decrypt with your private key, a shared key or the password. The XML editor's context menu offers Encrypt Element… / Decrypt…. See XML Encryption.
  • Signature algorithms: RSA, RSA-PSS and ECDSA, a selectable digest and canonicalization; new certificates with RSA or EC keys. See Digital Signatures.
  • fxt-cli sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt (also --inspect). See Command Line.

More

  • fxt-cli query runs XPath, XQuery and JSONPath; the XQuery profiler shows where a query spends its time (Run ▾ → Profile Query, fxt-cli transform --profile).
  • Regression checks for scenarios: compare a scenario's output with an expected result (Check, Differences, Accept; fxt-cli scenario --check). See Projects.
  • XML compare: ignore XPaths, XMLUnit placeholders and a numeric tolerance.
  • XSpec templates in File → New.
  • Problems, Query Console hits and FundsXML data-quality findings open in the document's current view (Tree or Graphic) instead of switching to the Text view.
  • Grid: a click elsewhere keeps the value you are editing (like Enter) and closes an open context menu; the XSD diagram's context menu closes the same way.
  • One look for every dialog, light and dark; banner and dialog images in the Windows installers.

• XSD Overview view: a new view mode for schemas lists all top-level components - imports, includes, annotations, elements, types, groups, attribute groups, attributes, notations - in one table. Insert, append, move (also by drag and drop), sort by type or name, rename with the references, edit annotations in place, add imports and includes. Tabs below edit the selected component's attributes (Default/Fixed offer the enumeration values), identity constraints, XSD 1.1 assertions and the schema's namespace prefixes. See XSD Tools.
  • XSD saving keeps your order: the top-level components are no longer re-sorted on every save; schema-level xs:annotation, xs:notation and xs:defaultOpenContent are no longer lost when the schema is edited.
  • Named types in frames (Graphic view): the content an element gets from a named complex type is drawn in a light-yellow, dashed frame titled with the type's name; the base of an xs:extension gets a nested frame. The content is read-only there - double-click the frame title or choose Edit Type '…' to open the type in its Type Editor. A type used inside a Type Editor now opens in a further Type Editor tab, so nested types can be followed level by level. See XSD Tools.
  • Constraints on their target nodes (optional, off by default): a key, unique or keyref can also show on the node its field points to (e.g. BenchmarkID lists the key Fund declares). In the Graphic view, switch it in the new DISPLAY section at the top of the Properties pane or under View → Show Constraints on Target Nodes. In the XSD documentation, use Show constraints on their target elements: it adds a row to the diagram box and a Referenced by Identity Constraints section to the element's page. See XSD Tools.
  • Flatten Schema: the dialog asks for the output file, preset to <name>_flattened.xsd next to the original schema; the result is written there and opened. See XSD Tools.
  • Downloaded imports are saved next to your schema: a missing xs:import / xs:include (e.g. xmldsig-core-schema.xsd of FundsXML4) is saved under its original name in the folder of the schema that references it and loaded from there - also in validation, Schema Analysis, flattening and documentation - instead of an md5-named cache file. Existing files are never overwritten. See XSD Tools.
  • XML → Excel: the workbook now has the same look as the Data Dictionary export. With a bound XSD, numbers, booleans and dates go into number, boolean and date cells instead of text. Importing the workbook gives back the original values. The CSV export adds a Data Type column and quotes only text. Excel → XML and CSV → XML also read the values with the XSD (from the new Schema (XSD) field, or the one the file declares). Dates, booleans and numbers that were entered by hand or reformatted by a spreadsheet application (31.01.2024, 1.234,50, TRUE) come out valid. Values that contain the delimiter, quotes or line breaks now import back correctly. See XML Editor.
  • Favorites from everywhere: a star in the header bar lists every favorite on every activity and page (also Settings, Schema Library and Signature); the Explorer has a star and FAVORITES | RECENT tabs at the bottom; and the menu bar has File → Open Favorite. See Favorites.
  • Explorer TOOLS: besides Open file… and Clear recent, the list offers Open from URL…, Compare files…, Spreadsheet Converter… and Generate XSD from XML files…. Compare and Generate XSD use the files selected in the workspace tree (two selected files are compared with each other); the tree's context menu adds Compare Selected Files and Generate XSD from Selected. See Unified Shell.
  • Query Console: a close button (✕) at the top right, and the XPath | XQuery mode is a clear switch; the active mode is also named on the Run button (Run XPath / Run XQuery) and in the hint below the input. See Query Console.
  • Side panels are collapsed and re-opened only with the editor toolbar's toggle buttons (or Ctrl+L / Ctrl+Shift+P), and collapsing one no longer changes the width of the other. See Unified Shell.
  • Fixes: the grid's scroll bars can be dragged when the content is less than twice the height of the view; in the XSD documentation, nested compositor symbols are centred over their children.

• XSD Graphic view, new card layout: every node is one card with a symbol, name and type line; cardinality and attribute use are pills, optional cards are dashed and repeating ones have a second outline. A title chip (top left) names the selected card, a zoom control sits at the bottom right, and the light theme has more contrast. Element and attribute cards list their constraints and assertions (View → Show Constraints in Diagram). The ComplexType editor tab shows the same cards. See XSD Tools.
  • XSD Graphic view: cards open in large schemas too; inherited xs:extension content, group and attribute group references, wildcards, inherited attributes and placeholder cards are shown; a bar names includes and imports that could not be loaded; relative references inside schemas loaded over HTTP now resolve; xs:redefine and xs:override are resolved, and every file of a namespace split over several xs:imports is loaded; changes to included and imported files on disk are noticed, and open cards stay open when the schema is rebuilt. See XSD Tools.
  • Schema files on disk: a changed date alone no longer asks to reload, and an XML document follows the schema bound to it even without a tab for that schema. The check pauses on a slow drive.
  • xs:redefine and xs:override also work inside included files, and they now count in the Type Library, statistics, quality checks and the Inspector of an XML document.
  • Facets: a restriction of a named type offers the facets of what that type comes down to, and restrictions of list and union types offer only the facets XML Schema allows there.
  • XSD documentation (PDF and Word): an Element Reference with a section per element and attribute (diagram, properties, documentation, restrictions, children, constraints) and a section per complex and simple type, all linked from the data dictionary, the index and the tables, with bookmarks; a namespace overview that names each namespace, the option XSD source in each section; in the PDF vector (SVG) diagrams and an overview diagram of the whole schema; in Word real headings, so the table of contents and the navigation pane work. Large schemas no longer run out of memory. Fixed: wrong root in the schema diagram, HTML in restrictions, cut-off text, usage counts. See XSD Tools.
  • XSD documentation diagrams: element boxes list constraints and assertions (option Show constraints in diagrams, with Also in the page's own element box); constraint rows link their selector, fields and key; the choice symbol is drawn as a switch. Show documentation in diagrams is now off by default.
  • Go to Definition from an XML document (Graphic, Tree and Text view, Ctrl+Click in text) opens the bound XSD in the Graphic view, expanded along the element's path with its card selected. See XML Editor.
  • Grid: the header adapts to a narrow column (icon-only buttons, then the tools move into the ⋯ menu); the scroll range follows tables whose cells are opened.
  • Side panels list their tools first; the Tools menu has Generate XSD from XML and Generate XSD from XML Files… (batch, always available).
  • Fixes: schemas whose DOCTYPE names a missing DTD (such as XMLSchema.xsd) load everywhere; absolute schema locations in xsi:schemaLocation bind; right-clicking in the editor no longer stalls on a large clipboard; user errors are no longer reported as app errors.

• Grid: opened table cells are full grids at any depth (select, edit, navigate, search, resize and drag & drop inside them); select whole table rows/columns and open nested cells with + / −; the entry helpers panel (Siblings / Children / Values) beside the XML grid. JSON grid: change a value's type via its type icon, drag & drop, Table submenu. See Grid View.
  • Network: complete proxy settings (system / manual / none, exceptions, authentication incl. NTLM/Kerberos, timeouts, Test Connection); every HTTP connection uses them. See Settings.
  • Settings: old log files are deleted automatically (LOG FILES card); the clear buttons show the space in use.
  • XSD documentation: type definitions, SVG overview and metadata are on by default; the Data Dictionary Excel export has the look of the HTML documentation.

• Editable grid for XML: block layout with docked tables and inline previews, table cell ranges and TSV copy/paste with spreadsheets, flip rows/columns, sortable and movable columns, multi-selection, split view, sticky scroll header, sibling groups for huge containers, validation markers, XQuery filters (Filter to Focus) and formulas, drag & drop, Edit as Raw Text (Ctrl+Alt+R), Wrap in Element, configurable cell colours. See Grid View.
  • XSD editor: only structural edits that keep the schema valid are allowed; create global complex and simple types; set type, cardinality and more when adding a node; drag & drop in the Graphic view; a type picker with explanations. See XSD Tools.
  • IntelliSense: attribute and value completion for XSLT and XSD-bound XML. See Auto-Completion.
  • Editor tabs can be reordered by drag and have a context menu (Reload, Close Others, Copy Path, Reveal…); problem rows can be copied.

• Interactive debugger for XSLT, XQuery and Schematron (at the .sch lines): DEBUG dock below the editor, conditional breakpoints, hit counts, logpoints, template / function / mode and input-node breakpoints, break on errors and xsl:message, Pause (F6), line stepping, Smart Step Into (Shift+F7), Run to Cursor (Ctrl+F10), debug configurations and Re-run Last Debug, Evaluate (Alt+F8), structured variables, watches, inline and hover values, changed-value markers, Explain Match, coverage, output so far and output-to-source mapping. See Debugger.
  • Memory: the heap limit follows the installed RAM and is adjustable in Settings; large files are guarded. See Settings → Memory.
  • Files: every opened file goes into Recent (configurable limit); files picked, dropped or chosen from favorites open in the editor; "Open with" works on all platforms; quitting asks about unsaved documents.

• Streamlined workflows: Settings, Schema Library and Signature open as pages in the main area; Help is a menu (header ? and F1); the Welcome page has a task list and Open an Example.
  • Properties inspector redesign, and editing the bound XSD from an XML document (type, cardinality, facets, documentation) with Open in schema. See Properties Inspector.
  • Large documents and schemas stay responsive: typing, highlighting, folding, view switches, saving and formatting no longer block the window.

• Installation via package managers: updates of Scoop / Homebrew / winget / Flatpak installs show the matching upgrade command. See Installation.
  • SHA256SUMS.txt with every release; Linux desktop entry, AppStream metadata and icons.
  • Code signing policy.

• macOS: packages signed and notarized by Apple; native system menu bar.
  • Menu bar (File, Edit, View, Tools, Help) with every action by name; Ctrl/Cmd+W closes the tab, Ctrl/Cmd+, opens the settings.
  • Files changed outside the app are detected (also on network drives) and can be reloaded.

• Schema Analysis tool with types, statistics, quality checks and report export (CSV, JSON, HTML, PDF, XLSX). See XSD Tools.
  • Workflow colours for every activity; labelled action rows in all side panels.
  • Grid: wrapped values, measured column widths, zoom, resizable columns.
  • Settings are stored in ~/.freeXmlToolkit/FreeXmlToolkit.properties.
  • 2.3.1: no more UI freezes on large diffs, minified files and web-imported schemas; log files roll over automatically.

• Anonymous usage statistics and error reports (opt-out). See Privacy & Telemetry.
  • JSON grid view; .jsonc / .json5 open as JSON. See JSON Editor.
  • A much more reliable sample XML generator and the Schema Analysis tool tab.

docs.title: Where the former tabs went
docs.text:
The Unified Shell consolidates what used to be separate sidebar tabs. The earlier standalone editors - XSD Editor, XSD Validation, JSON Editor, XSLT Viewer, Schematron, Schema Generator, Digital Signatures and FOP/PDF - have been retired and their functionality now lives in the shell:

Former tab Now in the shell XSD Editor / Tools Open an .xsd: Text/Tree/Graphic views + inspector; Schema activity (Type Library panel) for type editing, documentation, flatten and schema analysis XSD Validation Validation activity (single + batch, XSD & Schematron) JSON Editor Open a .json / .jsonc / .json5: Text / Tree / Graphic (grid) views + inspector; JSONPath via the Query Console; JSON Schema validation in the Validation activity XSLT Viewer Transform panel (set stylesheet, transform, preview, browser) Schematron Validation activity: check rules, templates, tester, builder, documentation, CSV/JSON export Schema Generator Editor toolbar Schema ▾ → Generate XSD from XML Digital Signatures Signature activity (sign, validate, trust validation, certificate creation) FOP / PDF FOP activity (XSL-FO → PDF + preview) XSLT Developer Transform panel + editor: run/live transform, parameters, and the OPTIONS & TOOLS section (batch, profile, trace, debugger) — see XSLT Developer XML Editor The shell's editor itself: every XML document opens with IntelliSense, Text/Tree/Graphic views and the Properties inspector

docs.title: XML Editor Features
docs.text: This page has been merged into the XML Editor guide: Search, Auto-Completion, Code Folding, Schematron Integration and the Grid View.

docs.title: XML Editor
docs.text: The XML Editor is the main feature of FreeXmlToolkit. It provides a powerful and easy-to-use interface for working with XML files.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The XML Editor in text mode with syntax highlighting

The XML Editor in the Graphic view (grid) for structured editing

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
The editor toolbar is a single slim row. Related actions sit in split buttons with a visible ▾ arrow menu (e.g. Save As / Save All under Save ▾, Minify under Format ▾); secondary tools are icon-only buttons with tooltips. See Unified Shell - Toolbar for the full reference.

With an XML file active, the toolbar offers:

Button Shortcut Description New Ctrl+N Open the guided New File dialog Open Ctrl+O Open one or more files Save ▾ Ctrl+S Save the current file; the arrow menu holds Save As… (Ctrl+Shift+S) and Save All Undo / Redo Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y Undo / redo the last change (icon buttons) Format ▾ Shift+Alt+F Pretty-print the document; the arrow menu holds Minify. (Note: Ctrl+Shift+F opens Find in Files, not document search.) Query Console Ctrl+Shift+X Toggle the bottom XPath/XQuery console (icon button) Transform XSLT - Pick a stylesheet and transform the active XML (icon button) Schema ▾ - Set XSD Schema… for IntelliSense and validation; the arrow menu also holds Generate Documentation… and Type Editor… (enabled for XSD files) and Generate XSD from XML / Generate XSD from XML Files… Validate F8 Validate the document (the toolbar's primary action, filled in Validation green - see Colours: workflows and actions)

Insert Template… (Ctrl+T, Edit menu), Compare with File… and Spreadsheet Converter… (Ctrl+E, both in the Tools menu) are menu commands, not toolbar buttons. Without an open document (for example on the Welcome page) the toolbar shows only New and Open.

The Run ▾ button and the Input dropdown ("Input: …") appear when a query, XSLT, or XProc document is active - see Query Documents.

docs.title: Opening and Saving Files
docs.text:
The shell header and the editor toolbar with the New, Open, Save ▾, and Format ▾ buttons

  • Open Files: Click "Open" or use Ctrl+O to browse for XML files
  • Save Files: Click "Save" or use Ctrl+S to save changes to the current file
  • Save As: Use Ctrl+Shift+S (or the Save ▾ arrow menu) to save the current file with a new name
  • Save All: Pick Save All from the Save ▾ arrow menu to save every open document tab at once (untitled tabs prompt you for a file name)
  • Create New: Click "New" (Ctrl+N) to open the guided New File dialog - pick a file type, an optional template or schema, and start editing
  • Drag & Drop: Drag files from your file explorer into the editor
  • Recent Files: Reopen recently used files from the Explorer panel's RECENT section or the Welcome page

docs.title: Multiple Files
docs.text: Open multiple XML files in separate tabs. Each tab shows the file name and indicates unsaved changes with an asterisk (*).

docs.title: Text Mode
docs.text:
Text editor with syntax highlighting

The text editor provides:

  • Syntax Highlighting: XML elements, attributes, and values are color-coded
  • Line Numbers: Every line is numbered for easy reference
  • Code Folding: Click arrows to collapse or expand sections
  • Auto-Completion: Type < to see suggestions for valid elements
  • Error Highlighting: Invalid XML is highlighted in red
  • Edit Properties: Move the text cursor into an element and edit its properties in the Properties inspector - see Properties Inspector

docs.title: Tree View
docs.text:
Tree view showing XML structure

  • See your XML document as a hierarchical tree
  • Click any node (element, text, comment, CDATA, or processing instruction) to select it
  • Edit the selected node's properties in the Properties inspector - see Properties Inspector
  • Right-click for context menu options

docs.title: Graphic View (Grid)
docs.text:
For XML documents (and XSLT / Schematron), the Graphic view shows the editable grid.

An XML document in the Graphic view (grid editing)

  1. Open an XML file and switch to the Graphic view with the view switch
  2. Click cells to edit values directly; move with the arrow keys
  3. Add, delete, wrap or move nodes through the right-click context menu or drag & drop
  4. Select a row to view and edit its properties in the Properties inspector

Repeating elements appear as embedded tables (sortable, flippable, copy/paste with spreadsheets), cells can be opened to show their nested content as a grid of their own, and the entry helpers side panel offers the siblings, children and values the bound XSD allows. All views share one model, so changes show up in the Text view immediately.

See the Grid View page for every grid feature.

docs.title: Code Folding
docs.text:
Code folding - collapse XML sections to focus on the parts that matter

For large XML files, you can collapse sections to focus on what you're working on:

  • Collapse: Click the minus (-) icon next to an element
  • Expand: Click the plus (+) icon to show the content again
  • Nested Folding: Collapse parent elements to hide all children

docs.title: Properties Inspector
docs.text:
The Properties inspector lets you view and edit a node's properties in all three XML views - Text, Tree, and Graphic.

The Properties inspector shows the details of the currently selected node and lets you change them. Toggle the panel with the toggle at the right end of the editor toolbar; it appears on the right side of the editor. The Properties Inspector page describes it for every document type.

docs.title: Selecting a Node
docs.text:
How you select a node depends on the active view:

  • Text view - Move the text caret into an element. That element is selected automatically and shown in the inspector. If the caret is not inside a well-formed element, the inspector shows a read-only view with the node's name and XPath. In large files (from 8 MB) the inspector follows the caret right away after edits in the grid. After you type, it shows no node until you pause for about 1.5 seconds. The file is then parsed again in the background, which takes a few seconds for very large files (about 5 seconds for 150 MB).
  • Tree view - Click a node in the tree (element, text, comment, CDATA, or processing instruction).
  • Graphic view - Select a row in the grid.

docs.title: What You Can Edit
docs.text:
Depending on the node type, the inspector lets you edit:

  • Element name - click the name in the node header at the top of the inspector to rename it
  • Namespace (prefix and URI) - in the NAMESPACE section, right below NODE & XPATH
  • Attributes - in the framed list of the VALUE & ATTRIBUTES section: click a name to rename it, click a value to edit it (Enter saves, Esc cancels), point at a row and click the trash icon to delete it, and use the row below the list to add one. You can also reach the rows with Tab: Enter edits the value, Delete removes the row
  • Text content of leaf elements
  • Text of comments, CDATA sections, and processing instructions

Editable values look like plain text; the field frame appears when you point at or click them. Long values wrap instead of being cut off. NODE & XPATH shows the element's Depth (the root element is 0) and has Copy XPath and Copy Node (XML) buttons next to the XPath. Sections without content are not shown. The ⋮ menu at the top of the inspector offers Copy XPath, Copy Node (XML), Expand All Sections and Collapse All Sections, and the star next to it adds the file to your Favorites. For the full layout, see Properties Inspector.

Your edits are written straight back to the document, so the source text always stays in sync. In the Text view, edits are applied as a minimal change that keeps your caret and scroll position in place.

docs.title: Schema Information
docs.text:
When the XML file is bound to an XSD schema, the inspector also shows what the schema says about the selected element. The node header's validation pill shows Valid, the number of errors, or Well-formed · no schema bound when no schema is bound.

  • Schema facts - Type, Base type, Derivation (with list item type / union member types), the facets including enumeration values, minOccurs/maxOccurs, Use, Order (the element's position in its parent sequence or choice, e.g. 3 of 3 · sequence), nillable, default and fixed values, Since … / Deprecated: …, the schema's appinfo, and identity constraints, assertions and type alternatives in CONSTRAINTS.
  • Declaration box - Declared in X.xsd · local element · type T with an Open in schema link that opens the XSD in the Graphic view, expanded along the element's path in the document, and selects this element there.
  • Editing the schema from here - where the declaration is editable, Type, minOccurs/maxOccurs, Nillable, Fixed, Default, the facets and the documentation/appinfo change the declaration in the XSD. The XSD opens as a background tab (your XML stays in front), the change is one undo step there, and after you save the XSD the XML document's schema facts are reloaded. Declarations from included/imported schemas and cached Schema Library copies are read-only. See Properties Inspector - Editing the bound schema.
  • Documentation - the element's documentation from the schema ("No documentation in the schema" when there is none).
  • Value check - "Value matches the schema facets" in green, or an amber warning such as "Value should be one of: …" when the current text breaks a facet.
  • EXAMPLE VALUES - shown as chips; click one to use it as the element's text.
  • VALID CHILDREN - shown as chips; click one to add that child element (None when the element allows no children).
  • USED IN - the containing element and its type.
  • Attributes - each row shows its declared type as a badge (* = required); attributes the schema does not declare are marked undeclared; enumerated attributes get a drop-down. DECLARED, NOT SET chips (e.g. + id *) add a missing declared attribute, with a default or fixed value filled in.

docs.title: Shared Across Views
docs.text:
All three views share a single in-memory model for each open document. This means your edits - and your full Undo / Redo history - are preserved when you switch between the Text, Tree, and Graphic views.

Switching views also keeps your place. The node at the caret is selected and opened in the Tree and the grid. Coming back to the Text view, the caret goes to the node you last selected, and the node's lines are tinted (see View Modes).

Note: Adding, deleting, or moving whole nodes (structural editing) is done in the Graphic view (the grid) via its right-click context menu. The Text and Tree views provide property editing through the inspector.

docs.title: Search (Find)
docs.text: Search works in every view mode — Text, Tree and Graphic — for XML documents, XSD schemas and JSON documents.

docs.title: Finding Text in Your Document
docs.text: Press Ctrl+F to open the Find feature and type the text you are looking for. Use the up and down arrows (Find Previous / Find Next, or Enter / Shift+Enter) to move between matches. When you reach the last match, the search wraps around and continues from the beginning.

docs.title: Search Works in All Views
docs.text:
You can search in the Text, Tree or Graphic view of a document:

  • Text view - Matches are highlighted in the source code. Replace is available here.
  • Graphic view (XML instances) - The search looks through element names, attribute names, and values across the whole document, including the cells of embedded tables. When you press the up/down arrows, the editor jumps directly to the matching node: if the match is inside a collapsed node, its parent nodes are expanded automatically, the matching row is selected, and it is scrolled into view.
  • Tree and Graphic views (XSD schemas) - The search looks through the schema nodes themselves: element/attribute/type names, documentation and appinfo, type references, fixed/default values, enumeration and facet values, and comments. Matching nodes are revealed (collapsed branches expand), selected, and scrolled into view — in the Graphic diagram this includes loading lazily rendered subtrees.
  • Tree and Graphic views (JSON documents) - The search looks through the keys and values of the document. Matches inside collapsed objects or arrays are revealed, selected, and scrolled into view, the same way as in the XML grid.

Searching is case-insensitive in all views.

docs.title: Switching Views While Searching
docs.text: If you switch the view mode (Text / Tree / Graphic) or the file tab while the search bar is open, the search automatically re-targets the view you switched to, so you can keep navigating without retyping your search term.

docs.title: Where Search Is Available
docs.text:
Pressing Ctrl+F opens an inline search bar at the top of the editor, with up/down chevron arrows for Find Previous / Find Next and a replace toggle (Text view only). The same bar works in every view mode, for every XML-family document type and for JSON documents.

Note: In the Tree and Graphic views, search is for finding and navigating only - Replace is not available there (the replace toggle is disabled). To replace text, use the Text view.

Note: HTML documents have a rendered, read-only Preview view instead of Tree/Graphic (see HTML Preview). Pressing Ctrl+F there searches the document's underlying markup text, not the rendered page.

docs.title: Searching Across Many Files
docs.text:
Ctrl+F searches the active document. To search - and replace - across all files of a folder, by plain text or by an XPath expression, use the Search activity in the Unified Shell: press Ctrl+Shift+F (Find in Files) or Ctrl+Shift+H (Replace in Files), or click the magnifying-glass icon in the activity bar. See the Search Panel guide.

Changed shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+F used to format the document - Format Document is now Shift+Alt+F.

docs.title: Auto-Completion (IntelliSense)
docs.text:
Auto-completion popup showing element suggestions

The editor automatically suggests valid elements and attributes based on your XSD schema:

  1. Type < to see a list of valid child elements
  2. Navigate through suggestions with arrow keys
  3. Press Enter to insert the selected element
  4. Press Escape to close the suggestions

The suggestions are context-sensitive - only elements valid at your current position are shown.

docs.title: Attribute Suggestions
docs.text:
Inside a start tag, type a space (or press Ctrl+Space) to see the element's attributes:

  • Schema-bound XML - the attributes your XSD declares for the element (including attribute groups), required ones first, with type and documentation in the tooltip
  • XSLT stylesheets - the attributes of every XSLT 3.0 element from a built-in catalog, no schema needed
  • Attributes with fixed values (XSD enumerations and booleans, XSLT values such as xml, html, text for xsl:output method) show their values right after insertion; Ctrl+Space inside the quotes brings them back
  • Attributes already in the tag are not offered again; accepting one inserts name="" with the cursor between the quotes

docs.title: Auto-Closing Tags
docs.text:
When you type an opening tag like <element>, the editor automatically adds the closing tag </element> and places your cursor between them.

Learn more: Auto-Completion Guide

docs.title: Binding an XSD Schema
docs.text:
Bind an XSD to the active document directly from the editor.

If your XML does not reference its schema (or you want to use a different one), you can bind an XSD by hand:

  1. Click the "No XSD" indicator in the status bar (it shows "XSD: name" once a schema is bound), or click the toolbar's Schema button (Set XSD Schema…).
  2. Choose an .xsd file.

The binding applies to the active document and drives both features at once:

  • IntelliSense - auto-completion suggests the elements and attributes the schema allows.
  • Schema validation - Validate (F8) and continuous validation check against the bound XSD.

docs.title: Go to Definition
docs.text:
Jump from an element in your XML document to the place in the bound XSD that declares it:

  • Graphic view (grid) and Tree view: right-click an element → Go to Definition
  • Text view: right-click inside an element → Go to Definition (Ctrl+Click), or hold Ctrl and click the element

The XSD opens in front (in its own tab, if it was not open yet) in the Graphic view. The diagram is expanded along the element's path from the document root, and the card of the declaration is selected. Because the path is followed, elements with the same name in different places - for example a Name inside Customer and a Name inside Product - each lead to their own declaration. If the path cannot be found in the schema (for example an element allowed by a wildcard), the first declaration with that name is selected instead.

The entry is available for elements only, and only when a schema is bound to the document.

docs.title: Pretty Print
docs.text:
Before pretty print

Click Format or use Shift+Alt+F to format your XML with proper indentation. (The Format ▾ arrow menu also offers Minify to strip all insignificant whitespace.)

After pretty print

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Validation panel showing errors and warnings

docs.title: How to Validate
docs.text:
1. Click Validate or press F8
  2. If your XML references a schema, it's loaded automatically - or bind one yourself, see Binding an XSD Schema
  3. Errors and warnings appear in the PROBLEMS panel below the editor (and in the Validation activity's PROBLEMS list)
  4. Click an error to jump to the problem location

docs.title: Supported Validation Methods
docs.text: Method Description Well-Formed Check Ensures basic XML syntax is correct XSD Validation Validates against XML Schema files Schematron Validates against business rules

docs.title: Supported Schema Formats
docs.text: Format Support XSD (XML Schema) Full support (1.0 and 1.1) Schematron Full support DTD, RELAX NG Validation and IntelliSense (Schema Support) RelaxNG Not supported

docs.title: Schematron Integration
docs.text: Schematron validation in the Validation panel - the bound rules file in SOURCES, the findings in the PROBLEMS list

docs.title: What is Schematron?
docs.text: Schematron lets you create custom validation rules for your XML documents. While XSD schemas validate the structure, Schematron validates business rules - for example, "if field A contains X, then field B must not be empty."

docs.title: How to Use Schematron
docs.text:
1. Open an XML file in the editor
  2. Open the Validation panel from the activity bar
  3. In the SOURCES section, click Change on the Schematron row and pick a .sch file - or pick a favorited Schematron from the row's star menu, or simply drop a .sch file onto the row
  4. Click Run Validation - the findings appear in the PROBLEMS list (each row tagged with a Schematron badge); click a problem to jump to the offending element
  5. Enable Validate while typing (the panel's ⋮ menu) to check as you type

Problems whose rules define quick fixes can be corrected in place: click the yellow lightbulb in the editor gutter (or press Alt+Enter / Ctrl+.), or right-click the problem row and pick a fix from the Quick Fix submenu. See Schematron Quick Fixes.

docs.title: Saving Schematron Files as Favorites
docs.text:
Save frequently used Schematron files for quick access: - Add them to your Favorites (for example with Add current in the Favorites panel while the .sch file is open) - Organize them in favorites folders like "Business Rules" - Bind a saved rules file in one click via the star menu on the Validation panel's Schematron row - or via Validate with Other Schematron ▸ Favorites in the Explorer's right-click menu

Learn more: Schematron Support | Favorites System

docs.title: XPath and XQuery
docs.text:
The Query Console docked below the editor - XPath query on the left, the result on the right

Use XPath and XQuery to find and extract data from your XML documents. The fastest way is the Query Console, a panel that docks along the bottom of the editor and always runs against the active document.

docs.title: Using the Query Console
docs.text:
1. Toggle the console with Ctrl+Shift+X or the toolbar's terminal icon
  2. Choose XPath or XQuery with the mode toggle
  3. Enter your expression - it is syntax-highlighted, and IntelliSense suggests element names, functions, and axes as you type (or on Ctrl+Space)
  4. Click Run or press Ctrl+Enter (Enter inserts a new line; the hint below the query says so)
  5. The result appears in the read-only results pane on the right, with syntax highlighting; Copy puts it on the clipboard

Save stores the current expression as a named snippet, and the Snippets menu loads any saved XPath or XQuery snippet back into the console. See Query Console for the full reference.

docs.title: XPath Examples
docs.text: Expression Description //element Find all elements named "element" //element/@attr Find all "attr" attributes on "element" /root/child[1] Find the first child of root count(//item) Count all item elements //text() Find all text nodes

docs.title: XQuery Examples
docs.text:
Expression Description for $x in //item return $x Return all items for $x in //item where $x/@id='1' return $x/name Filter and return

Use the Examples menu for quick insertion of common expressions.

docs.title: Bundled Example Collections
docs.text:
Your FreeXmlToolkit installation ships ready-to-run query collections in the examples folder next to the application:

  • examples/xpath/ - 32 XPath 3.1 expressions (one per file, each with a comment header). Files 01-20 cover the basics; files 21-32 are a reporting series that joins positions, asset master data and transactions and outputs CSV, ASCII tables/charts, Markdown tables or JSON.
  • examples/xquery/ - 17 XQuery 3.1 scripts. Files 01-11 are data-quality checks with HTML reports; files 12-17 are reporting/export examples (CSV export, ASCII dashboard, Markdown fund report, JSON export, pivot table, two-fund comparison).
  • examples/xproc/ - 8 XProc 3.0 pipelines, from a minimal identity pipeline to multi-step chains: slimming with p:delete, CSV/JSON export by orchestrating the bundled stylesheets, metadata stamping, p:for-each iteration, p:choose branching and a Schematron SVRL report. See the folder's README.md.
  • examples/xspec/ - 5 XSpec test files for an XSLT stylesheet, an XQuery module and a Schematron (with the code under test next to them); 05-failing-demo.xspec fails on purpose to show what a failure looks like. Open one and choose Tools → Run XSpec Tests.

All examples target the FundsXML4 sample documents in examples/xml/. The simplest way to run one: open the file directly and press the toolbar's Run button (Ctrl+Enter) - query, XSLT and XProc files are first-class editor documents that run against the Input dropdown's selection (by default the most recently active XML document). Alternatively paste a query into the query panel or the Query Console - the map:, array: and math: function namespaces are pre-declared, so expressions using map:merge(), array:size() etc. run without any prolog. Each folder contains a README.md describing every example.

docs.title: XML/Excel/CSV Converter
docs.text:
Choose Tools → Spreadsheet Converter… (Ctrl+E) to open the converter dialog:

  • XML to Excel: Export XML data to Excel spreadsheet
  • XML to CSV: Export XML data to CSV file
  • Excel to XML: Import Excel data as XML
  • CSV to XML: Import CSV data as XML

The Excel workbook looks like the Data Dictionary export: a dark header row that stays in view while you scroll, striped rows, XPaths in a monospace font, and container elements in bold. It also has an AutoFilter and prints one page wide.

When an XSD is bound to the document, each value goes into a cell of its schema type. The type is followed through derived simple types, xs:simpleContent and imported schemas:

Schema type Excel cell xs:integer, xs:int, xs:long, … Number, format 0 xs:decimal Number, showing as many decimals as the XML value (10.50 → 10.50) xs:double, xs:float Number, General format xs:boolean (true / false) TRUE / FALSE xs:date, xs:dateTime, xs:time Date / time, yyyy-mm-dd / yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss / hh:mm:ss

Some values stay text, so that importing the workbook gives back exactly the same XML:

  • values with more than 15 digits;
  • leading zeros or +;
  • 0 / 1 booleans;
  • dates with a timezone or before 1900;
  • times more precise than milliseconds;
  • lists, unions and values that do not match their type.

Without a schema, every value is text.

Excel to XML turns typed cells back into their XML form. It also uses an XSD, so that cells you entered or changed by hand still give valid values:

  • the date cell 31.01.2024 under xs:dateTime becomes 2024-01-31T00:00:00;
  • a plain number such as 45322 under xs:date becomes 2024-01-31;
  • a date-formatted cell under xs:decimal stays a number;
  • 1 / 0 or the text TRUE under xs:boolean become true / false;
  • 42.0 under xs:int becomes 42;
  • blanks around a number or date are removed;
  • a formula gives its result instead of the formula text (this also applies without a schema).

CSV to XML uses the XSD too. A CSV holds only text, so the import repairs values that do not fit their type yet. This is typical after the file went through a spreadsheet application:

In the CSV XSD type Imported 1.234,50 · 1,234.50 · 1 234,50 xs:decimal 1234.50 31.01.2024 · 2024/01/31 xs:date 2024-01-31 31.01.2024 10:15 xs:dateTime 2024-01-31T10:15:00 9:05 xs:time 09:05:00 TRUE · WAHR · yes xs:boolean true

A value that is already valid for its type is never changed. For example, 007 under xs:int and 1.234 under xs:decimal stay as written. Text values are not touched.

The delimiter decides ambiguous values. In a semicolon file (as European Excel writes it) a single comma is the decimal separator and 01/02/2024 is 1 February. In a comma file it is the other way round. Values that stay ambiguous (1,234 in a tab file) are imported as written, and validation shows the error. Text cells in an Excel import are repaired the same way, as far as that is unambiguous.

The import (Excel or CSV) takes the XSD from the Schema (XSD) field of the converter dialog. If you leave the field empty, it uses the schema the file declares: the root element's xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation / xsi:schemaLocation, resolved relative to the workbook's folder, or the Schema Library entry for its namespace. The imported document is bound to that XSD. Without a schema, the cells' own types and formats decide, as before. A value that does not fit its type is imported as written, and validation shows the error.

The CSV export uses the bound XSD as well. CSV has no cell types, so the file gets an extra Data Type column with each value's XSD built-in type (decimal, date, dateTime, …). Values that are valid for their type are written without quotes; all text fields are quoted:

"XPath";"Value";"Type";"Data Type"
"/FundsXML4/ControlData/ContentDate";2021-11-30;"element";"date"
"/FundsXML4/ControlData/DataSupplier/Name";"Erste Asset Management";"element";"string"

Values are written exactly as in the XML. A timezone or a leading zero stays as it is. A value that contains the delimiter, a quote or a line break is always quoted, with inner quotes doubled. CSV to XML reads such values back correctly, including line breaks inside a value, and ignores the Data Type column. Without a schema, the CSV keeps the plain format: no Data Type column, and quotes only where needed.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Choose Edit → Insert Template… (Ctrl+T) to insert a snippet:

  • Insert pre-defined XML snippets
  • Create your own templates (Settings → Editor → TEMPLATES)
  • Organize templates by category

Learn more: Template Management

docs.title: Schema Generator
docs.text:
With the XML document active, open the editor toolbar's Schema ▾ menu (click the small arrow next to the Schema button) and choose Generate XSD from XML (or Generate XSD from XML Files… for several files) to generate an XSD schema from your XML. Both entries are also in the menu bar's Tools menu; Generate XSD from XML Files… works there even without an open document, because it asks for its files itself:

  • Analyze XML structure
  • Generate matching XSD schema
  • Customize type detection

docs.title: Favorites
docs.text:
Save frequently used files for quick access:

  • Add Favorite (Ctrl+D) - Save the current file to favorites
  • Favorites activity - Click the star icon in the activity bar to open the Favorites panel; click any entry to open it as a tab
  • Your favorites appear as star menus next to the file rows of the Transform, Validation, PDF/FOP panels and the Signature page

Learn more: Favorites System

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
The complete list is on the Keyboard Shortcuts page (and in the app under Help → Keyboard Shortcuts).

Especially useful while editing XML:

Shortcut Action Ctrl+Space or < Open auto-completion Shift+Alt+F Format / pretty-print F8 Validate Ctrl+T Insert a template Ctrl+Alt+X / Ctrl+Alt+C Grid view: copy the XPath / the node as XML Ctrl+Click Text view: Go to Definition in the bound XSD Ctrl+mouse wheel, Ctrl+0 Zoom (Text: font size, Graphic: the grid) / reset

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Multiple Files: Open multiple XML files in different tabs
  • Remember Location: The editor remembers the last folder you used
  • Font Size / Zoom: Hold Ctrl and scroll the mouse wheel to adjust the font size in the Text view (Ctrl+0 resets); in the Graphic view the same gesture zooms the whole grid
  • Quick Validation: Errors are highlighted as you type
  • Drag & Drop: Drag files directly into the editor window
  • Recent Files: Reopen recent files from the Explorer panel's RECENT section or the Welcome page

docs.title: XML Encryption
docs.text:
FreeXmlToolkit encrypts and decrypts XML according to W3C XML Encryption 1.1: single elements, the content of elements, whole documents or any file, for certificates, public keys, shared keys and passwords - on the Sign & Encrypt page, from the XML editor's context menu and on the command line (fxt-cli encrypt / fxt-cli decrypt).

Encryption works on the saved file. The encrypted result is written next to it (name.encrypted.xml) and opened; a decrypted document opens as a new, unsaved tab - it is written to disk only when you save it.

docs.title: The Page
docs.text:
Open Sign & Encrypt in the activity bar. Its side panel lists the actions; three of them are about encryption:

Action What it does Encrypt Encrypts the document, the element at the editor's caret or the elements an XPath selects, for one or more recipients Decrypt Decrypts every EncryptedData your key opens - also several layers (super-encryption) Inspect Encryption Shows what is encrypted, for whom and with which algorithms - without a key

The DOCUMENT row follows the active editor document; Browse picks another file.

In the XML editor, right-click an element → Encrypt Element… opens Encrypt with that element as target; Decrypt… (shown when the document contains EncryptedData) opens Decrypt.

docs.title: Encrypt
docs.text:
1. What to encrypt
    • Whole document - the document element with everything in it.
    • Element at the caret - the element the editor's caret was in.
    • XPath - every element an XPath 1.0 expression selects. Namespace prefixes declared on the document element can be used; //*[local-name()='card'] works without any.
    • Only the content - the element's children are encrypted, the element itself (with its attributes) stays visible (Type=…#Content).
  2. Data algorithm - the block cipher of the data. AES-256-GCM is the default and the recommendation; see the algorithm table.
  3. Recipients - who can decrypt. Every recipient gets its own EncryptedKey with the same data key, so each of them opens the document alone. Add them with the buttons after Add:
    • Certificate - a recipient's certificate or public key (PEM or DER). RSA keys use RSA-OAEP, EC keys ECDH-ES, X25519/X448 keys their key agreement.
    • From keystore - the certificate of the alias in the KEYSTORE section above.
    • Key file - a shared symmetric key (16, 24 or 32 bytes as hex, Base64 or raw). You can give it a KeyName so the receiver knows which key to take.
    • Password - the key is derived from a password with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations, HMAC-SHA256).
  4. Encrypt. The status line says how many elements were encrypted; legacy algorithms add a warning.

docs.title: Advanced options
docs.text: Option Meaning RSA key transport RSA-OAEP 1.1 (default), RSA-OAEP MGF1P, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (legacy) OAEP digest / OAEP mask Digest (SHA-1 … SHA-512) and mask generation function (MGF1 with SHA-1 … SHA-512) of RSA-OAEP 1.1 Key derivation (EC keys) ConcatKDF (default) or HKDF after ECDH-ES / X25519 / X448, and its digest Key wrap The key wrap for shared keys, passwords and key agreement (default: AES matching the data key); none uses the key file itself as data key (one recipient only) Certificate reference How an EncryptedKey names the recipient's certificate: issuer and serial number (default), the whole certificate, subject key identifier, subject name or nothing Recipient attribute A name written into every EncryptedKey (Recipient="…") EncryptedKeys next to the data The EncryptedKeys are written beside the EncryptedData with a ReferenceList, the EncryptedData points at them with RetrievalMethod Encryption properties Free name=value pairs, written as EncryptionProperties

docs.title: Decrypt
docs.text:
Choose the key:

Key source What to give Keystore The KEYSTORE section above: a .jks / .p12 file, the alias (or none if the keystore holds one key) and the passwords Private key (PEM) Your private key as PEM (PKCS#8 or traditional, also encrypted - then its password) Key file The shared symmetric key; optionally the KeyName it stands for Password The document's password

Decrypt replaces every EncryptedData the key opens - outer layers first, so super-encrypted content opens too - and removes EncryptedKeys that pointed at it from outside. The result opens as a new tab. A document that is a single EncryptedData of non-XML data (a file encrypted as binary) is decrypted to its original bytes, which you save where you like.

CipherReference (cipher data in a separate file) is supported for files next to the document; other locations are refused.

docs.title: Inspect Encryption
docs.text: Lists every EncryptedData with its location, type, algorithm, cipher data and the ways to its key: EncryptedKeys with method and recipient, KeyName, certificate reference (issuer and serial, subject, SKI), key agreement and derivation, password parameters - plus warnings for legacy algorithms. No key is needed.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
Kind Algorithms Legacy Data AES-128/192/256-GCM, AES-128/192/256-CBC, Camellia-128/192/256-CBC, SEED-128-CBC, TripleDES-CBC all CBC modes, TripleDES Key transport (RSA) RSA-OAEP 1.1 (xmlenc11#rsa-oaep, digest and MGF selectable), RSA-OAEP MGF1P, RSA-1_5 RSA-1_5 Key wrap AES-128/192/256 KW, Camellia KW, SEED KW, TripleDES KW Camellia, SEED, TripleDES Key agreement ECDH-ES, X25519, X448 finite-field Diffie-Hellman (decryption only) Key derivation ConcatKDF, HKDF, PBKDF2 (passwords) –

Legacy algorithms are there for old partners: CBC block ciphers have no integrity protection (padding oracles), RSA-1_5 is open to Bleichenbacher attacks, TripleDES has a 64-bit block. They work, but every use shows a warning, and an administrator can switch them off (below). For new data use AES-GCM with RSA-OAEP or ECDH-ES.

The full list with URIs: fxt-cli encrypt --list-algorithms.

docs.title: Sign and Encrypt
docs.text:
Signing and encrypting are two steps on the same page:

  • Encrypt, then sign - sign the encrypted file: the signature covers the encrypted form, anyone can check it without decrypting.
  • Sign, then encrypt - encrypt the signed file: the receiver decrypts first, then verifies.

The Decryption Transform for XML Signature (signatures that exclude later-encrypted parts) is not supported: decrypt first, then verify.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
# the card elements for a partner's certificate
fxt-cli encrypt order.xml -x '//p:card' --ns p=urn:pay --cert partner.pem
# the whole document for two certificates and a password from an environment variable
fxt-cli encrypt report.xml --cert alice.cer --cert bob-ec.pem --password-env REPORT_PW -o report.enc.xml
# decrypt with a keystore, a PEM key, a shared key or a password
fxt-cli decrypt order.encrypted.xml --keystore me.p12 --storepass-env KS_PW -o order.xml
fxt-cli decrypt report.enc.xml --password            # prompts
# what is encrypted - no key
fxt-cli decrypt --inspect -f json order.encrypted.xml

All options: Command Line → encrypt / decrypt.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Encrypted documents are read without any DOCTYPE, external entities or network access; Santuario runs with secure validation.
  • At most 10,000 EncryptedData elements, 64 EncryptedKeys per EncryptedData and 10 million PBKDF2 iterations are accepted; a CipherReference may only name a file next to the document (up to 512 MB).
  • Passwords are never written to logs or telemetry; the telemetry counts encryptions with the algorithm families, the number of recipients and whether a legacy algorithm was used.
  • Administrators can disable XML encryption (xmlenc.allowed=false) or the legacy algorithms (xmlenc.legacyAlgorithms.allowed=false), see Administration.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: release/examples/encryption/ (in the installation's examples folder) holds an order encrypted in every variant, demo keys and their passwords - see its README.md.

docs.title: XProc Pipelines
docs.text:
XProc 3.0 pipelines (.xpl, .xproc) are first-class editor documents, executed with the embedded XML Calabash 3 engine:

The bundled 03-positions-csv.xpl example after Run Pipeline: the pipeline runs the CSV export stylesheet (referenced with a relative href) against the Automatic target and streams the result into the OUTPUT panel.

  • Run Pipeline (the toolbar's Run button or its ▾ menu, or Ctrl+Enter) runs the active pipeline. The primary input (source port) is the document chosen in the Input dropdown — by default the most recently active XML document, exactly like Run Query and Run Transform.
  • Relative hrefs in the pipeline (p:document, p:xslt stylesheets, Schematron schemas) resolve against the pipeline file's directory.
  • Results appear in the OUTPUT panel; XML, HTML, text/CSV and JSON outputs are routed to the matching view automatically.
  • Self-contained pipelines (no input ports, or ports with default bindings) run without a target.
  • File → New offers an XProc skeleton (p:declare-step with source/result ports and p:identity).
  • Ready-to-run examples ship in examples/xproc/ — see Bundled Example Collections.

Saxon-HE limitations

p:validate-with-xml-schema and p:xsl-formatter require Saxon-EE and are not available; use the Validation activity (Xerces, full XSD 1.1) and the PDF/FOP activity instead. p:validate-with-json-schema is not supported in this bundle.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
Pipelines are programs, so by default they run with restrictions:

  • Pipelines that use p:os-exec (run a program), p:run (run a pipeline computed at run time) or p:http-request are not run, also when the step is in an imported library. The message names the step.
  • Documents, imports and doc() may only be local files; loading from http:, https: or ftp: fails with a message that says so.
  • Reading and writing local files (p:store, p:file-copy, p:file-delete, …) works as before, with your rights: run only pipelines you trust.

Settings → Network & Security → Run XProc pipelines without restrictions lifts all of it (an administrator can lock it, see Administration & Policies). The same rules apply to fxt-cli transform. See also the Threat Model.

docs.title: XSD Tools
docs.text:
Note: The standalone XSD Editor tab has been retired. XSD editing — the Text/Tree/Graphic views, the inspector, the Type Library, type editing, documentation generation, schema flattening and schema analysis — now lives in the Unified Shell (open an .xsd file; "go to schema definition" from the XML editor opens the schema's graphic view at the element). The capabilities below are unchanged; they are reached through the shell rather than a dedicated sidebar tab.

This part of the application provides tools for working with XML Schemas (XSD). These tools help you understand, document, and use XSD files effectively.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When you open an .xsd file in the Unified Shell, the editor host and the Schema activity provide several capabilities, each with a specific purpose:

Capability Description Graphic View Visual schema editor with interactive tree Overview View All top-level components in one table: reorder, sort, add, rename, attributes, identity constraints, assertions, namespaces Type Library Browse and analyze all types in your schema Type Editor Edit ComplexTypes and SimpleTypes graphically Text View Raw XSD source code editor Schema Analysis Statistics, type library with unused-component cleanup, quality checks, identity constraints and XPath validation - exportable as CSV / JSON / HTML / PDF / Excel Documentation Generate HTML, Word, or PDF documentation Preview The editor's Preview view renders HTML files, e.g. generated documentation opened in the shell Generate Example Data Create sample XML from schema with customizable rules and profiles Flatten Schema Merge includes into one standalone file, with optional reduction for server-side validation

docs.title: 1. Graphic View
docs.text:
The Graphic View lets you explore and edit your schemas visually.

An XSD open in the Unified Shell's Graphic view, with the Schema activity panel on the left

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Visual Tree: See your XSD as an interactive, hierarchical tree
  • Easy Navigation: Click on elements to explore their structure
  • Edit Documentation: Add or edit documentation for schema elements using the inline tab-based editor (no modal dialogs)
  • Constraints on the Cards: Element and attribute cards list their key, keyref and unique constraints and the assertions of their type, including inherited ones - see Constraints on the Cards
  • Named Types in Frames: The content of a named complex type is drawn in a light-yellow, dashed frame titled with the type's name; it is read-only there and edited in the type's editor - see Named Types in Frames
  • Type Picker: Choose an element's or attribute's type from a list of the schema's own types and all XSD built-in datatypes, each explained in a side pane
  • Add Examples: Include example values for elements
  • Drag and Drop: Move or copy elements, compositors, group references and attributes by dragging their cards - see Moving and Copying by Drag and Drop
  • Reorder and Duplicate: Move nodes up and down, copy, cut, paste and duplicate them from the context menu
  • Full Undo/Redo: Go back and forward through your changes
  • Export: Save the diagram as PNG, SVG or PDF, or copy it as an image (File → Export View…, Edit → Copy View as Image, or right-click the empty canvas) - see Exporting a Graphical View

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Open your XSD file in the editor host and switch to the Graphic view
  2. The schema appears as an interactive tree
  3. Select an element by clicking on it
  4. Edit properties in the panel on the right (name, type, cardinality/occurrence, use, form, constraints, documentation, and facets)
  5. Add children using the context menu (right-click)
  6. Reorder nodes by dragging them to a new place, or with Move Up / Move Down from the context menu; Delete removes the selected node

Editing properties from any view: The same Properties pane is available in the Text view as well as the Graphic and Tree views. See Editing Schema Properties from Any View below.

docs.title: Reading a Card
docs.text:
Every node is a card with two lines: the name and, below it in a monospace font, the type (xs:string, DataSupplierType) - or the kind of node when it has no type (element, group). The cards of one sequence, choice or all share the width of the widest one.

What you see Meaning Symbol </> Simple content (a simple type, no children) Symbol of a small tree Content of its own: a complex type, or an element with children Symbol @ Attribute Folder symbol Group or attribute group reference Symbol colour Kind of node: blue element, teal attribute, green simple type, grey complex type or group Pill 0..1, 1..*, 2..5 Cardinality; none is shown for the default 1..1 Pill req / opt Attribute use: required or optional Dashed outline Optional (minOccurs="0", or an attribute that is not required) A second outline behind the card Repeats (maxOccurs above 1 or unbounded) Button with › / ‹ Opens / closes the card; a blue dot means its children load when you open it Small box with lines, signpost or stack xs:sequence, xs:choice, xs:all; a cardinality other than 1..1 is written below it Small blue I in the corner The node comes from an included file

The title chip at the top-left names the selected card (or the diagram's root when nothing is selected) with its kind, type and content model, e.g. DataSupplier element · DataSupplierType · sequence. The zoom control at the bottom-right zooms out and in; click the percentage to return to 100 % (also Ctrl −, Ctrl +, Ctrl 0).

docs.title: Constraints on the Cards
docs.text:
A card lists what limits its node below the type lines, one row per constraint:

Label Meaning Row shows KEY xs:key Name and fields UNIQ xs:unique Name and fields REF xs:keyref Name and the key it refers to ASSERT xs:assert or xs:assertion The test, shortened

An element reference shows the constraints of the global element. Assertions come from the card's type and its base types. A card shows up to four rows, followed by +N more.

Hover over the rows to see every constraint in full: selector, fields, the complete test, and the type it was declared in. To add or delete a constraint, use the CONSTRAINTS section of the Properties pane; it lists what is declared directly on the selected node, so an assertion inherited from a type is changed in that type.

To hide the rows, turn off View → Show Constraints in Diagram. The setting applies to all open diagrams and is remembered.

Constraints on target nodes. A key, unique or keyref is declared on one element but checks the values of another: its field target. For example, in FundsXML4 the element Fund declares the key benchmarkID with the selector FundStaticData/Benchmarks/Benchmark and the field BenchmarkID. Turn on Constraints on target nodes, and the BenchmarkID card also lists ← benchmarkID @ Fund. The row has an outlined label and muted text, so you can tell it apart from the card's own constraints. An attribute field (@code) shows on the attribute card. A type used in several places matches only where its path fits the selector. Only fields count, not the elements the selector picks. The option is off by default.

Both switches are in the DISPLAY section at the top of the Properties pane, which appears for XSD documents, and in the View menu (Show Constraints on Target Nodes). They change open diagrams at once and are remembered.

docs.title: Named Types in Frames
docs.text:
When an element uses a named complex type (<xs:element name="Address_EU" type="EU-Address"/>), the content it gets from that type is drawn inside a light-yellow frame with a dashed border. The type's name is the frame's title, top left. Everything inside the frame belongs to the type, not to the element: the same content appears wherever the type is used.

  • The frame is read-only. Renaming, deleting, moving, cutting or pasting a node inside it, and adding new content to the element that holds the frame, are refused with a short explanation. The context menu of such a node starts with Edit Type '…' and greys out the changing actions; Copy Node and Copy XPath stay available. The Properties pane shows "Part of type '…'. It is read-only here" with an Edit type button and disables its editors.
  • To change the content, edit the type: double-click the frame title, choose Edit Type '…' in the context menu, or use Edit type in the Properties pane. The type opens in its own Type Editor tab, where its content can be edited. This works inside a Type Editor tab too: a type used there opens in a further Type Editor tab (of the same schema), so nested types can be followed level by level. A type that is already open just has its tab brought to the front.
  • The element itself stays editable: its name, cardinality, type and documentation belong to the element's declaration, so they can still be changed on its card.
  • Extensions show the base type as a nested frame. For a type defined by xs:complexContent/xs:extension, the frame of the derived type contains a second frame titled with the base type, holding the inherited content; the extension's own content follows below it. In the type editor of the derived type only the base type's frame is shown (and read-only), its own content is editable.
  • Anonymous types defined inline in an element are not framed: their content belongs to the element and is edited in place.

Address_EU uses the type EU-Address: its content is drawn in the type's frame. The selected street belongs to the type, so the Properties pane shows it read-only with Edit type. Expanding Branch (which extends EU-Address) shows the base type's frame nested inside the Branch-Address frame.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Right-click for a context menu with common actions (Add Element… / Add Attribute… with all properties - see Adding an Element or Attribute, Rename…, Change Type…, Change Cardinality…, add/move/delete). Change Type… opens a small dialog with the type picker, pre-filled with the current type - the same dialog as in the Tree view
  • Edit the name and every other property in the Properties pane on the right
  • Only edits that keep the schema valid are possible; see Only Valid Changes
  • Ctrl+Z to undo, Ctrl+Y to redo
  • Ctrl+S to save (a backup is created automatically - Settings → Schemas & Validation → XSD lets you turn this off or change the number of kept versions, 3 by default)
  • The toolbar's Save ▾ split button saves the schema; its arrow menu offers Save As… (Ctrl+Shift+S, save under a new name) and Save All (saves every open tab)

docs.title: What the Diagram Shows
docs.text:
• Expanding cards. Click a card's expand button to open it. In a large schema the diagram builds the first few thousand cards up front; the rest loads when you open the card that holds it. Simple types and built-in types have no content to open, so they have no expand button.
  • Inherited content. A type built with xs:extension also shows the content of its base type. A type built with xs:restriction shows its own elements, because a restriction restates the content model, plus the attributes of its base type, except those it redeclares or prohibits.
  • Wildcards. xs:any and xs:anyAttribute appear as cards named any and anyAttribute, with the allowed namespace and the validation mode. Their right-click menu offers Delete and Copy XPath.
