  • Redefined files. The file named by xs:redefine or xs:override is loaded, and its global elements appear like those of an include. Its definitions are shown in their changed form: a redefined type builds on the original, an overridden one replaces it. They are read-only, and saving leaves the file and your xs:redefine as they are.
  • Group references. xs:group and xs:attributeGroup references appear as their own cards, labelled group: Name and attributeGroup: Name. Attribute group cards stay closed until you open them. The right-click menu of these cards offers only Delete and Copy XPath: Delete removes the reference, not the shared definition.
  • Placeholder cards. When the diagram cannot show something, a card names it, and it has no right-click actions:
    • Unresolved type: X, Unresolved group: X, Unresolved attribute group: X: the definition was not found, often because it is in a file that could not be loaded.
    • External: ...: a referenced element was not found. It usually belongs to another namespace whose schema is not loaded.
  • Files changed on disk. The schema's own file and every local file it pulls in are watched: includes at any depth, imports and the targets of xs:redefine/xs:override. When such a file changes, is deleted or appears, one question names the files for each schema tab. A file with a new date but the same content asks nothing. Reload rebuilds the schema from the current editor text, so unsaved text stays, but the undo history of diagram edits is cleared. Ignore keeps the current view until the file changes again. Open and closed cards, zoom and scroll position survive any rebuild. An XML document watches the schema bound to it the same way, also without a tab for that schema. Its schema facts and IntelliSense then refresh without asking, because the document stays as it is.

  • Warning bar for missing schemas. A bar above the diagram names the includes and imports that could not be loaded, also those inside imported schemas and nested includes. Circular includes are not failures. Dismiss hides the bar until the set of failures changes. A schema you have not saved yet has no file location, so it cannot resolve its includes: save it first.

For what the diagram leaves out, see Supported XSD Features.

docs.title: Moving and Copying by Drag and Drop
docs.text:
In the Graphic view you can rearrange the schema by dragging its cards: elements, compositors (sequence, choice, all), group references and attributes.

  1. Press the left mouse button on a card and move the mouse a few pixels - the drag starts. While you drag a card, the diagram does not pan (dragging on empty space still pans it).
  2. Point at the target and watch the feedback:
    • A blue line above or below a card: the node is dropped before or after that card (point at the upper or lower quarter of the card).
    • A green frame around a card: the node is dropped into it (point at the middle). Elements go into the card's sequence, choice or all; attributes go into its complex type. Sequence, choice and all symbols only accept drops into them.
    • A red frame: the drop would not produce a valid schema. If you release there, a message explains why and nothing changes.
  3. Release the mouse button to move the node. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on macOS) while releasing to copy it instead. The copy keeps its name, or gets the suffix _copy if a sibling already has that name.

More details:

  • Near the edge of the visible area the diagram scrolls automatically.
  • Press Esc to cancel the drag.
  • Named types are read-only in their frames. Dropping into an element whose content comes from a named complex type, next to a node inside such a frame, or moving a node out of it is refused - edit the type in its type editor instead. Copying a node out of a frame (Ctrl) is allowed.
  • Shared definitions ask first. Dropping into or out of a named global group, or into a named type in its type editor, that is used by more than one declaration changes every place that uses it. A confirmation dialog tells you how often the definition is used ("This changes a shared definition … used N times").
  • Not possible (shown with a red frame):
    • moving a global declaration into a content model - use a reference (ref) instead
    • moving a local declaration to the top level of the schema
    • dropping attributes among elements, or elements among attributes
    • dropping into an element with a simple type (such as xs:string)
    • changing nodes that come from an imported schema
    • changing the content of a named type inside its frame (see above)
  • Every drop is one undo step - Ctrl+Z reverts it. The Text view shows the change right away.
  • As an alternative without the mouse, use Move Up / Move Down from the context menu.

docs.title: Adding an Element or Attribute
docs.text:
Add Element…, Add Root Element and Add Attribute… (right-click in the Graphic or Tree view) open one dialog in which you set the new node's properties right away. You do not have to fill them in afterwards in the Properties pane.

  • Name: pre-filled and selected, so you can type over it.
  • Type: the type picker with built-in types and the schema's own types. Leave it empty for no type. Attributes are offered simple types only.
  • Occurs (elements): min, max and unbounded. A top-level element has no cardinality, so the row is hidden for Add Root Element.
  • Use (attributes): optional, required or prohibited.
  • Documentation: written as xs:annotation/xs:documentation.
  • More (collapsed): Default or Fixed value, Form (qualified / unqualified / schema default), nillable, and for top-level elements abstract and Substitution group.

The input is checked while you type. A red note names the problem and OK does nothing until it is fixed. For example, the name must be a valid XML name, min may not be greater than max, a node cannot have both a default and a fixed value, and an attribute with a default must be optional. The new node is added with all its properties as one undo step.

docs.title: Only Valid Changes
docs.text:
The graphical editor only lets you make changes that keep the schema valid XML Schema. This applies to the Properties pane, the right-click menus of the Graphic and Tree views, Paste and drag & drop alike.

  • Menu entries that cannot apply are disabled. An element with a simple type such as xs:int cannot contain child elements or attributes, so Add Element…, Add Container Element… and Add Attribute… are greyed out for it. An element reference (ref="…") takes its type and content from the referenced element, so its Type field and Change Type… are locked. Child elements need a Sequence, Choice or All first.
  • A change that would replace existing content asks first. Setting a type on an element that defines its own content (an inline complex type, for example a sequence with child elements) would leave both in the schema. Instead a dialog explains what would be lost and offers Replace with xs:int. Confirming removes the inline content and sets the type. Cancel keeps the schema unchanged. Adding a Sequence, Choice or All to an element that has a type works the same way: the dialog offers Remove type and add sequence.
  • Everything is one undo step. Ctrl+Z brings back the inline content or the type you replaced.
  • Switching a compositor keeps its children. Changing a Sequence into a Choice or All moves the child elements over. An All is refused when it would hold a nested Sequence or Choice, or, in an XSD 1.0 schema, an element with maxOccurs greater than 1.
  • Attributes land in the right place. For an element whose type is a named complex type, a new attribute is added to that type. For a complex type with simple content it goes into the xs:extension.

When an edit is not possible, a short message says why.

docs.title: Automatic Resolution of Imported Schemas
docs.text:
Some schemas import other schemas that are not shipped alongside them. For example, many financial schemas contain:

<xs:import namespace="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#"
           schemaLocation="xmldsig-core-schema.xsd"/>

If xmldsig-core-schema.xsd is not next to your schema, FreeXmlToolkit resolves the import automatically, trying these sources in order:

  1. Next to the declaring file - a relative schemaLocation is resolved against the folder of the schema that declares the import (also for imports declared inside an imported or included file).
  2. The Schema Library - your own mappings, registered XML catalogs and the bundled standards, matched by the declared location (system ID) first and then by the import's namespace. A hit here loads without any network access.
  3. The schema cache - a previously downloaded copy under ~/.freeXmlToolkit/cache/schemas/, again without network access.
  4. The declared URL - an http(s) schemaLocation is downloaded (following redirects, using your proxy settings).
  5. The namespace URL - as a last resort the schema is fetched from the import's namespace URL, which is how the W3C hosts the XML signature schema, for instance.

Downloaded content is verified to be a real XML Schema, then stored in the cache and saved next to the schema that references it, under its original name - for the example above as xmldsig-core-schema.xsd in your schema's folder. From then on that file is used: it is what Schema Analysis shows as Resolved path, what Open Referenced File opens, and it works offline. A relative location keeps its folder layout (../common/types.xsd lands one folder up, in common); an absolute http(s) location is saved under its file name next to the referencing schema (http://www.w3.org/2001/xml.xsd → xml.xsd), and the schemaLocation in your schema stays as it is. Imports are resolved transitively: an imported schema's own xs:import and xs:include declarations (and imports declared inside an included file) are followed too, with circular imports detected and a nesting depth cap of 10.

A few things to know:

  • Your files are never overwritten. A downloaded schema is only saved next to your schema when no file of that name exists there yet; the referencing schema itself is never rewritten. If the folder is not writable (or the schema has not been saved yet), the cached copy is used as before. This applies everywhere imports and includes are resolved: the schema views, validation, the Type Library, Schema Analysis, flattening, sample validation and documentation generation.
  • Only imports whose namespace is an http:// or https:// URL are looked up by namespace (step 5).
  • xs:include references are resolved relative to the including file, or through an XML catalog / Schema Library entry for their location - they are not looked up by namespace.
  • If an include or import still cannot be loaded, the Graphic view names it in a bar above the diagram.
  • Internal and private network addresses are never contacted - see Security Features.
  • Clearing the cache (Settings → Files & Cache → TEMP & CACHE, or the Schema Library's Cache tab) is safe: the copies next to your schemas stay, and anything else is re-downloaded the next time it is needed.
  • Advanced: -Dfxt.schema.localCopies=false keeps downloaded schemas in the cache only.
  • Advanced: to turn remote downloads off entirely (for example in fully offline environments), start the application with the system property -Dfxt.schema.namespaceFallback=false - local files, catalog hits and already-cached copies still resolve.

docs.title: Overview View
docs.text:
The Overview view mode (the table icon in the view switch, or View → Overview View) lists every top-level component of the schema in one table: imports, includes, redefines and overrides, schema-level annotations, global elements, complex and simple types, groups, attribute groups, global attributes and notations - in the order they have in the file. It is offered for XSD documents only.

The component table

Column Shows Kind import, element, complexType, annotation, … with its icon Name The component name, or the location of an import/include. Double-click (or F2) to rename Details Type of an element/attribute, base type and derivation of a type, namespace of an import, identifiers of a notation Annotation The first documentation line. Double-click to edit it in place
  • Insert adds a new component in front of the selected row, Append at the end. The new row gets a free default name (NewComplexType, newElement, …) and its name is ready to type. An Annotation adds a schema-level xs:annotation at that position.
  • Import / Include adds an xs:import, xs:include, xs:redefine or xs:override. Choose the file with Browse…: the location is made relative to the schema, and for an import the chosen schema's target namespace is filled in.
  • Move up / down (Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓) or drag rows to reorder them. Several selected rows move together. Imports and includes always stay in front of the components - XSD requires that, so a move that breaks the rule is refused with an explanation.
  • Sort orders the components Type, then Name or Name, then Type. Imports and includes keep their place on top; a comment or annotation stays with the component that follows it. Sorting is one step you can undo.
  • Rename a type, element, group or attribute: when the schema references it, you are asked whether to update the references (type, base, ref, substitutionGroup, itemType, memberTypes) as well. References inside included or imported files are not changed.
  • Delete (Del) removes the selected components. If they are still referenced, you are asked first.
  • Included also lists the components of included files - read-only and in italics.
  • The header edits the target namespace and the elementFormDefault / attributeFormDefault of the schema.
  • Double-click a type to open it in the Type Editor, an element to show it in the Graphic View, an import to open its file.

The tabs below the table show the selected component:

Tab For What you can do Details imports/includes, notations, annotations Edit namespace and location (Browse…, Open File), public/system identifiers, the documentation text and its language. For other components a summary with Open in Type Editor / Show in Graphic View Attributes elements, complex types, attribute groups Edit Name, Type, Use, Default and Fixed in place. Default and Fixed offer the enumeration values of the attribute's type. Add attributes and attribute group references, delete them. For an element with a named type the attributes of that type are shown - changes apply to every use of the type Identity Constraints elements Add a key, unique or keyref, and edit name, selector, fields (comma-separated) and refer in place Assertions complex types (also an element's anonymous one) Add XSD 1.1 xs:assert and edit the test and xpathDefaultNamespace Namespaces the schema Add, edit and remove namespace prefixes. A prefix that is still used, or the prefix of the XML Schema namespace, cannot be removed

The selected row also drives the Properties pane on the right, so all other properties (cardinality, facets, documentation in several languages, …) are edited there. Every change is a normal edit of the document: it shows up in the Text view, and Undo/Redo is shared with the Tree and Graphic views.

docs.title: Order of the Components When Saving
docs.text: The schema is saved in the order you see in the Overview (and in the Text view). Earlier versions sorted the top-level components on every save; now the order only changes when you Sort explicitly. Schema-level annotations, xs:notation and xs:defaultOpenContent are kept at their positions.

docs.title: 2. Type Library
docs.text:
The Schema activity's side panel is your type library: it lists the active schema's top-level declarations so you can browse, find, and open every type in the schema.

The Schema activity's Type Library, with the schema diagram in the editor host

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Feature Description Grouped lists Declarations grouped into GLOBAL ELEMENTS, COMPLEX TYPES, and SIMPLE TYPES (collapsible sections) Filter A filter field on top narrows all three lists by name as you type Reveal in Tree Click a declaration to reveal it in the schema's Tree view Open Type Editor Double-click a type to open it in its own Type Editor tab Find Usage Right-click a type to find the places where it is used New type The + button in the COMPLEX TYPES / SIMPLE TYPES header (or right-click → New Complex Type… / New Simple Type…) declares a new top-level type - see Creating a New Type Schema tools Labelled rows in the TOOLS section at the top of the panel, above the filter field (open by default): Generate Sample XML…, Sample XML with Options…, Flatten Schema…, Schema Analysis, and Generate Documentation… Generate XSD from XML Not in the Schema panel: Generate XSD from XML and Generate XSD from XML Files… are in the editor toolbar's Schema ▾ split menu

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Open your XSD file
  2. Open the Schema activity from the activity bar
  3. Browse the grouped lists, or type in the filter field to narrow them
  4. Click a declaration to reveal it in the Tree view
  5. Double-click a type - or right-click and choose Open Type Editor - to edit it; right-click also offers Reveal in Tree and Find Usage

Tip

The whole panel is a drop zone: drop an .xsd file from your file manager anywhere on it to open that schema as a document.

docs.title: 3. Type Editor
docs.text:
The Type Editor provides dedicated editing for ComplexTypes and SimpleTypes.

A named type opened in its own Type Editor tab in the editor area

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Feature Description Tab-Based Editing Each type opens in its own tab in the editor area; a named type used inside a Type Editor opens in a further Type Editor tab (double-click its frame title or Edit Type '…') - see Named Types in Frames ComplexType Editor Graphical editing in the card diagram of the Graphic view SimpleType Editor Form-based editing with facet panels

docs.title: ComplexType Editor
docs.text:
For ComplexTypes, the tab shows the same card diagram as the Graphic view - see Reading a Card for what each card shows:

  • The type is the root card of the diagram, with its compositors, child elements and attributes below it
  • A title chip at the top left names the selected card (or the type), and the zoom control at the bottom right zooms out, in, or back to 100%
  • A bar above the diagram edits the type's Name, Abstract and Mixed settings. These apply to the schema right away and can be undone there (Ctrl+Z in the schema's tab)
  • Add, delete and modify elements, attributes and Sequence / Choice / All compositors through the cards' context menus, as in the Graphic view; the properties pane beside the diagram edits the selected node
  • Changes to the diagram are kept in the tab until you click Save to schema (or press Ctrl+S); they are then written into the schema. Close the tab with Close, Esc or its ×

docs.title: SimpleType Editor
docs.text:
For SimpleTypes, you get a 5-panel form editor:

Panel Description General Name and Final attribute Restriction Base type and facets List Item type (enabled for list types and types without derivation yet) Union Member types (enabled for union types and types without derivation yet) Annotation Documentation and AppInfo

The Base type, Item type and Add Member Type… fields are the same type picker as in the inspector, limited to what a simple type may derive from: the schema's other simple types and the built-in datatypes (complex types, xs:anyType and the type itself are left out).

docs.title: Creating a New Type
docs.text:
New top-level types can be declared from three places:

  • Graphic view: right-click the schema node or an empty area of the diagram → Add Complex Type… / Add Simple Type…
  • Tree view: right-click the schema (root) node → New Complex Type… / New Simple Type…
  • Schema panel: the + button in the COMPLEX TYPES or SIMPLE TYPES section header

A small dialog asks for the kind and the name. A free name is suggested (NewComplexType, NewComplexType2, …); the name is checked while you type - it must be a valid XML name (no spaces or :) and must not be used by another simple or complex type of the schema, so OK stays disabled until it is.

Kind Starts as Complex type An empty xs:sequence - add child elements and attributes right away Simple type A restriction of xs:string - pick another base type and add facets

The new type is added next to the schema's other types of the same kind, appears in the Type Library and opens in its own Type Editor tab. The diagram itself shows global elements only; assign the new type to an element with the type picker. One Undo removes the type again.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. In the Schema panel's Type Library, find the type (use the filter field for large schemas)
  2. Double-click it - or right-click and choose Open Type Editor. Alternatively, pick Type Editor… from the editor toolbar's Schema ▾ menu and choose a type by name.
  3. The type opens in its own Type Editor tab in the editor area
  4. Make your changes
  5. Click Save or use Ctrl+S

docs.title: 4. Text View
docs.text:
The Text View provides raw XSD source code editing.

The XSD in the Unified Shell's Text view (Schema activity panel on the left, inspector on the right)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Full Code Editor: View and edit the raw XSD source code
  • Syntax Highlighting: Color-coded code for easy reading
  • Search and Replace: Find and change text quickly
  • Query Console: Query the schema with XPath/XQuery (Ctrl+Shift+X)
  • Save as Favorite: Quick access to frequently used schemas
  • Editable Properties pane: Move the text caret into a schema construct to select it and edit its properties without leaving the text editor (see below)

docs.title: Editing Schema Properties from Any View
docs.text:
You can edit a schema node's properties directly from the Text view, the same way as in the Tree and Graphic views.

The XSD editor has three views - Text, Tree, and Graphic - and all three share one in-memory schema model. The Properties pane works in every view:

  • Tree and Graphic views: Select a node to edit its name, type, cardinality/occurrence, use, form, constraints, documentation, and facets.
  • Text view: Move the text caret into an XSD construct - such as an xs:element, xs:complexType, xs:simpleType, xs:attribute, a compositor (xs:sequence, xs:choice, xs:all), or a facet - and the Properties pane selects the matching schema node and shows it editable. You get the same property editing as in the Tree and Graphic views, without leaving the source editor. Your edits round-trip back into the schema text as a minimal change that preserves your caret and scroll position.

If the caret is not inside a recognizable construct - for example inside an xs:annotation, a comment, or blank space - the pane falls back to a read-only caret/XPath view.

Because all three views share one model, your edits and your Undo/Redo history are preserved when you switch between Text, Tree, and Graphic.

docs.title: What You Can Edit in the Properties Pane
docs.text:
For the selected schema node you can edit:

  • Name, type, cardinality/occurrence, use, form - The core properties of the node. The Type field is a picker: it lists the schema's own simple and complex types (including included and imported ones, with their namespace prefix) and every XSD built-in datatype, filters as you type and explains the highlighted type in a side pane; free text is still accepted for references it does not know. See Choosing a type with the type picker for the keyboard shortcuts and what the side pane shows. Compositors (xs:sequence, xs:choice, xs:all), group references and xs:any also show editable minOccurs/maxOccurs and their Order in CARDINALITY & USE.
  • Facets - Add, edit, and remove facets such as patterns, enumerations, and length limits. In the facet list, click a value to edit it (Enter saves, Esc cancels), point at a row and click the trash icon to delete it, and use the row below the list to add one, which offers only the facets the base type allows, also through named, list and union types. Facets inherited from a base type appear in italics and are read-only. When all facets come from a named type, the add row is replaced by "Facets come from T – click to edit them there."; click it to select that type.
  • App info (xs:appinfo) - The machine-readable metadata attached to the node (for example the technical tags described in Documentation Generator).
  • Multi-language documentation (xs:documentation) - One row per language. Use Add language to add a translation and the ✕ button to remove one.
  • Comments - Select an XSD comment in the tree to edit its text. To add a comment, choose Add Comment… from a node's right-click context menu.
  • Constraints - In the CONSTRAINTS section, select a key, keyref, unique, or assert constraint and click Delete constraint to remove it.

The pane also shows information you cannot edit directly: the Base type and Derivation (restriction / extension / list / union), final for a simple type (in ADVANCED), the Order of the node in its parent compositor (e.g. 2 of 5 · sequence), and USED IN - for a global type, element or group every place that references it (click an entry to select the referring node), for a local declaration the global component that contains it. Editable values look like plain text until you point at them. See Properties Inspector for the full layout.

In the Tree/Graphic view, the Copy XPath and Copy Node buttons in NODE & XPATH copy the schema XPath and the XSD source of the selected node.

Tip: You can also edit a declaration from an XML document that uses this schema: select the element there and change type, cardinality, facets or documentation in its inspector - see Properties Inspector - Editing the bound schema.

Note: Structural editing (adding, deleting, and moving nodes) remains a Tree and Graphic capability via the right-click context menu. The Text view provides property editing through the Properties pane.

docs.title: 5. Schema Analysis
docs.text:
The Schema Analysis row in the Schema panel's TOOLS section (at the top of the panel; expand it if collapsed) analyzes the active XSD and opens the report as a tool tab in the editor area. The analysis runs in the background on the current editor text (unsaved changes included); imports and includes are resolved relative to the file. The header shows the document, the quality score, the number of issues, the number of unused types and - when unused components drag further components along - the size of the unreachable set; Refresh re-runs the analysis, and opening the tool again while the tab is already open re-analyzes the active document instead of adding a second tab.

The Schema Analysis tool tab with its five sub-tabs, opened from the Schema activity

Every finding is a link into the schema: selecting a row, an unused type, a usage location or an affected element switches the document to the Tree view and reveals the node.

Export in the header writes the complete report - every section of every sub-tab - as CSV, JSON, HTML, PDF, or Excel. Each sub-tab additionally has its own Export menu that writes just that section in the same formats. All formats carry the same content: CSV as one block per section (facts as Key,Value, then each table), JSON as sections keyed by id with tables as arrays of objects, HTML with a table of contents, PDF with one chapter per section, and Excel with one sheet per section (in the same look as every other Excel export: dark header row, striped rows, highlighted findings in their status colour).

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
The Statistics tab opens with a row of tiles for the declaration counts (elements, attributes, complex and simple types, groups, attribute groups), followed by detail cards:

Card Metrics Schema XSD version (1.0/1.1), target namespace, form defaults, namespaces, total nodes Files Schema files, includes / imports, unresolved references, and node counts per file for multi-file schemas Constraints Counts of xs:key, xs:keyref, xs:unique, and assertions Documentation Coverage bar (green ≥ 75 %, yellow ≥ 40 %, red below), documented nodes, appinfo nodes, documentation languages, the most frequent appinfo tags (@deprecated, @since, …) Cardinality Optional vs. required elements as a two-segment bar, plus the unbounded element count Complexity Deepest element nesting (hover for the XPath), longest type-derivation chain, widest complex type, average declarations per type, abstract types / elements, substitution-group heads / members, anonymous types, mixed content, extensions / restrictions, XSD 1.1 features Facets Total facets and enumeration values, plus a count per facet kind (pattern, maxLength, …)

Below the cards:

Section Content Schema references One row per xs:include / xs:import with its location, resolution status (error in the tooltip), namespace and the number of elements, types and groups it contributes; shown only for multi-file schemas Most used types The named types with the most references; the usage bar is relative to the most used type Unused types Every named type that is never referenced, listed by name - click one to reveal it Unused groups / attribute groups Global xs:groups and xs:attributeGroups nothing references Circular references Type-derivation cycles (a type deriving from itself - an error) and recursive content models (Folder → FolderType → Folder, legal); click one to reveal its first member

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
The Types tab is the type library of the schema: one row per global complex type, simple type, group and attribute group with its kind, name, base (extends X, restricts X, list of X, union of A, B), first documentation line, usage count and - for multi-file schemas - the include file it comes from. The usage chip is red for 0 usages, orange for one to three, green otherwise. The chips above the table filter by kind, Unused (never referenced), Unreachable (not reachable from any global element or attribute, directly or through other components - the cascading unused set) and Single use (named types used exactly once, candidates for an inline anonymous type); the text field searches name, base and documentation.

Selecting a row reveals the component in the Tree view and fills the Used in list with every reference to it (element and attribute types, base types, list item and union member types, refs, substitutionGroups - references from included files are marked with the file name, references from imported schemas with [import]); selecting a usage reveals the referring node. The Documentation box shows the full documentation text.

Remove unused (N)… deletes every unreachable component of the analyzed document in one step: a confirmation lists what will be removed; components declared in included files are skipped (they belong to another file). The deletion goes through the editor's command stack, so Ctrl+Z in the document restores all of them at once, and the analysis re-runs afterwards.

docs.title: Quality Checks
docs.text:
The Quality Checks tab shows a score (0-100) with its rating, the number of checks passed, the dominant naming convention and its distribution (chips per convention, the dominant one in green), and the issues found. The count chips next to the score (by severity and by category) are clickable filters - click one to show only those issues, click it again to clear. The filter bar offers the same severity and category selection plus a free-text search and reports how many issues are currently shown. Every row carries a severity icon; the File column names the include file of a finding (full path in the tooltip) and the location column shows the XPath. Select an issue to read its suggestion and location and to jump to the affected elements.

Check Severity Description Naming Convention Warning Element, attribute, type and group names that deviate from the schema's dominant convention (UpperCamelCase, lowerCamelCase, snake_case, kebab-case) Best Practice Info / Warning / Suggestion xs:any / xs:anyAttribute wildcards and unbounded content without limits (info), elements nested deeper than the Max nesting limit (warning), anonymous complex types (suggestion) Deprecated Warning Components marked as deprecated in xs:appinfo Constraint Conflict Error Enumeration values that conflict with length facets Inconsistent Definition Warning The same name defined with different content in several places Duplicate Definition Info Different names with identical structure Duplicate Element in Container Error The same element declared twice in one sequence, choice, or all (ambiguity error) Unresolved Reference Error A type, ref, base, itemType, memberTypes, substitutionGroup or XSD 1.1 alternative type naming a component that is declared nowhere (XSD built-ins, prefixes bound to other namespaces and unknown prefixes are ignored) Circular Reference Error / Info A type deriving from itself, directly or indirectly (error); a recursive content model (info) Unused Component Info A named type, group or attribute group that nothing references, or that is only referenced from other unused components Missing Documentation Suggestion A global component without xs:documentation Inline Candidate Suggestion A named type used exactly once as an element or attribute type - could be declared inline (abstract types and types from included files are not suggested)

Max nesting (top right of the tab, default 5) is the limit of the deep-nesting check: it counts element levels declared inside one another through anonymous types - compositors and the types themselves do not count, and an element with a named type starts a new declaration. Changing the value re-runs the analysis; the setting is remembered.

The score is the share of checked declarations (every named element, attribute, type and group) that no Error or Warning counts against: a naming deviation or a too deeply nested element costs one declaration, a duplicate element every occurrence, and an inconsistent definition the declarations that deviate from the most frequent variant of that name. The informational checks (unused components, recursion, missing documentation, inline candidates) never lower it; documentation coverage has its own percentage on the Statistics tab.

docs.title: Identity Constraints
docs.text: The Identity Constraints tab lists every xs:key, xs:keyref, xs:unique, and xs:assert with its parent element, selector, fields, referenced key or test expression, and a validation status - for example a keyref whose refer points to a key that does not exist. The count chips above the table filter by kind (key, keyref, unique, assert) and by status (errors, warnings); click a chip again to clear the filter. Selecting a row reveals the constraint in the Tree view and fills the details pane with the validation message, the parent element (a link), selector and fields, and - for a keyref - a link that selects the referenced key.

docs.title: XPath Validation
docs.text:
The XPath Validation tab lists every XPath expression used by identity constraints and assertions - each selector, each field and each assert test is one row - with its status: Valid, or the most severe finding for it (syntax errors, element names that do not occur in the schema, empty assert tests). The status chips above the table are clickable filters, and the details pane shows the full expression, the findings and a link to the parent element. The expressions are checked statically against the schema; they are not evaluated against a sample XML document.

Note

Identity constraints (xs:key, xs:keyref, xs:unique, xs:assert) can also be inspected and deleted per node in the Properties inspector's CONSTRAINTS section - see What You Can Edit in the Properties Pane.

docs.title: 6. Documentation Generator
docs.text:
Create professional documentation from your XSD file automatically.

The Documentation generator open as a tab in the editor area, with source, format, and options

docs.title: Output Formats
docs.text: Format Description HTML Interactive web documentation with navigation Word Microsoft Word (.docx) document PDF PDF document using Apache FOP

docs.title: How to Generate Documentation
docs.text:
1. Open your XSD file in the editor host
  2. Click Generate Documentation… in the Schema panel's TOOLS section (or pick it from the editor toolbar's Schema ▾ menu) - the generator opens as a tab in the editor area. The generator reads the saved schema file: if it has unsaved changes, you are asked to Save and Continue, Use Saved Version or Cancel
  3. Check SOURCE & OUTPUT: the active schema is pre-filled; choose the output folder (HTML) or file (PDF/Word)
  4. Select your output format (HTML, PDF, or Word) and the diagram format (SVG, PNG, or JPG)
  5. Configure options (PDF and Word add page-layout and content options)
  6. Click Generate - the PROGRESS log streams the pipeline's messages live, and the run can be cancelled
  7. Open the result automatically or from the output location

Tip

Generation works from the schema's last-saved version on disk so that relative xs:include / xs:import references resolve correctly - save the XSD first to document your latest edits. Remote imports are resolved through the Schema Library, XML catalogs and the schema cache (see Automatic Resolution of Imported Schemas); the generator never modifies your schema file or writes into its folder.

docs.title: Generation Options
docs.text:
Option Description Markdown rendering All documentation (default), Per node (@markdown), or Off - see below Include type definitions in source code Show the type's XSD source on the detail pages (on by default) Show documentation in diagrams Print the documentation text inside the SVG element boxes (off by default) Show constraints in diagrams List keys, unique and keyref constraints and assertions inside the element boxes, as in the Graphic view: a coloured label (KEY / UNIQ / REF / ASSERT) and the text, at most four lines plus "+N more", full details as tooltip; assertions include those of derived and base types (on by default, also for PDF and Word) Also in the page's own element box Off: only the child boxes list constraints; the page's own ones are in the sections below the diagram (off by default) Show constraints on their target elements Also list a key, unique or keyref on the element its field points to (e.g. BenchmarkID for a key on Fund). It shows as a row in that element's diagram box (with Show constraints in diagrams on) and in a Referenced by Identity Constraints section of its page, linked to the element that declares it. An attribute field shows on the attribute's element (off by default) Generate SVG overview page Interactive full-schema SVG (on by default) Add metadata in output Generator name, date and schema information in the output (on by default) Deduplicate data dictionary by type List each type once in the Data Dictionary instead of per usage Image format SVG (default), PNG or JPG for the diagrams Favicon (HTML) A custom icon file for the HTML output Open the generated documentation after creation Opens index.html (HTML) or the generated file in your system viewer

When you pick PDF or Word, a PDF OPTIONS / WORD OPTIONS section appears below the general options:

Option Formats Description Page size PDF, Word A4 (default), Letter or Legal; the PDF also offers A3 Orientation PDF, Word Portrait (default) or Landscape Cover page PDF, Word A title page in front of the document (off by default) Table of contents PDF, Word A table of contents listing the chapters (on by default) Data dictionary PDF, Word The table of every element and attribute path with its type, cardinality and description (on by default) Schema diagram PDF, Word A chapter with the diagram of the root element; the PDF adds an overview of the whole schema for schemas up to 400 elements (on by default) Element diagrams PDF, Word A diagram in every element and type section (on by default) Element reference PDF, Word One section per declaration (default), Every occurrence or Off - see Element reference below XSD source in each section PDF, Word Shows the XSD source of every element and type in its section (off by default; makes the document considerably longer) Color scheme PDF The accent colour of the document: Blue (default), Green, Purple, Grayscale or Professional Watermark PDF None (default), Draft, Confidential or Internal Use Only, printed across every page Page numbers PDF Page numbers in the footer (on by default) PDF bookmarks PDF A bookmark tree for the chapters and every element and type section (on by default)

docs.title: Element reference (PDF and Word)
docs.text:
The PDF and the Word document are built from the same chapters, each one switched by the options above: cover page, table of contents, Schema Overview, Namespace Overview, Schema Diagram, Complex Types, Simple Types, Data Dictionary, Element Reference and Index. The schema diagram starts at the schema's root element. The index lists every element and attribute with its path (without sequence/choice containers) and says which of the two it is. Restrictions are written as plain text (for example Base: xs:string; MaxLength: 256), and long paths, restrictions and descriptions wrap in their column instead of being cut off. Type usage counts include derived types.

The PDF and the Word document have an Element Reference: one section per element and attribute with what the HTML detail page shows:

  • the diagram (all levels), with Element diagrams on;
  • the properties: type, cardinality or use, namespace, default / fixed / nillable;
  • the documentation in every selected language;
  • the restrictions with their values, including the full enumeration list;
  • the children and attributes;
  • identity constraints (selector, fields, refers to), assertions, type alternatives, wildcards and open content;
  • appinfo.

One section per declaration describes an element once, however many paths its type is used at. The section lists the other paths, and they link to it. Every occurrence gives each path its own section, as the HTML documentation does; for large schemas this makes the PDF much longer.

Paths in the data dictionary, names in the index and in the children tables link to their section, and the PDF bookmarks list every section under Element Reference.

The Complex Types and Simple Types chapters list every global type in a table, then give each type its own section:

  • documentation;
  • base and derivation;
  • the content model of a complex type: diagram plus children and attributes;
  • the facets of a simple type with their values, and each enumeration value with its documentation;
  • assertions;
  • Used In: the elements and attributes of this type, with links;
  • the types derived from it.

Type names link to these sections wherever they appear: overview tables, data dictionary, element properties, children tables and index.

Deduplicate data dictionary by type also applies to PDF and Word: each named type is listed once in the data dictionary.

The Word document has the same element and type sections as the PDF:

  • each section is a bookmark;
  • paths and types in the data dictionary, names in the index, the type tables, children tables and Used In lists are links to it;
  • chapters use real Word headings (Heading 1 to 3), so the table of contents, the navigation pane and the outline view work. Section headings appear in the navigation pane, while the table of contents lists the chapters (Word fills it when the document is opened);
  • the Namespace Overview says what each namespace is and lists the imports and includes;
  • diagrams are embedded as sharp PNG images in their own proportions, fitted to the text width.

More in the PDF:

  • Diagrams follow Diagram image format. With SVG (the default) they are vector graphics: sharp at any zoom and searchable. PNG and JPG embed images.
  • The Namespace Overview lists the prefixes the schema declares (target namespace, XML Schema, imported, declared), plus a table of its imports, includes, redefines and overrides with their locations.
  • The Schema Diagram chapter adds an overview of the whole schema, as on the HTML overview page. Schemas with more than 400 elements get a note instead, because the overview would not be legible on one page.
  • XSD source in each section (PDF and Word, off by default) shows the XSD source of every element and type. Leaf elements and attributes show a Sample value.

docs.title: Markdown rendering
docs.text:
xs:documentation text can be rendered as Markdown, so **bold**, lists and links show up formatted on the generated pages. The choice has three settings:

Setting Effect All documentation (default) Every node's documentation is rendered as Markdown, unless that node itself says @markdown is false Per node (@markdown) Only nodes whose annotation says @markdown is true are rendered - everything else, including nodes that say nothing, stays plain text Off Nothing is rendered, whatever the nodes say

A node's own @markdown always beats the chosen setting - only Off is absolute. Where an element and its type disagree, the element wins; the type's @markdown applies to every element using it that does not state its own. The same rule drives the complexType, simpleType, attribute and enumeration documentation on the generated type pages.

Documentation that is not rendered as Markdown appears literally: **bold** stays visible as typed instead of being formatted. If you want text formatted, write Markdown and leave the rendering on.

Unrendered text is HTML-escaped everywhere it appears in the generated HTML, so markup written straight into xs:documentation shows as the tags themselves instead of being applied. The PDF, Word and Excel outputs are unaffected: they flatten the documentation to plain text and drop the markup as before.

Formatting is a feature of the HTML output. The PDF, Word and Excel outputs are plain text: the documentation is flattened for them, but paragraphs, list items and headings each keep their own line instead of running together.

The per-node switch lives in the schema itself and is edited in the Inspector's Markdown choice (Not set / Markdown / Plain text):

<xs:element name="Transaction">
    <xs:annotation>
        <xs:documentation>A **single** financial transaction.</xs:documentation>
        <xs:appinfo source="@markdown">true</xs:appinfo>
    </xs:annotation>
</xs:element>

docs.title: Language Settings
docs.text:
For multi-language schemas, you can:

  1. Click Scan languages to detect the xml:lang values used in the schema
  2. Untick the languages you do not want in the output
  3. Choose a fallback language for missing translations

De-selected languages are dropped everywhere: element detail pages, type pages, attribute and enumeration documentation, the Data Dictionary (HTML and Excel), the search index, the SVG diagrams and the Source Code snippets on the detail pages. Documentation without an xml:lang attribute ("default") is always kept as a fallback. The schema files copied next to the documentation are left untouched. Leaving every language ticked (or not scanning at all) includes all of them.

docs.title: Adding Technical Notes to Your Schema
docs.text:
You can add structured technical information directly in your XSD files:

Full tag reference

All supported tags, their semantics and examples are listed in the XsdDoc Tags reference.

The tag goes into the source attribute of an xs:appinfo, its value into the element's text content.

Supported tags:

  • @since - When a feature was introduced
  • @version - Version detail of the component
  • @see - References to other elements (may occur several times)
  • @deprecated - Mark elements as deprecated
  • @markdown - true/false, whether this node's documentation is rendered as Markdown (see Markdown rendering)
  • {@link /path/to/element} - Create clickable links inside @see and @deprecated

Example values are a separate block rather than a tag. They appear as Sample Data on the detail pages and also feed the sample-XML generator and IntelliSense.

Example in your XSD:

<xs:element name="Transaction">
    <xs:annotation>
        <!-- User-friendly documentation -->
        <xs:documentation xml:lang="en">A single financial transaction.</xs:documentation>
        <xs:documentation xml:lang="de">Eine einzelne Transaktion.</xs:documentation>

        <!-- Technical notes for developers -->
        <xs:appinfo source="@since">4.0.0</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@version">1.2</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@see">{@link /FundsXML4/ControlData}</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@deprecated">Use {@link /FundsXML4/NewTransaction} instead.</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@markdown">true</xs:appinfo>

        <!-- Example values -->
        <xs:appinfo>
            <fxt:exampleValues xmlns:fxt="http://freexmltoolkit.org/xml-schema-extensions">
                <fxt:example value="TRX-0815"/>
                <fxt:example value="TRX-0816"/>
            </fxt:exampleValues>
        </xs:appinfo>
    </xs:annotation>
</xs:element>

Older schemas keep working. The form that packs tag and value into the attribute alone - <xs:appinfo source="@since 4.0.0"/>, used throughout FundsXML - is still read, and so is altova:exampleValues. Both are rewritten into the form above the next time you save the schema from the toolkit; the generated documentation is the same either way. An altova:exampleValues block is only converted once you actually change the example values.

docs.title: 7. Sample XML Generator
docs.text:
Create sample XML files based on your XSD schema. This is useful for testing, data migration, or as a starting template.

The advanced sample generator dialog with its per-XPath rules table

Unified Shell: In the Unified Shell, sample-data generation lives in the Schema panel. It offers two actions: Generate Sample XML for the basic generation described below, and Sample XML with Options… for the rule-based, batch-capable generation shown above.

docs.title: Quick Start (Basic Generation)
docs.text:
For simple use cases, you can generate sample XML in seconds:

  1. Load your XSD file
  2. Choose Generate Sample XML… in the toolbar's Schema ▾ menu or under Tools (or in the Schema panel's TOOLS section at the top of the panel). If the schema has unsaved changes, choose Save and Continue or Use Saved Version when asked
  3. Choose your options:
    • Only mandatory elements: Include only required elements
    • Max. repetitions: Limit repeating elements
    • Realistic values: Honor enumerations, patterns and value ranges when inventing values
  4. Click Generate
  5. Validate the generated XML against the schema
  6. Save or copy the generated XML

docs.title: Profiled Generation (Advanced)
docs.text:
For more control, you can define rules that specify exactly how each element or attribute gets its value. Open it from Sample XML with Options… in the Schema panel. It includes:

Feature Description XPath-Based Rules Set a generation strategy for each element or attribute by its XPath 11 Strategies Auto, Fixed Value, Omit, Empty, XSD Example, Enum Cycle, Sequence, XPath Reference, Random from List, Template, and Null Auto-Fill XPaths Automatically extract all XPaths from your schema to populate the rules table Saveable Profiles Save your generation configuration and reload it later Profile Sharing Export and import profiles to share with colleagues Batch Generation Generate multiple files at once with configurable file naming (for example, order_001.xml, order_002.xml)

For a complete guide with step-by-step instructions and examples, see Profiled XML Generation.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The generated sample is pretty-printed like Format Document (Shift+Alt+F) and opens as a normal editor tab (Sample.xml) that is already bound to the schema it was generated from, so you can validate it right away:

  1. Click Validate (F8) - the result is Valid or a list of problems, not merely Well-formed
  2. Problems appear in the PROBLEMS list - click one to jump to its line

The sample's root element references the schema by file name (xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="FundsXML4.xsd", or the xsi:schemaLocation pair for a namespaced schema) rather than by an absolute file: path, so it can be moved and shared. Saving it for the first time into another folder rewrites the reference to a relative path (for example ../xsd/FundsXML4.xsd), so it keeps resolving there - also in other tools.

docs.title: 8. XSD Flattener
docs.text:
Combine multiple XSD files into a single, standalone file. Useful when your schema is split across several files via <xs:include>, or when you want a minimal schema for a validation server.

The Flatten Schema options dialog over an open schema — all reductions enabled by default

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Open your main XSD file in the editor
  2. In the Schema activity's side panel, click the Flatten Schema… tool button
  3. The Flatten Schema dialog opens. Output file is preset to the folder of your schema with _flattened.xsd appended to its name (FundsXML.xsd → FundsXML_flattened.xsd). Change it, or pick another file with Browse…
  4. Pick which reductions you want (see below) and click OK
  5. The flattened schema is written to the output file and opened in a new editor tab. If the file already exists you are asked before it is overwritten; the original schema itself can never be chosen as the output

Leave Output file empty to open the result as an unsaved tab (Flattened.xsd) instead — this is also the default for a schema that has not been saved yet.

docs.title: Flatten Options
docs.text:
Before flattening, a dialog lets you reduce the output. The four reduction options are checked by default, which produces the smallest possible schema — ideal for deploying to a validation server:

Option What it does Remove annotations (documentation, appinfo) Strips all xs:documentation and xs:appinfo content — the human-readable descriptions a validator does not need Remove XML comments Strips all XML comments, including comments at the top of the file Remove unused global types and groups Removes global types, groups and attribute groups that are not reachable from any global element or attribute — dead weight in large schema libraries. (Skipped automatically if the schema uses xs:redefine or xs:override.) Minified output (no indentation) Collapses the whitespace between tags for the smallest file size Track source files (xs:appinfo) Off by default. Adds an fxt:sourceFile annotation to every global component that came from an included file, naming that file — see below

Uncheck all four reduction options for a plain flatten that keeps documentation, comments and formatting — the previous behavior.

docs.title: Keeping Track of Where Components Came From
docs.text:
Flattening merges every included file into one document, which normally loses the information about which file a type or element originally came from. Tick Track source files to keep it: each global element, type, group, attribute group and attribute that was pulled in from an xs:include gets an annotation naming its origin.

<xs:complexType name="PersonType">
    <xs:annotation>
        <xs:appinfo>
            <fxt:sourceFile xmlns:fxt="http://freexmltoolkit.org/schema/flattening">types.xsd</fxt:sourceFile>
        </xs:appinfo>
    </xs:annotation>
    ...
</xs:complexType>

The markers are added after the reductions, so they survive Remove annotations — you can combine a fully reduced schema with full origin tracking. Components defined in the main file are not marked, and a stale marker from an earlier flatten is replaced rather than duplicated. The option needs a saved file: for unsaved content there is no directory to resolve includes against, so nothing is merged and nothing is marked.

The reduced schema is verified to still compile as a valid schema before it is shown, so you can deploy it with confidence.

docs.title: What Happens to Includes and Imports
docs.text:
• xs:include — Included schemas (same namespace) are merged into the output, and the resolved include directives are removed: the flattened schema is standalone. If an include cannot be resolved, its directive is kept in the output so you can see what is missing.
  • xs:import — Imported schemas (different namespaces) are not merged; the import declarations stay untouched.

When saving schemas from the graphical editor, xs:include and xs:import declarations are preserved. The flattener only merges included content when you explicitly flatten — it does not alter your original schema structure.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Deploying a minimal, resource-efficient schema to a validation server
  • Distributing schemas to partners
  • Tools that don't support includes
  • Simplifying complex schema sets
  • Creating self-contained schemas

docs.title: Supported XSD Features
docs.text: Category Features Elements Elements, attributes, groups, attribute groups, xs:any / xs:anyAttribute Types ComplexTypes, SimpleTypes (restriction, list, union), simple/complex content with extension and restriction Compositors Sequence, Choice, All Constraints Facets: patterns, enumerations, length limits, value ranges, digits, whiteSpace, assertion / explicitTimezone (XSD 1.1) References Import, Include, Redefine and Override (resolved, also transitively). Redefined and overridden definitions replace the originals in the Graphic view, the Type Library, statistics, quality checks and the Inspector of an XML document. XSD 1.1 Assertions (xs:assert, xs:assertion) are loaded, shown and analysed; xs:alternative and xs:openContent are honored by the XSD 1.1 validator but not shown in the graphical views Identity Key, KeyRef, Unique

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
The complete list is on the Keyboard Shortcuts page (and in the app under Help → Keyboard Shortcuts).

In the XSD Tree and Graphic views, Delete removes the selected node, and Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo every schema edit.

docs.title: XSD Validation
docs.text:
Note: The standalone XSD Validation tab has been retired. Validation — XSD and Schematron, single-file and batch — now lives in the Unified Shell's Validation activity panel. The capabilities below are unchanged; they are reached through the shell's Validation panel rather than a dedicated sidebar tab.

Validate your XML files against XSD schemas to check if documents follow the rules defined in the schema. Supports both single file and batch validation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The XSD Validation tool provides two modes:

Mode Description Single File Validate one XML file at a time Batch Validation Validate multiple XML files at once

XSD and Schematron validation now live in the Unified Shell's Validation activity panel

docs.title: What Does It Check?
docs.text: Check Description Structure Are elements in the right order? Required Fields Are all mandatory elements present? Data Types Are values the correct type (text, number, date)? Constraints Do values meet length, range, or pattern requirements? XSD 1.1 Assertions Do values pass custom assertion rules?

docs.title: Single File Validation
docs.text: Use this mode to validate one XML file against a schema.

docs.title: Step 1: Load Your Files
docs.text:
1. Open the XML file in the editor (Ctrl+O, the Explorer, or drag & drop).
  2. Schema selection:
  3. Automatic: Schema references inside the XML (xsi:schemaLocation / xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation) are found automatically. The reference is re-read from the editor content before every validation run, so adding, changing, or removing it takes effect immediately - no save needed, and untitled documents work too. If you remove the reference, validation falls back to a well-formedness check and the status bar shows "No XSD". A schema you bound manually is never overridden by this automatic detection. If the document has no xsi:schemaLocation, the Schema Library is consulted by root namespace (or root element) - see Schema Library. A declared location is also checked against your XML catalogs and library mappings before anything is downloaded, and the status bar indicator shows how the schema was found: "XSD: name" (declared), "(catalog)", "(library)" or "(manual)".
  4. Manual: Bind an XSD yourself - click the "No XSD" chip in the status bar (or click the toolbar's Schema button - Set XSD Schema…), pick a schema in the Validation panel's SOURCES section, or simply drop an .xsd file from your file manager onto the panel's XSD source row or onto the status bar's XSD indicator. The binding drives both validation and IntelliSense.

docs.title: Step 2: Validate
docs.text: Click the toolbar's Validate button or press F8 to start validation.

docs.title: Step 3: View Results
docs.text:
The panel's status line reports the outcome right away:

Status line Meaning Valid The document conforms to the bound XSD (and Schematron, if one is bound) Well-formed · no schema bound No schema is bound - only the well-formedness check ran and it passed (neutral, not green: bind an XSD in SOURCES to validate) 1 problem / N problems Problems were found; they are listed in the PROBLEMS panel below the editor

In Single file mode the side panel does not repeat the problem list: below the status line it shows a row such as "3 problems — show below the editor". Click it to expand and focus the PROBLEMS panel below the editor.

Each entry in the problem list reads [source] Ln N: message:

  • Source - XSD, Well-formed, or Schematron, so you can tell which check reported it
  • Line number - where the problem is
  • Severity icon - red ✕ for errors, orange ⚠ for warnings

Selecting a problem shows it in the current view (Text: its line; Tree and Graphic: its element). The same problems are mirrored in the PROBLEMS panel below the editor, whose header shows error and warning counters; see Jump to Validation Errors for navigation details.

Validate while typing (on by default, toggle in the panel header's ⋮ menu) re-runs validation shortly after every edit, tab switch, or schema change, so the list stays current without pressing F8.

docs.title: Batch Validation
docs.text:
Validate multiple XML files at once. Useful for testing entire folders of XML documents.

Batch validation with multiple files

docs.title: Which Schema Is Used
docs.text:
There is no per-run schema picker. A batch run validates every selected file against the XSD (and Schematron) currently bound to the active document - the ones shown in the Validation panel's SOURCES section and in the status bar's XSD indicator:

Bound in SOURCES What the batch run does XSD Every file is validated against that one schema Schematron Every file is additionally checked against that Schematron (nothing bound) Every file gets a well-formedness check only

The files' own xsi:schemaLocation references are not consulted during a batch run. To validate a folder against a particular schema, open any XML document, bind the XSD (Change in the SOURCES row, the ★ favorites menu, drag & drop, or the toolbar's Schema button), then start the batch.

docs.title: Running Batch Validation
docs.text:
In the Validation panel's Batch mode, Run Validation opens a small menu so you can pick files or a whole folder in one step.

  1. Open the Validation panel and switch the mode toggle to Batch.
  2. Click Run Validation and choose how to pick the files:
  3. Select XML files… - a file chooser where you select one or more XML files.
  4. Select folder… - a folder chooser; every *.xml file in the folder and all of its subfolders is validated.
  5. Watch progress while the files are validated.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The RESULTS list shows one row per file:

Indicator Description Status icon Red ✕ = errors, orange ⚠ = warnings only, green ✓ = valid File name Name of the XML file Badge Number of problems found in that file

The RESULTS list and the panel's PROBLEMS list are only shown in Batch mode (starting a batch run switches to it). Select a row to see that file's problems in the PROBLEMS section; double-click a row to open the file in the editor. A plain-text report of the run (schema names plus one line per file) opens as a document via Open Last Batch Report in the panel's REPORTS & CHECKS section. A running batch can be cancelled from the progress bar; the results collected so far are kept.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The RESULTS header shows a summary of the run, for example:

RESULTS · 2 OF 25 FAILED

and the panel's status line repeats it ("2 of 25 file(s) failed").

docs.title: Exporting Results
docs.text:
There is one export: the Export Problems to Excel row (Excel icon) in the panel's REPORTS & CHECKS section. It is enabled whenever the list contains problems and writes exactly the problems currently shown:

  • after a single-file run, the active document's problems;
  • after a batch run, the problems of the file selected in RESULTS - pick a row first, then export. There is no all-files export; use Open Last Batch Report for a per-file overview of the whole run.

The suggested file name is <document>-problems.xlsx. The workbook contains:

Sheet Content Summary Source file, export timestamp, application version, and counts (total, errors, warnings) Problems One row per problem: #, Source, Severity (errors in red, warnings in amber), Line, Message - with a frozen header row and an auto-filter

All Excel files FreeXmlToolkit writes share one look - the Data Dictionary, the Schema Analysis report, the XML → Excel conversion and this export: a dark header row, striped rows with a thin rule, no gridlines, coloured sheet tabs, and an info sheet with a title and sections. Every sheet prints one page wide.

docs.title: Favorites Integration
docs.text:
Save frequently used XML and XSD files to favorites for quick access:

  • Ctrl+D - add the active document to favorites
  • Ctrl+Shift+D - show the Favorites side panel (or collapse it when it is already shown)
  • The ★ menu on each SOURCES row lists your favorites of that type (XSD, Schematron, or JSON) - one click binds the schema without a file chooser.

docs.title: Validation panel
docs.text: Control Description REPORTS & CHECKS Section at the top of the panel: Validation Report (enabled after a run with a bound Schematron), Export Problems to Excel, Open Last Batch Report. (FundsXML validation lives in the FundsXML panel.) SCHEMATRON AUTHORING Section at the top of the panel: Rule Templates, Schematron Tester, Rule Builder, Check Rules, Schematron Documentation. SOURCES · XSD row Two lines: icon, caption XSD, ★ and Change on the first; the bound file's name on the second (shortened in the middle, full path as tooltip). While nothing is bound it reads "No XSD bound — choose or drop a file" and a click acts like Change. Click the name to open the schema in the editor, ★ to pick a favorite, Change to browse; drop an .xsd onto the row to bind it. SOURCES · Schematron row The bound Schematron (.sch), with the same layout and name / ★ / Change / drop behavior ("No Schematron — choose or drop a file" while empty). SOURCES · JSON Schema row Shown instead of the two rows above while a JSON document is active. Single file / Batch Segmented toggle that decides what Run Validation does. Run Validation Single file: validates the active document. Batch: opens the Select XML files… / Select folder… menu. Status line Valid, Well-formed · no schema bound, 1 problem / N problems, batch summaries, or a precondition hint (e.g. No document open). "N problems — show below the editor" (Single file mode.) Expands and focuses the PROBLEMS panel below the editor. RESULTS (Batch mode only.) Per-file rows of the last batch run (collapsible section). PROBLEMS (Batch mode only.) The problems of the file selected in RESULTS (collapsible). ⋮ menu Validate while typing.

docs.title: Editor toolbar and status bar
docs.text: Control Shortcut Description Validate F8 Validates the active document - well-formedness, or against the bound XSD / Schematron Schema (primary click) - Set XSD Schema… - bind an XSD (or a JSON Schema for JSON documents) to the active document Schema ▾ menu - Set XSD Schema…, Generate Documentation…, Type Editor…, Generate XSD from XML, Generate XSD from XML Files… XSD indicator (status bar) - Shows No XSD (a clickable chip), Detecting XSD…, XSD: name (with (catalog) / (library) / (manual)), or XSD error; click it to bind a schema, or drop an .xsd onto it. While an XSD schema itself is the active document it shows XSD 1.1 schema / XSD 1.0 schema instead (from vc:minVersion).

docs.title: Supported Standards
docs.text:
Standard Support XSD 1.0 Full support XSD 1.1 (with assertions) Full support

The validation engine uses Xerces 2.12.2 with full XSD 1.1 support.

A schema may start with a <!DOCTYPE …> naming a DTD, as the W3C's own schemas do (XMLSchema.dtd). The DTD plays no part in validation and is never loaded, neither from disk nor from the network, so a missing DTD file does no harm.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• If your XML already references its schema via xsi:schemaLocation, just open it - the schema is bound automatically and the status bar shows how it was found
  • Use Batch Validation for testing multiple files efficiently - remember that all files are checked against the XSD bound to the active document
  • Export to Excel when working with large documents or sharing results; the Problems sheet has an auto-filter, so you can narrow it by source or severity in Excel
  • There is no filter inside the panel: in a batch run, the red ✕ / orange ⚠ icons and the count badges in RESULTS show at a glance which files need attention, and the PROBLEMS panel below the editor counts errors and warnings separately in its header
  • Double-click a file in RESULTS to open it in the editor; select a problem to jump to its line

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action F8 Validate the active document Ctrl+O Open a file Ctrl+D Add the active document to favorites Ctrl+Shift+D Show the Favorites panel

docs.title: XsdDoc Tags
docs.text: JavaDoc-style annotations in xs:appinfo - how FreeXmlToolkit reads, renders and edits them, in the HTML documentation generator and in the XSD editor's Properties Inspector.

docs.title: Where the Metadata Lives
docs.text:
Everything structured hangs off xs:annotation with its two children:

  • xs:documentation - human-readable prose, multi-language via xml:lang.
  • xs:appinfo - machine-readable metadata. Its source attribute carries the JavaDoc-style tag, the element's text content its value: <xs:appinfo source="@since">4.0.0</xs:appinfo>.

Legacy encoding

Older schemas (FundsXML among them) packed tag and value into the attribute alone: <xs:appinfo source="@since 4.0.0"/>. That form is still read - as is the duplicated <xs:appinfo source="@since 4.0.0">@since 4.0.0</xs:appinfo> some older versions of the editor produced - and is rewritten into the canonical form the next time the schema is saved from the toolkit. The generated documentation is identical either way.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Prefix Namespace URI Used for fxt http://freexmltoolkit.org/xml-schema-extensions fxt:exampleValues - the toolkit's example values fxt http://freexmltoolkit.org/schema/flattening fxt:sourceFile - origin tracking when flattening (details) altova http://www.altova.com/xml-schema-extensions altova:exampleValues - read for compatibility, never written

Both extension blocks declare their prefix on the xs:appinfo child itself rather than on xs:schema, so a schema edited by the toolkit does not collect namespace declarations it does not otherwise need.

docs.title: The Supported Tags
docs.text:
Tag Meaning HTML documentation XSD editor (Inspector) @since Schema version that introduced the component "Since" field in the JavaDoc block Text field @since @see Cross reference; may occur several times "See Also" list, {@link} resolved to hyperlinks List with Add/Remove + {@link} autocomplete @deprecated Deprecation marker plus reason Red warning box at the top of the detail page "Deprecated" checkbox + note field @version Version detail of the component Only under "Additional Information" Text field @version @author Author Only under "Additional Information" No field - but preserved unchanged on edit {@link XPath\|Name} Inline link inside @see / @deprecated Link to the target's detail page Autocomplete popup over the schema's element paths @markdown true/false - whether this node's documentation is rendered as Markdown (details) Honored in every Markdown rendering mode except Off - a node can opt in or out whatever the mode says "Markdown" choice (Not set / Markdown / Plain text) fxt:exampleValuesaltova:exampleValues Example values. Written as fxt:; the Altova form (the FundsXML convention) is still read "Sample Data" on the detail page "Example values" list; also feeds sample-XML generation and IntelliSense fxt:sourceFile Records which included file a component came from when a multi-file schema is flattened (details) - Not shown; passed through untouched anything else Arbitrary source string or text content "Additional Information" section (HTML-escaped) Preserved untouched

On top of that, xs:documentation/@xml:lang gets special treatment: it drives the language switcher on the generated pages, the Scan languages filter of the documentation generator, and one row per language in the Inspector.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
<xs:element name="Transaction">
    <xs:annotation>
        <xs:documentation xml:lang="en">A single financial transaction.</xs:documentation>
        <xs:documentation xml:lang="de">Eine einzelne Transaktion.</xs:documentation>

        <xs:appinfo source="@since">4.0.0</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@version">1.2</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@see">{@link /FundsXML4/ControlData}</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@see">{@link TransactionType}</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@deprecated">Use {@link /FundsXML4/NewTransaction} instead.</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo source="@markdown">true</xs:appinfo>
        <xs:appinfo>
            <fxt:exampleValues xmlns:fxt="http://freexmltoolkit.org/xml-schema-extensions">
                <fxt:example value="TRX-0815"/>
                <fxt:example value="TRX-0816"/>
            </fxt:exampleValues>
        </xs:appinfo>
    </xs:annotation>
</xs:element>

{@link} resolution

The target may be an absolute XPath (/FundsXML4/ControlData - synthetic CHOICE_n / SEQUENCE_n path segments are stripped before matching) or a plain element name (first match wins). A target that cannot be resolved degrades to plain code text instead of failing the documentation run.

docs.title: @markdown - Per-Node Markdown Rendering
docs.text:
xs:documentation content can be rendered as Markdown. The documentation generator offers three choices under Markdown rendering:

Choice Effect All documentation (default) Every node's documentation goes through the Markdown renderer, unless that node itself says @markdown = false. Per node (@markdown) Only nodes whose annotation says @markdown = true are rendered; every other node - including nodes that say nothing - stays plain text. Off Nothing is rendered, whatever the nodes say. 
<xs:element name="Transaction">
    <xs:annotation>
        <xs:documentation>A **single** financial transaction.</xs:documentation>
        <xs:appinfo source="@markdown">true</xs:appinfo>
    </xs:annotation>
</xs:element>

A node's own @markdown always beats the chosen mode; only Off is absolute. The same rule applies to the documentation of named types, attributes and enumerations on the generated type pages, each of which decides from its own annotation.

In the Inspector the tag is a three-state Markdown choice: Not set (no tag is written), Markdown (true) and Plain text (false). Like the other tags it is read from the element's own annotation and from the annotation of its resolved type - a type-level @markdown therefore applies to every element using that type unless the element states its own.

  • Documentation that is not rendered as Markdown is emitted literally: **bold** stays visible as typed instead of being formatted. Write Markdown (or turn the node's Markdown on) if the text is meant to be formatted.
  • Unrendered text is HTML-escaped wherever it is written into the generated HTML, so markup written straight into xs:documentation shows as the tags themselves rather than being applied.
  • PDF, Word and the Excel data dictionary are plain-text formats: rendered documentation is flattened for them, with paragraphs, list items and headings kept on separate lines and HTML entities decoded. Only the HTML output shows the formatting itself.
  • @markdown is a rendering hint, not documentation: it never appears in the "Additional Information" section of a generated page.

docs.title: fxt:sourceFile - Origin Tracking When Flattening
docs.text:
This is the toolkit's own xs:appinfo extension, in the namespace http://freexmltoolkit.org/schema/flattening (prefix fxt). It answers a question that flattening otherwise destroys: which of the included files did this component come from?

<xs:complexType name="PersonType">
    <xs:annotation>
        <xs:appinfo>
            <fxt:sourceFile xmlns:fxt="http://freexmltoolkit.org/schema/flattening">types.xsd</fxt:sourceFile>
        </xs:appinfo>
    </xs:annotation>
    ...
</xs:complexType>
  • Written by Flatten Schema… (Schema activity → TOOLS) when Track source files (xs:appinfo) is ticked (off by default). Only global components get the marker - elements, complex and simple types, groups, attribute groups and attributes. The markers are added after the other reductions, so they survive Remove annotations, and a marker from an earlier flatten is replaced rather than duplicated. The schema must be saved: unsaved content resolves no includes and is therefore never marked.
  • Read and kept everywhere else: the appinfo statistics of the Schema Analysis count it as an @sourceFile tag, and the Inspector never shows it but carries it over untouched, so editing @since on a flattened component does not lose its origin marker. Saving writes it back as a clean fxt:sourceFile element.

Origin of nodes in an unflattened schema

The per-file node counts in the Schema Analysis statistics and the file column of its quality issues work on any multi-file schema, flattened or not - they do not need this marker. fxt:sourceFile is the form of origin information that survives writing a flattened schema to disk and opening it again.

docs.title: XSLT Developer
docs.text:
Note: The standalone XSLT Developer tab has been retired. Its capabilities now live in the Unified Shell's Transform panel (stylesheet, input, output method, parameters) together with the Debug button next to Run Transform (the interactive debugger with breakpoints, stepping, variables, call stack, watches and live messages in a dock below the editor; also Tools → Debug with XSLT… / Shift+F5), and the run options and advanced tools in the panel's OPTIONS & TOOLS section — Batch Transform…, Profile run, and Trace run. This page describes how to do XSLT and XQuery development in the shell, plus a collection of ready-to-use XSLT and XQuery patterns. XPath / XQuery queries against the open document run in the Query Console.

FreeXmlToolkit is a full-featured environment for creating and testing XSLT stylesheets and XQuery scripts. It includes live transformation, parameter support, batch processing, and debugging tools.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
